explanationHtml:
Radiation is the predominant mechanism of heat loss from the anode disc to the envelope in X-ray tubes.

Heat is produced in the X-ray tube when high-speed electrons from the cathode strike the anode target, since over 99% of this energy is converted to heat rather than X-rays.

This heat is released into the environment through the layers of the tube: anode → glass/ceramic envelope → surrounding oil bath → external housing → air. The mechanism at each step differs:

  • Anode to tube envelope: radiation (as infrared radiation)
  • Tube envelope to oil: convection
  • Oil to housing: conduction
  • Housing to air: convection

The anode and the rotor are connected by a thin molybdenum stem. Because this stem is narrow, only a small amount of heat is conducted through it, making radiation the dominant pathway for heat loss from the anode disc.

explanationHtml:
Silver bromide is the most commonly used optically sensitive component of an X-ray film.

X-ray films are coated with a photosensitive emulsion containing silver halide crystals. The emulsion mainly contains silver bromide (AgBr), which forms the majority (90–99%) of the halide crystals. The remaining 1–10% is silver iodide (AgI), and together they form silver iodo-bromide crystals.

The emulsion responds to X-rays and hence is the most important layer for image formation. Silver bromide has optimal photosensitivity to X-rays and visible light while being chemically stable enough for film processing.

Standard radiographic films have emulsion on both sides. In contrast, mammography films are single-emulsion films, with coating present on only one side.

Note: X-ray films are most sensitive to blue light and least sensitive to red light. Therefore, red safelights are used in the darkroom.

correctAnswer: B. When high-speed incident electrons decelerate near target nuclei
explanationHtml:
X-rays are produced when the electron beam decelerates close to the nucleus of the atom in the anode. This mechanism describes bremsstrahlung radiation, the commonest mechanism of X-ray production.

An X-ray tube consists of a cathode (heated tungsten filament) and an anode (tungsten target). When electricity heats the filament, electrons are emitted and accelerated across the tube by a high potential difference (kV), striking the anode with high kinetic energy.


Most interactions (99%) only produce heat. A small fraction produce diagnostic X-rays through two mechanisms.

  1. Bremsstrahlung radiation accounts for 80% of X-ray production. When electrons pass near a target nucleus, they decelerate and change direction, releasing kinetic energy as X-ray photons. This produces a continuous spectrum of X-ray energies.
  2. Characteristic radiation occurs when incoming electrons displace inner-shell (K-shell) electrons from target atoms, creating a vacancy. An outer-shell electron fills this vacancy and releases energy as a characteristic X-ray. This produces a discrete line spectrum with energies specific to the target material.

correctAnswer: D. An inner-shell electron with binding energy lower than the energy of the photon
explanationHtml:
The photoelectric effect occurs when an incident photon displaces an inner-shell electron with a binding energy lower than the energy of the photon.

The photoelectric effect is initiated when an incident photon interacts with an inner-shell electron and displaces it. For this interaction to take place, the binding energy of the inner shell electron should be lower than the energy of the incident photon. The inner shell electron completely absorbs the photon's energy and is ejected, and is then designated as a photoelectron.

Following photoelectric emission, the vacancy created in the inner shell is filled when an outer shell electron moves to the inner shell, releasing energy in the process. The energy can be transferred to a photon and released as a characteristic X-ray or to an electron, which is released as an Auger electron.


Photoelectric effect is the major interaction responsible for the absorption of the X-ray beam in the patient. Higher density tissues (e.g., bone) absorb more X-rays through photoelectric absorption, preventing them from reaching the receptor. These areas appear radiopaque (bright). X-rays pass more through lower-density tissues (e.g., lungs), which appear radiolucent (darker) on the image. This differential absorption is what creates image contrast and helps distinguish various tissue types in an X-ray image.

Compton effect, on the other hand, occurs when an incident photon interacts with a loosely bound outer shell electron, losing some of its energy and changing its direction. Compton effect produces scatter radiation, which degrades image contrast.

Spiral (helical) CT is based on slip ring technology.

Modern CT technology is built on two key advances: slip ring technology (enabling spiral/helical scanning) and multidetector arrays (enabling faster acquisition and larger coverage).

In older generation CT scanners, electric cables connected the rotating gantry to the power supply and computer system. This limited the gantry to stopping and unwinding between rotations.

The slip ring technology solved this. It consists of a metal ring on the outer gantry and a connector linking the detector arrays to this ring, enabling continuous gantry rotation while maintaining electrical contact. This was introduced in sixth-generation CT scanners, allowing three- and four-dimensional imaging in a single breath hold.

Seventh-generation CT scanners combine spiral CT with multiple rows of detectors, called multidetector CT (MDCT), using a cone beam. This allows larger z-axis coverage per rotation, faster scanning, and thinner slices for better resolution.

explanationHtml:
Hounsfield unit (HU) depends on the linear attenuation co-efficient.

The linear attenuation coefficient (μ) represents the proportion of X-ray beam energy absorbed or scattered by a material for each unit thickness through which the beam travels. It depends on three main factors: tissue density, atomic number and energy of the X-ray photons

HU quantifies the radiodensity of the tissue by measuring X-ray attenuation values in CT scanning.

HU is calculated using the formula:

HU = 1000 × (μ_tissue - μ_water) / μ_water

Where μ is the linear attenuation coefficient.
question: What does the Hounsfield unit depend on?

explanationHtml:
Hounsfield Unit (HU) is zero for water.

Hounsfield Unit (HU) is a standardised, dimensionless CT unit that quantifies the radiodensity of the tissue by measuring X-ray attenuation of a tissue relative to that of water at room temperature(μ_water).

During a CT scan, the scanner measures how much each small volume of tissue attenuates the X-ray beam, giving a linear attenuation coefficient (μ). Linear attenuation coefficient (μ) is the fraction of incident energy removed from an X-ray beam per unit thickness of the medium it passes through. It depends on three main factors: tissue density, atomic number and energy of the X-ray photons.

This value is then converted into HU using a formula that compares the material's μ to that of water (μwater).

HU= 1000 x (μ_material – μ_water) / μ_water

According to this scale, water is defined as 0 HU, air is around –1000 HU, compact bone roughly +1000 HU, and most soft tissues lie between these two extremes.

explanationHtml:
Ultrasonography (USG) works based on the principle of the piezoelectric effect.

The tip of ultrasound transducer is made up of piezoelectric crystals like lead (Pb) zirconate titanate (PZT). When electric current passes through the transducer, these crystals starts to vibrate and produce ultrasound waves. This is called reverse piezoelectric effect.

The sound waves propagate through different tissues and are reflected back to the transducer. These waves are then converted back into electrical impulses by the transducer crystals. This is called piezoelectric effect. These impulses are further processed to form an ultrasound image on the screen by pulse-echo principle. Both reverse piezoelectric effect and piezoelectric effect are used in diagnostic ultrasound.

explanationHtml:
Lead (Pb) zirconate titanate (PZT) is the most widely used piezoelectric material in the ultrasound transducers/probes. It has replaced the previously used barium titanate.

Ultrasound technology is based on the pulse-echo principle, which is enabled by the piezoelectric material located at the tip of the ultrasound probe.


When a piezoelectric crystal is electrically pulsed, it changes shape and vibrates, producing a sound beam thus converting electric voltage to ultrasound pulse. This is called reverse piezoelectric effect.

The reflected echoes reach the crystal which causes it to vibrate and produce electrical voltage, thus converting into electrical impulses. This is called piezoelectric effect.

These impulses are further processed to form an ultrasound image on the screen by pulse-echo principle.

Harmonic imaging is a technique used in sonography (ultrasonography).

Harmonic imaging is an ultrasound technique that involves tuning the receiver to detect harmonic (high) frequencies. When sound passes through tissue, nonlinear propagation generates harmonic frequencies at deeper levels. Harmonic imaging captures these frequencies instead of the fundamental frequency, improving image quality.

Harmonic imaging provides better image quality by eliminating artifacts from superficial tissues (such as reverberation and noise), improving the ability to distinguish adjacent structures (better lateral resolution), and producing clearer images with less background interference. It is particularly useful in obese patients.

Clinical imaging scanners have magnets with field strengths ranging from 0.2 to 3 Tesla (and more recently 7 Tesla). Routinely used MRI has a field strength of 1.5 Tesla, which is created by superconductors.

Doppler effect is seen due to the relative change in frequency of sound waves.

Doppler ultrasound works by detecting the Doppler effect, in which sound waves reflected from a moving structure undergo a change in frequency. Comparing the difference between the incident and returning frequencies (Doppler shift frequency) of blood cells gives the blood velocity.

In colour Doppler, the frequency shifts are encoded as colours displayed on top of B-mode ultrasound. Most commonly, red denotes motion toward the transducer, whereas blue denotes motion away from the transducer.

Spectral Doppler shows the range of Doppler frequencies or velocities as a spectrum over time. It can show values such as peak systolic velocity and end-diastolic velocity. The image given below shows a spectral Doppler of the carotid artery.

The correctly arranged sequence among the given options is Radio waves, Infrared, X-rays, Gamma rays.

The electromagnetic spectrum, arranged by increasing frequency and energy: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

Electromagnetic waves consist of perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields. Functional MRI (fMRI) uses the BOLD (blood oxygen level-dependent) technique. During activity, the corresponding brain area has increased oxygen consumption, producing signal changes that help detect functions of different brain parts.


MR angiography uses the time of flight (TOF) principle to visualize blood flow in vessels without contrast agents, by exploiting flow-related enhancement of blood protons entering the imaging field.

explanationHtml:
Compton effect occurs when an incident X-ray photon interacts with a loosely bound outer-shell electron. The photon transfers part of its energy to the electron, gets deflected from its original path, and produces scattered radiation.

Interactions of X-rays with matter:

  • Photoelectric effect: The incident photon is completely absorbed by an inner-shell electron, leading to ejection of the electron. This improves image contrast.
  • Compton scattering: The incident photon interacts with a loosely bound outer-shell electron, loses energy, and changes direction. This produces scatter radiation and reduces image quality.


Production of X-rays:

  • Bremsstrahlung radiation: It is produced when high-speed electrons slow down after passing near the target nucleus. The sudden loss of kinetic energy is converted into X-rays. It forms most of the X-ray beam and produces a continuous spectrum.
  • Characteristic radiation: It is produced when an incident electron ejects an inner-shell electron from the target atom. An outer-shell electron then fills the vacancy and releases X-rays with energy specific to the target material. It produces a discrete spectrum.

explanationHtml:
The probe shown is a linear array transducer, typically used for vascular and other superficial high-resolution imaging.

Ultrasound transducers contain multiple piezoelectric elements arranged in an array. A single slab of PZT is cut into small subelements, each with its own connection, allowing different groups to be activated to shape and steer the beam.

1. Linear array transducers: have elements arranged in a straight line, activated sequentially in small groups (beam stepping). They produce a rectangular image and are used for vascular and high-resolution imaging.

2. Curvilinear (convex) array transducers: have elements along a curved surface, also activated by beam stepping. They produce a sector image with a curved top, useful for abdominal, obstetric and gynaecological imaging.

3. Phased array transducers: have a small footprint and use beam steering, i.e., all elements work together with small time delays to steer and focus the beam. They produce a sector image with a pointed top and are used for cardiac imaging, neonatal brain imaging, and endocavitary applications (e.g., endovaginal probes).

4. Vector (trapezoidal) transducers: combine beam stepping and beam steering, producing a trapezoidal image with a flat top. They are useful for abdominal, cardiac, and Doppler studies.

The correctly matched parameters and SI units are as follows:

Parameter SI unit
1. Absorbed Radiation d. Gray
2. Total Radiation Exposure c. Coulomb/kg
3. Radioactivity a. Becquerel
4. Dose equivalent b. Sievert

Radioactivity: Becquerel measures radioactivity by measuring disintegration per second. It describes how active a radioactive material is, regardless of whether that radiation reaches a person.

Radiation Exposure: Exposure measures the number of ionizations, calculated by measuring the difference of charge in an ion pair and dividing it by mass of air. It is depicted by the SI unit Coulomb per kilogram.

Absorbed Dose: Gray (Gy) is the SI-derived unit of absorbed dose in Joules per kilogram. It measures the physical energy deposited in a material or tissue, hence describing how much radiation energy was actually absorbed by the body.

Dose Equivalent: Equivalent dose is used in radiation safety purposes and is measured in Sieverts (Sv). It is obtained by multiplying dose by a weighting factor (WF) that corrects for the type of radiation.

The harmful effects of radiation may be classified into two general categories: deterministic and stochastic effects.

Deterministic effects are predictable tissue reactions that occur when radiation dose exceeds a threshold level. Severity increases with increasing dose. E.g., skin erythema occurs after a threshold dose of 2 Gy is crossed.

Stochastic effects are random, chance-based effects where severity does not depend on dose but the probability of occurrence increases with increasing dose.

Acute radiation syndrome is characterized by three main presentations:

Lymphocytopenia, granulocytopenia, followed by thrombocytopenia, is the correct chronological order for radiation effects on peripheral blood components.

Radiation mainly affects hematopoietic stem cells. While most mature blood cells are relatively resistant, mature lymphocytes are radiosensitive and undergo apoptosis.

Cytopenias occur as the naturally dying mature blood cells are not being replaced by the damaged stem cells. Therefore, the chronology of cytopenias of various blood cells depends on their lifespan.

  • Lymphocytes: Most radiosensitive; levels fall earliest, within hours.
  • Granulocytes: Fall later because mature cells survive initially; lowest levels are reached by about 2–4 weeks.
  • Platelets: Usually reach their lowest level by about 2–4 weeks.
  • Erythrocytes: Relatively radioresistant; anemia after radiation is usually due to bleeding rather than direct RBC destruction.

A radiation of 3–4 Gy in a single exposure, in the absence of medical management, is considered the Mean Lethal Dose (LD50) for humans. This threshold is increased to 8 Gy with medical management.

All the given options are principles of radiation protection, except shielding.

The ICRP (International Commission on Radiological Protection) has proposed three key principles of radiation protection:

1. Justification: Any imaging procedure involving ionizing radiation should be used only if its benefits outweigh the potential risks.

2. Optimization: During imaging, radiation exposure should be kept as low as reasonably achievable. This includes reducing both the dose delivered and the number of people exposed, such as by using low-dose CT protocols when appropriate.

3. Dose limitation: The radiation dose received by a person should remain within the recommended national limits. These limits define the maximum allowed dose for different population groups.

explanationHtml:
The ALARA principle aims to achieve minimal radiation dose to patients while still maintaining adequate diagnostic image quality.

ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) principle of radiation safety is used for dose optimization. It is applied to both patients and personnel during the imaging procedure. It is based on three key measures:

  1. Time: less time near the source leads to less dose exposure
  2. Distance: more distance equals less dose (inverse square law)
  3. Shielding: use of barriers (lead apron, gonadal shields, lead glass, walls)


ALARA does not aim for the absolute minimum dose possible, nor does it compromise image quality, and it does not directly deal with legal radiation limits.

Clinical benefit outweighing the radiation risk is assessed before the procedure as a part of the justification principle, whereas ALARA is applied while conducting the procedure as a part of the optimization principle.

explanationHtml:
The correct statement out of the given options is: Gadobenate has the lowest risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis as it is hepatocyte specific and excreted by the liver.

Gadolinium is the most commonly used MRI contrast agent, chelated as Gd-DTPA to reduce toxicity. GBCAs reduce both T1 and T2 relaxation times, but the predominant effect is on T1, making post-contrast images T1-weighted.

The most common adverse effects are mild reactions like nausea and headache. NSF is the most concerning adverse effect, seen in renal failure patients (GFR under 30 ml/min), but not the most common.

Macrocyclic Gadolinium based contrast agents (GBCAs), e.g., Gadobutrol, Gadoteric acid, Gadoteridol, are preferred over linear GBCAs due to their stability and lesser side effects. Gadopiclenol (Elucirem/Vueway) is a newer macrocyclic GBCA with higher relaxivity, allowing use at a much lower dose.

GBCAs are category C in pregnancy and should only be used when the benefits outweigh the risk, the information cannot be obtained otherwise, and waiting until after delivery is not safe.

From the given list, intraocular foreign bodies, insulin pumps, and certain intra-aortic balloon pumps are generally considered MR-unsafe.

MR-Unsafe Devices and Conditions:

  • Insulin pumps - contain ferromagnetic components and sensitive electronic circuits that can be damaged by MRI, causing dangerous insulin delivery and life-threatening blood sugar changes. External pumps must be removed before the scan. Implantable pumps are contra-indications.
  • External fixator orthopaedic devices
  • Hemodynamic monitoring devices, ventricular assist devices, temporary pacing devices, and intra-aortic balloon pumps

Other MR Conditional or Special Situations

  • Cardiac pacemakers (older models) - newer MRI-conditional pacemakers are safe under supervision
  • Cochlear implants (older models) - newer MRI-conditional models are safe.
  • Older vascular clips, usually made of ferromagnetic materials (newer clips since the 1990s are MRI safe)
  • Claustrophobia (can be managed with sedation or general anaesthesia)
  • Gadolinium-based contrast agents should be avoided in pregnancy as they are category C drugs. It should only be used when the benefits outweigh the risk, the information cannot be obtained otherwise, and waiting until after delivery is not safe.
  • Contrast MRI is contraindicated in severe renal failure due to the risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF).

MR-Safe devices: Certain devices are MRI safe because they are made of non-ferromagnetic materials like titanium. They are also usually fixed within the body. Examples include surgical sutures, orthopaedic implants, dental implants, vena cava filters, embolisation coils, coronary and peripheral arterial stents, cardiac occluder devices, prosthetic cardiac valves, and most vascular clips (especially those manufactured after the 1990s).

The microbubbles used as ultrasound contrast agents are excreted via the lungs.

Ultrasound contrast media are microbubbles of inert gas compounds like perfluorocarbons and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) that are encapsulated by a phospholipid or polymer layer to increase stability. These inert gas compounds are excreted through the lungs, hence are not toxic to kidneys, making them ideal in patients with renal impairment who cannot undergo contrast-enhanced CT or MRI.

explanationHtml:
Diabetic patients undergoing FDG PET imaging need optimisation of blood glucose levels before the procedure.

Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is a glucose analogue, and its uptake is directly influenced by blood glucose and insulin levels.

High glucose concentration results in glucose competing with FDG for cellular uptake, leading to reduced tracer accumulation in target tissues and lesions, thereby decreasing image sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy.

In addition, exogenous insulin promotes increased FDG uptake by skeletal muscles and adipose tissue, causing non-specific background activity and potentially obscuring pathological foci.

Proper preparation, including fasting, optimisation of blood glucose levels, and appropriate timing of insulin or oral hypoglycaemic agents, ensures optimal tracer biodistribution, improves contrast, and allows reliable interpretation of PET images.

explanationHtml:
A transabdominal USG for pelvic pain requires a full urinary bladder. A full bladder acts as an acoustic window, displaces bowel loops, and improves pelvic organ visualisation in transabdominal ultrasound.

Preparation before ultrasound:

Pelvic / Renal / lower abdomen / obstetric ultrasound – Requires a full urinary bladder. Patients should be advised to drink 3–4 glasses (600–800 mL) of water and finish drinking about 1 hour before the appointment. Patients should be advised not to void urine until after the scan.

Transvaginal sonography is performed with an empty urinary bladder.

Upper abdominal ultrasound (liver, gallbladder, pancreas, aorta, spleen, etc.) – Requires fasting to reduce bowel gas and gallbladder contraction. Patients should be advised to eat or drink nothing after midnight or fast for at least 6 hours.

Routine radiographic studies like X-ray KUB or X-ray abdomen do not need bladder preparation.

Intravenous urography (IVU) does not require a full urinary bladder as patient preparation. IVU uses IV iodinated contrast that is renally excreted to opacify the pelvicalyceal systems, ureters, and bladder sequentially. A postvoid scout film is taken at the start, and the patient is asked to void again at the end to assess drainage and residual bladder volume. Bladder filling occurs naturally during the procedure.

Diatrizoate is contraindicated for angiography as it is ionic and high-osmolar.

Contrasts with high osmolarity and ionicity cause higher adverse effects, such as reactions and nephropathy, and therefore are contraindicated for vascular and intrathecal use. Non-ionic and low-osmolar contrasts such as iohexol are preferred for these procedures.

Water-soluble: Used for CT enhancement, angiography, and luminal studies. Can be ionic or non-ionic.

  • Ionic contrast: Dissociate into ions in solution and have higher adverse reaction rates. Most are high osmolar, with a few exceptions.
    • High osmolar (HOCM): Ionic monomers (e.g., diatrizoate, iothalamate). Not used for intravascular studies due to high risk. Used for luminal GI and GU studies due to lower cost.
    • Low osmolar: Ioxaglic acid, iocarmic acid.
  • Non-ionic contrast: They do not dissociate into ions, thus resulting in much lower adverse reaction rates. Modern standard for most procedures
    • Low osmolar (LOCM): Non-ionic monomers (e.g., iohexol, iopamidol). Most commonly used for IV, intra-arterial, routine CT studies, and intrathecal use (CT cisternography and myelography).
    • Iso-osmolar (IOCM): Non-ionic dimers (e.g., iodixanol). Osmolality similar to plasma but higher viscosity. Least nephrotoxic. Contraindicated for intrathecal use.

Water-insoluble: Example: lipiodol (ethiodized poppy seed oil). It is used for lymphangiography and transarterial chemoembolization (TACE)

explanationHtml:
Bile is anechoic on ultrasound.

Echogenicity refers to how bright or dark a tissue appears on ultrasound. It depends on how much of the ultrasound beam passes through the tissue and how much is reflected back. Reflection is influenced by the tissue’s acoustic impedance, which depends on its density and the speed of sound through it.

Homogeneous fluids like bile have uniform density with no internal interfaces, so sound waves pass through without producing echoes, resulting in an anechoic (black) appearance.

M-mode is a one-dimensional ultrasound technique that tracks motion along a single beam over time. It has low spatial but high temporal resolution, making it ideal for assessing rapidly moving structures in echocardiography and lung ultrasound-driven approaches such as evaluation for pneumothorax, left ventricular systolic function, cardiac tamponade, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.


Other USG modes:

  • A-mode (Amplitude) - 1 dimensional (1D) representation: Signal amplitude at a certain depth represented by a graph with spikes along a line, instead of an image. Used mainly in ophthalmology.

  • B-mode (Brightness) - 2D: echo amplitude is depicted as dots of different brightness which are compiled to form grayscale images. Most common mode for routine diagnostic imaging (abdomen, obstetrics, soft tissue).

  • Doppler - 2D + flow: Measures blood flow velocity and direction. Used in vascular studies to detect arterial/venous flow patterns (e.g., triphasic waveform in normal arteries).

Many pulse sequence techniques are used in MRI, and the most classic are T1 and T2 weighted images.

  • T1-weighted images: White matter is brighter than grey matter. CSF is dark (hypointense). Used for anatomical detail and post-contrast imaging.
  • T2-weighted images: Grey matter is brighter than white matter. CSF is bright (hyperintense). Used for detecting pathology such as edema, inflammation, and lesions.
  • FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery): An inversion recovery sequence that nulls CSF signal. Grey matter is brighter than white matter (similar to T2), but CSF appears dark. Used for detecting periventricular lesions and MS plaques.


STIR (Short Tau Inversion Recovery): An inversion recovery sequence with TI chosen to null fat signal. Fat appears dark. Used for detecting bone marrow edema in musculoskeletal imaging.

MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) is a non-invasive MRI-based technique that produces high-contrast images of the biliary and pancreatic ducts without contrast injection. It depicts the ducts as hyperintense (bright) structures against the hypointense (dark) background liver, making it excellent for detecting luminal pathology and ductal anatomy.


HIDA scan (Cholescintigraphy) involves intravenous injection of Tc-99m labeled iminodiacetic acid. The tracer is taken up by hepatocytes and excreted by the biliary system, allowing both anatomical and functional assessment of the biliary tree and liver.


PTC is performed under fluoroscopic guidance after gaining access into the biliary tree through a cutaneous puncture needle. Iodinated contrast is injected and ducts are identified. It is often the first step for percutaneous biliary intervention.


During ERCP, an endoscope is introduced vvia the esophagus to reach the duodenal papilla and contrast is injected into the biliary tract. ERCP has the advantage of good spatial resolution and also allows tissue sampling and therapeutic procedures to be conducted in the same sitting.

explanationHtml:
All of the above are applications of DWI except white matter fibre tracking for pre-operative planning, which is a function of diffusion tensor imaging (DTI).

DWI detects restricted diffusion in areas where water molecule movement is limited.

  • Acute infarct can be detected within minutes to early hours, when CT and routine MRI have low sensitivity.
  • Epidermoid cysts appear bright on DWI, differentiating them from arachnoid cysts which do not restrict.
  • Brain abscess shows restricted diffusion, differentiating it from necrotic tumours.
  • Herpes encephalitis can be detected earlier on DWI than CT due to early high signal intensity.

Image below shows MRI brain in acute infarct. DWI (right) shows hyperintense signal; ADC map (left) shows corresponding hypointensity, confirming true restricted diffusion.


Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is used for white-matter fibre tracking. It measures directional diffusion of water molecules along white matter tracts and is used for tractography and pre-operative planning, which is not possible with DWI alone.

The gallstone in the image appears brighter than the surrounding tissue; hence, it is hyperechoic.

Echogenicity refers to how bright or dark a tissue appears on ultrasound. When sound waves hit a boundary between two tissues, some waves are reflected back to the probe. The amount reflected is determined by the difference in acoustic impedance between the two tissues. A large difference causes more reflection, making the tissue appear brighter (hyperechoic). A small difference causes less reflection, making it appear darker (hypoechoic).

Structures that contain fluid, like simple cysts, have no internal boundaries to reflect sound. These appear completely black (anechoic) because there are no internal echoes.

explanationHtml:
Cortical bone appears hyperdense (bright) on CT due to high X-ray attenuating properties.

CT terminology uses "density" because it measures X-ray attenuation of tissues, which depends on electron density. Materials with high X-ray attenuating properties like calcium appear hyperdense (bright), while tissues with lower X-ray attenuation appear hypodense (dark).

MRI uses "intensity" because it measures the intensity of radiofrequency signal, which depends on proton behavior (T1 and T2 relaxation times). On T1-weighted images, tissues with short T1 values (rapid recovery) appear hyperintense (bright), such as fat. On T2-weighted images, tissues with long T2 values (slow decay) appear hyperintense (bright), such as water.

The most likely explanation for the abnormal curvature of spine in this radiograph is motion artifact, where the straight radio-opaque marker (arrow) also appears bent at the height of the upper thoracic spine.

A radio-opaque reference marker is a straight metal strip placed on or near the patient during radiography to serve as a reference for alignment. In this image, the straight marker also appears bent at the upper thoracic level, confirming that the apparent spinal curvature is due to patient movement and not a true anatomical abnormality.

Artifacts are undesirable opacities or blemishes on a radiograph that do not correspond to actual anatomic structures and may cause incorrect interpretation. They are classified into two types:

  1. Exposure-related artifacts:
  • Patient movement can produce blurring or apparent displacement of structures on the image.
  • Improper screen-film contact or matching can reduce image clarity and obscure radiographic details.
  • Reusing cassettes may result in double exposure.
  1. Processing and handling artifacts:
  • Defective processor rollers cause fogging or "pi lines."
  • Excessive chemical usage results in dichroic stain.
  • Inadequate chemical usage results in the curtain effect.
  • Improper temperature or humidity leads to incorrect exposure.

During cardiac CT procedure, the images are acquired during mid-diastole using synchronous ECG gating.

The mid-diastole phase is the cardiac rest phase with least motion, minimizing motion artifacts. It occurs at around 75% of the R-R cycle (1 full cardiac cycle).

question: Which of the following is correctly matched regarding the labeled structures on the left cardiac border in this PA chest X-ray?

explanationHtml:
Out of the given options, miliary tuberculosis, disseminated histoplasmosis and hematogenous metastases show miliary shadows.

The miliary pattern consists of randomly distributed micronodules, occurring when organisms or cells enter the bloodstream and lodge in pulmonary capillaries.

Conditions producing miliary shadows:

  • Miliary tuberculosis: May occur in primary or post-primary TB; miliary nodules usually indicate active disease.
  • Fungal infections: Examples include histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, and coccidioidomycosis.
  • Hematogenous metastases: Often show lower-zone predominance; thyroid carcinoma is one example.
  • Septic emboli: Usually peripheral and lower-zone predominant; lesions may cavitate.
  • Adenocarcinoma of lung: Can rarely appear as multiple randomly scattered nodules.

Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis produces a "crazy-paving" pattern (ground-glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening), while idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis shows subpleural bibasal honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis. Neither produces a miliary pattern.
question:
The chest X-ray below shows miliary shadows. Which of the following conditions can present with this finding?

  1. Miliary tuberculosis
  2. Disseminated histoplasmosis
  3. Hematogenous metastases
  4. Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
  5. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

explanationHtml:
Eggshell calcification of lymph nodes is not a feature of bronchogenic carcinoma.

Eggshell calcification refers to fine calcification seen at the periphery of a lymph node. It may be seen in primary calcifying malignancies such as osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, colorectal, and ovarian tumours.
question: In which of the following conditions will you not see eggshell calcification of lymph nodes?

explanationHtml:
A history of fever, cough, and chest X-ray showing opacities in the right middle lobe suggest consolidation, describing a case of community-acquired pneumonia.

Community-acquired pneumonia presents with acute onset fever and cough, with or without sputum production, and shortness of breath. Pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxemia, or increased work of breathing may also be present.

Chest X-ray findings of CAP include lobar consolidation with air bronchograms, interstitial infiltrates, and/or cavitations. CT chest is used for better resolution or if chest X-ray is non-diagnostic.

Other options:

Lung abscess: Chest X-ray shows a thick-walled, irregular cavity containing an air-fluid level with surrounding pulmonary infiltrates.


Pleural effusion: shows blunting of costo-phrenic angle with a meniscus sign on chest X-ray.


Hydropneumothorax: Shows both a horizontal air-fluid level and hyperlucency on chest X-ray, with absence of lung markings above the fluid level. The fluid appears as a horizontal line (unlike the meniscus of pleural effusion) due to the presence of air above it.
question: An 35-year-old man presents with a history of fever and cough for 1 week. Chest X-ray is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Volume increase of the infected lobe displacing adjacent fissures
explanationHtml:
Bulging fissure sign occurs due to volume increase of the infected lobe, displacing adjacent fissures.

It is most characteristically seen in Klebsiella pneumonia, which causes dense lobar consolidation and early abscess formation, increasing the volume of the affected lobe. Typically involves the upper lobe, more commonly on the right, and usually occurs in elderly debilitated men.

On imaging, Klebsiella pneumonia shows lobar consolidation with air bronchograms, ground glass opacities, intralobular reticular opacity, and sharp margins of the advancing border. Complications include cavitation, lung abscess, pleural effusion, and empyema. Healing with fibrosis can mimic chronic fibrocavitary TB.

Other causes of the bulging fissure sign include Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia and pulmonary gangrene a rare complication of severe bacterial pneumonia, where necrosis within a lobar consolidation causes expansion and outward fissure displacement.

options.text: Volume increase of the infected lobe displacing adjacent fissures
Accumulation of fluid in the interlobar fissure
Fibrosis and retraction of the affected lobe
Compensatory hyperinflation of the adjacent lobe pushing the fissure outward

question: A chest X-ray of an elderly man with fever and productive cough is shown below. What is the mechanism behind the indicated finding?

explanationHtml:
The chest X-ray depicts a pneumatocele adjacent to the left heart border (black arrow in the image below). The most common cause of pneumatocele formation is Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia.

Pneumatocele is a thin-walled, air-filled cavity in the lung tissue, usually occurring as a complication of lung infection. Drainage of necrotic lung parenchyma forms a check-valve obstruction of the airway, resulting in trapping of air within the cavity.

It is classically associated with Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia in the pediatric age group. It may also occur with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, especially in patients with AIDS.

Note: Gallium lung scintigraphy is highly sensitive for pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia.

Conditions with similar appearance:

  • Lung abscesses: have thick, irregular walls with an air-fluid level, typically located in the posterior segments of the upper lobes and superior segments of the lower lobes.

  • Bulla: a sharply demarcated emphysematous space, ≥1cm in diameter with hairline-thin walls (<1mm), usually peripheral and associated with emphysema (not commonly associated with infections).
question: In patients with pneumonia, what is the most common causative organism that can lead to this condition?

explanationHtml:
The CT shows an air-fluid level with floating membranes (marked using yellow arrows in the image below) characteristic of a hydatid cyst. It is called a water lily or camalote sign. The most common location of hydatid cysts is the liver, followed by the lung.

When the inner membranes rupture, the cyst may become a cavitary lesion. On imaging, this can show characteristic features.

  • Air-fluid level
  • Water lily sign/ camalote sign - air-fluid level with a floating membrane
  • Double wall
  • Rising sun sign/ serpent sign - a double-wall, dry cyst with crumpled membranes lying at its bottom
  • Empty cyst sign - when all the contents are removed

Hydatid cysts result from infection by the Echinococcus species and can result in cyst formation anywhere in the body. Echinococcus granulosus species is the most common.
question: CT scan of a patient is being reviewed. Identify the given pathology.

explanationHtml:
The HRCT image shows the classical tree-in-bud sign, making endobronchial tuberculosis the most likely diagnosis among the given options.

Tree-in-bud sign describes small centrilobular nodules with branching linear opacities, giving a V- or Y-shaped appearance on CT. It is usually caused by dilated centrilobular bronchioles filled with mucus, pus, or fluid.

It is most commonly seen in infectious causes such as infectious bronchiolitis, bronchopneumonia, endobronchial TB, atypical mycobacterial infection and aspiration. It is also seen in cystic fibrosis and Kartagener syndrome.

The chest X-ray may be normal. HRCT is more sensitive. Patients may present with or without sputum.
question: A 56-year-old man presents with a one-month history of fever, fatigue, and non-productive cough. His chest X-ray is unremarkable, but HRCT is done and provided below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The X-ray shows Golden’s S-sign, representing right upper lobe collapse.

Golden’s S-sign/ reverse S-sign of Golden is named so as it resembles a reverse S shape seen as a central focal convexity and peripheral concavity. It can be seen on PA chest radiographs and on CT scans in right upper lobe collapse. This sign is most commonly due to bronchogenic carcinoma.

Image below shows the Golden's S-sign (bilateral breast implants incidentally noted):
question: The following x-ray was done on a patient with pulmonary tuberculosis. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Galaxy sign is a radiologic feature observed on HRCT in sarcoidosis (shown below), not on chest X-ray. It represents a coalescing granuloma with numerous smaller granulomas.

Depending on the stage of sarcoidosis, radiological features can range from a normal chest radiograph to pulmonary fibrosis. Pulmonary sarcoidosis can be classified on a chest radiograph into 5 stages. A normal chest radiograph indicates stage 0.

Other stages are -

options.text: Hilar lymphadenopathy with parenchymal lung changes

question: All of the following chest X-ray features can be seen in patients with sarcoidosis except:

explanationHtml:
The given scan shows the classic panda sign seen in sarcoidosis. This occurs because of the symmetrical uptake of Gallium-67 in the nasopharynx, lacrimal glands, and parotid glands, reflecting the bilateral involvement of the glands in sarcoidosis.

Other signs seen in sarcoidosis are:

  • The lambda sign refers to bilateral hilar and right paratracheal lymphadenopathy (seen on FDG PET Scan/ Ga scintigraphy).
  • Garland triad or 1-2-3 sign or Pawnbroker's sign is a lymph node enlargement pattern that is seen in sarcoidosis (seen on chest X-ray as shown below).

  • Galaxy sign (sarcoid galaxy) represents a coalescent granuloma seen in a minority of patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis, seen on HRCT as shown below


Wilson disease: classically shows “face of the panda” on T2W MRI of the brain, not Ga-67 scintigraphy.

Lymphoma and oromaxillary carcinoma: can show focal uptake in tumor and lymph nodes, not the symmetric lacrimal, parotid “panda” pattern of sarcoidosis.
question: A gallium-67 scan was performed on a patient and showed the following. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is aspergilloma. The CT images show the Monod sign, which refers to gas surrounding an intracavitary fungal ball, with the ball changing position between supine and decubitus views, confirming mobility.

Aspergilloma is a fungus ball of Aspergillus fumigatus forming in pre-existing cavities in lungs, most commonly post-tuberculous cavities. The air crescent sign (a crescent of air surrounding the fungus ball within the cavity ) is the classic CT finding. The ball is mobile and shifts on decubitus positioning (Monod sign).

The image below shows the fungal-ball at the posterior position when the patient is supine, and at the anterior portion of the cavity when the patient is prone, showing it shifting with gravity.


Other pulmonary manifestations of Aspergillus:

  • Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity reaction in asthmatics, showing finger-in-glove sign (mucoid impaction in dilated bronchi) and central bronchiectasis.

  • Angioinvasive aspergillosis occurs in immunocompromised patients. HRCT shows the halo sign: ground-glass opacity surrounding a nodule, representing hemorrhage. The air crescent sign in angioinvasive aspergillosis is a late finding, usually seen around 2 weeks after onset as the white blood cell count recovers. Since it can look like an intracavitary fungal ball, it may resemble an aspergilloma on imaging without showing the positional mobility.
question: A patient with a past history of pulmonary tuberculosis undergoes a CT scan, and the image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Popcorn calcification is seen in pulmonary hamartoma.

Popcorn calcification is defined as a pattern of calcification in rings and arcs that resemble popped corn kernels. The presence of fat in a well-circumscribed solitary pulmonary nodule on CT confirms the diagnosis of a pulmonary hamartoma.

Chest x-ray showing pulmonary hamartoma:


Patterns of calcification:

Pulmonary nodules:

  • Popcorn: rings and arcs within the nodule, seen in pulmonary hamartoma and chondrosarcoma
  • Lamellated/Central: calcification within the nodule, seen in granulomatous infections (TB, histoplasmosis)
  • Diffuse/Homogeneous: calcification throughout the nodule, associated with granulomatous infections
  • Eccentric or stippled: suggestive of malignancy. Eccentric calcifications are off-centre calcification within nodule, (carcinoma engulfing a granuloma).

Diffuse, laminated, central, and popcorn patterns are benign. Eccentric and stippled calcification suggests malignancy.

Within lymph nodes:

  • Eggshell: peripheral rim calcification, seen in silicosis (most characteristic), sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, post-radiation lymphoma
  • Icing sugar: light homogeneous calcification throughout the node; sarcoidosis
  • Complete/dense: entire node calcified; granulomatous infections (TB, histoplasmosis)
question: Which pattern of calcification is typically seen in pulmonary hamartoma?

explanationHtml:
The chest x-ray shown demonstrates the Luftsichel sign, making the most likely diagnosis left upper lobe (LUL) collapse.

Luftsichel (german for air-crescent) sign occurs when the superior segment of the left lower lobe undergoes compensatory hyperinflation to occupy the space between the aortic arch and the collapsed left upper lobe, creating a crescent of air between the two borders.

LUL collapse can produce a ‘veil sign’: The collapsed lobe falls flat over the anterior aspect, resembling a veil or sheet. This makes the left hemithorax appear brighter than the right on X-rays.

The CT below shows the collapse of the left upper lobe.
question: A 60-year-old male complains of recurrent cough and difficulty in breathing for 2 months. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the finding  in the chest X-ray provided below?

explanationHtml:
Plain CT is the investigation of choice for evaluating an incidentally detected solitary pulmonary nodule.

Solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN) is defined as a relatively well-defined, round or oval, pulmonary parenchymal lesion that is equal to or smaller than 3 cm in diameter. It is surrounded by pulmonary parenchyma and/or visceral pleura and is not associated with lymphadenopathy, atelectasis, or pneumonia.

According to ACR Appropriateness Criteria, CT chest without IV contrast is the usually appropriate next imaging study for adults ≥35 years with an incidentally detected indeterminate pulmonary nodule on chest radiograph. IV contrast is not required to initially characterise pulmonary nodules. Non-contrast CT allows assessment of size, margins, density, and calcification patterns.

Fleischner Society 2017 Guidelines are applied for the follow-up of incidentally detected pulmonary nodules. They are applicable to patients 35 years or older. Not applicable if immunocompromised or known/suspected malignancy.


The image below shows an incidentally detected SPN which showed spiculated margins on CT. Diagnosis was lung adenocarcinoma.
question: A solitary pulmonary nodule is incidentally detected on chest X-ray in a 50-year-old patient. What is the most appropriate next investigation in evaluating the risk of malignancy?

explanationHtml:
The chest X-ray showing a peripheral lung mass with spiculated margins (corona radiata appearance) is suggestive of malignancy. CECT chest is the next best investigation.

CECT detects nodal enlargement, pleural involvement, and chest wall and mediastinal invasion in evaluation of lung masses.

Bronchogenic carcinoma has varied imaging appearances. Peripheral tumours, most commonly adenocarcinoma, present as a solitary mass with spiculated margins. They may show ground-glass attenuation or resemble pneumonia.

Central tumours show hilar enlargement with distal collapse or consolidation. Cavitation is most common in squamous cell carcinoma. Lobar collapse in the right upper lobe may produce the Golden S sign.

Intrathoracic spread may involve hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, pleura, and chest wall.

Image below shows corona radiata in a case of bronchogenic carcinoma


HRCT chest is used primarily for evaluation of interstitial lung diseases. It provides detailed parenchymal assessment but is not used for staging of lung masses.

Bronchoscopy: allows direct visualisation and tissue sampling of central airway tumours. Has limited reach for peripheral lesions.

MRI is the investigation of choice for superior sulcus tumor (Pancoast tumor).
question: A 55-year-old smoker presents with a three-month history of cough and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a peripheral lung mass with corona radiata appearance. What is the next best investigation?

explanationHtml:
The chest X-ray depicts multiple, large, well-circumscribed, round pulmonary metastases that look similar to cannonballs. Hence it is known as cannonball metastasis.

The most common primaries to result in pulmonary metastases in adults include:

  • breast carcinoma
  • colorectal carcinoma
  • renal cell carcinoma
  • uterine leiomyosarcoma
  • head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

Uncommon metastatic patterns include endobronchial metastases, miliary pulmonary metastases, and tumor emboli. The miliary pattern is classically associated with tumors such as thyroid carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, and bone sarcomas.
question: A 72-year-old man presented with weight loss, decreased appetite, and iron deficiency anaemia. Chest X-ray was done and given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer that can mimic consolidation.

Adenocarcinomas with lepidic growth pattern (formerly termed bronchoalveolar cell carcinoma) can present with chronic consolidation, the most common type being lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma.

Adenocarcinoma presents as a peripheral upper lobe nodule that is ground-glass, part-solid, or solid with spiculated margins. Adenocarcinoma in situ appears as a pure ground-glass nodule >1 cm. Lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma shows consolidation with air bronchograms. Mucinous subtype may show multifocal bilateral consolidations. Among all lung cancers, adenocarcinoma is most commonly associated with pleural involvement.

CECT may show the “CT angiogram sign”: enhanced vessels inside the malignant consolidation, but it is not specific.

Shown below is chest X-ray and CT of a patient with non-resolving consolidation, biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma.
question: Which type of lung carcinoma can most commonly mimic consolidation on chest X-ray?

explanationHtml:
In the above clinical scenario, the CT chest shows the comet-tail sign. It is seen in cases of round atelectasis.

Round atelectasis is a form of parenchymal collapse condition characterised by the infolding of a redundant pleura, resulting in a parenchymal collapse that can mimic a mass on imaging. The comet-tail sign is produced by the distortion of bronchovascular bundles that appear pulled into the collapsed area, resembling a comet tail.

The most common cause of rounded atelectasis is occupational exposure to mineral dust: asbestos, pneumoconiosis, and mixed mineral dust.

The image below shows round atelectasis associated with pleural thickening and comet-tail sign:
question: A 62-year-old male, a retired construction worker,  presented with a 2-month history of mild cough and occasional dyspnea. CT chest was done as shown below.  What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The diagnosis in the above case is bronchiectasis. The HRCT shows a signet ring sign due to the dilated bronchus seen accompanying the pulmonary artery in the cross-section, suggestive of bronchiectasis.

Bronchiectasis is a suppurative lung disease with abnormal and irreversible dilatation of the bronchi. Clinically, the patients present with a chronic productive cough, clubbing, crackles, and rhonchi. HRCT is the investigation of choice for bronchiectasis.

Morphologically, bronchiectasis is described as cylindrical, varicose, or saccular. These reflect increasing severity of disease.

  • Cylindrical (tubular) - dilated bronchus with parallel, relatively smooth walls
  • Varicose - dilated bronchus with irregular walls
  • Saccular (cystic) - Most severe form. Bronchi become rounded and terminate as round cysts

The image shows cystic/saccular bronchiectasis with signet ring signs.
question: HRCT of a patient showed the following. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The HRCT shows subpleural reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, which are features of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP).

Imaging features of Interstitial lung disease (ILD) may be described as:

1. Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP): Subpleural bibasal reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis. Ground-glass opacity is not predominant. UIP is the classic pattern of IPF but also occurs in chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, asbestosis, and connective tissue disease.

2. Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP): Bilateral ground-glass opacities with fine reticulation, often peripheral or peribronchovascular. Honeycombing is minimal or absent. Associated with connective tissue disease, drug-induced lung disease, and chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
question: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive dyspnea and dry cough for 1 year. HRCT chest is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Bat-wing appearance is seen in pulmonary oedema.

The bat-wing distribution of pulmonary edema refers to bilateral perihilar air-space opacities with sparing of the lung peripheries.

Pulmonary oedema is defined as an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the extravascular compartments of the lung. Chest X-ray findings can be divided into: .

  • Vascular alterations (pulmonary venous hypertension)
    • Pulmonary venous engorgement / redistribution (cephalization)
  • Interstitial oedema
    • Kerley lines (esp. Kerley B)
    • Pleural effusion
    • Fluid in fissures (including “pseudotumour / vanishing tumour”)
  • Alveolar oedema
    • Air-space opacification in bat-wing distribution
    • Air bronchograms

The image below is a chest X-ray showing multiple signs of cardiogenic pulmonary edema (CHF).
question: Bat-wing appearance is seen in:

explanationHtml:
The CT shows a prominent systemic arterial vessel feeding the sequestered lung tissue, making the diagnosis pulmonary sequestration.

Pulmonary sequestration is a lung malformations in which a segment or lobe of dysplastic lung tissue is disconnected from the rest of the tracheobronchial tree (airways) and pulmonary arteries. It receives an anomalous vascular supply from systemic arteries, most commonly the aorta. It is a non-functional tissue. They most commonly occur in the lower lobes, with a left-sided preference.

Intralobar sequestrations are covered by the visceral pleura of the affected lobe, appear aerated on imaging, and are prone to recurrent infections. Treatment is elective surgical resection.

Extralobar sequestrations have their own separate pleural investment, appear as solid masses on imaging, and are typically asymptomatic with expectant management.

Images below show intralobar sequestrations:


Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) refers to a heterogeneous group of lung masses communicating with an abnormal bronchial tree. They have normal pulmonary arterial supply and normal pulmonary venous drainage. On imaging, type 1 appears as large cysts, type 2 as small cysts, and type 3 as microcysts appearing solid.

Image below shows CPAM:


Scimitar syndrome is a congenital pulmonary venous anomaly associated with underdevelopment of the right lung. In this condition, the right pulmonary vein drains abnormally, most often into the inferior vena cava above the liver. The anomalous vein may be seen on chest X-ray as a curved shadow along the right cardiac border, producing the scimitar sign.


Congenital lobar overinflation is due to partial obstruction of a lobar bronchus. Air enters the lobe but is not expelled normally, leading to progressive enlargement and increased translucency of the affected lobe. On imaging, the affected lobe shows increased lucency, widened intercostal spaces, and contralateral mediastinal shift. Most commonly affects the left upper lobe.
question: A young patient presents with recurrent lower respiratory tract infections. CT pulmonary angiography in oblique view is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Bilateral hilar with right paratracheal lymph nodes
explanationHtml:
The chest X-ray shows lymph node enlargement involving the bilateral hilar and right paratracheal nodes, a finding classically seen in sarcoidosis.

This characteristic pattern is called the Garland triad or 1-2-3 sign, also known as the pawnbroker's sign.

The lymph nodes involved are:

  1. Right paratracheal nodes
  2. Right hilar nodes
  3. Left hilar nodes

This is called the "1-2-3-4 sign" when the aortopulmonary nodes are also enlarged. In chronic disease, the lymph nodes may show eggshell calcification.

Image showing a pattern of lymph node enlargement (1-2-3 sign):


Subcarinal nodes are located at the level of the tracheal bifurcation. Paraesophageal nodes lie along the esophageal wall. Both these groups of lymph nodes are midline in location.

options.text: Bilateral paratracheal with right hilar lymph nodes
Bilateral hilar with right paratracheal lymph nodes
Bilateral hilar with subcarinal lymph nodes
Right paratracheal with paraesophageal lymph nodes

question: The chest X-ray of a patient with sarcoidosis is shown below. Which lymph nodes are enlarged in the classical radiological pattern?

explanationHtml:
The X-ray shows unilateral hyperinflation of the left lung with mediastinal shift to the right, suggesting a foreign body causing partial obstruction in the left main bronchus.

In partial obstruction, air enters the bronchus during inspiration but cannot escape during expiration due to a ball-valve mechanism. This results in unilateral hyperinflation of the affected lung with mediastinal shift to the opposite side.

Foreign body aspiration is common in toddlers and young children, typically presenting with sudden choking, coughing, or respiratory distress.

Most aspirated objects are radiolucent (nuts, plastic toys, food) and are not directly visible on X-ray. When the object is not visible, indirect signs include

  • unilateral hyperinflation from ball-valve mechanism in partial obstruction
  • lobar collapse in complete obstruction
  • mediastinal shift: away from hyperinflation in partial obstruction, and towards the collapsed lobe in complete obstruction.

Radio-opaque objects like coins and batteries are directly visible.

Chest X-ray showing partial left main bronchus obstruction:


Anatomically, in children <15 years, the right and left main bronchi are symmetrical, so aspiration is equal on both sides. But in adults, the right main bronchus is more vertical and shorter than the left, so obstructions are more common on the right side.
question: A 2-year-old was brought in with a choking episode. A foreign body was removed, and an immediate X-ray was taken. What was the likely site of obstruction based on the given X-ray?

explanationHtml:
The following chest X-ray findings in a patient with Marfanoid features point to a diagnosis of left-sided pneumothorax:

  • Hyperlucent area without vascular markings in the left hemithorax- indicating air in the pleural space,
  • Visceral pleural line - indicating partial lung collapse, and
  • Tracheal deviation towards the opposite side - indicating mediastinal shift.

Pneumothorax refers to the collection of air in the pleural space. Tall and thin young men, such as in Marfan's syndrome, are predisposed to developing spontaneous pneumothorax. In tall individuals, the pleural pressure at the lung apices is more negative, leading to the formation of subpleural apical blebs or bullae, which can rupture spontaneously and cause pneumothorax.


Marfan's syndrome is an inherited connective tissue disorder caused by a mutation in the gene that encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1 (FBN1). The FBN1 locus is on the long arm of chromosome 15.

It is a clinical diagnosis based on skeletal (arachnodactyly, overgrowth of long bones, pectus excavatum), cardiovascular (aortic root aneurysm, aortic dissection and rupture, valvular prolapse), ocular manifestations (ectopia lentis), and other systemic manifestations, like thoracic scoliosis and spontaneous pneumothorax.

Marfan's syndrome is one of the causes of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in adults.

question: A 21-year-old tall, thin male patient with long limbs and arachnodactyly presented with a sudden onset of breathlessness. His chest X-ray is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. PA view in full expiration
explanationHtml:
The patient most likely has pneumothorax. The best chest x-ray view to diagnose a pneumothorax is PA view in full expiration.

Standard chest X-ray in adults is obtained in PA view as it avoids magnification of the cardiac and mediastinal silhouettes and provides clearer visualisation of the lungs.

Expiratory chest X-ray increases the density of normal lung, which increases the contrast between lung and surrounding air, as in cases of pneumothorax and conditions causing air trapping (foreign body, partial bronchial obstruction).

Paired inspiratory and expiratory radiographs are often used when small pneumothorax or air trapping (as in COPD) is suspected.

Image showing left-sided pneumothorax:

Detection of a small/occult pneumothorax improves with an expiratory PA view, lateral decubitus view with the affected side up, or a horizontal beam “shoot through” lateral chest X-ray, which can identify anterior pneumothorax in patients who cannot be positioned erect.

CT is the most sensitive modality.

question: A 62-year-old man with COPD presents with left-sided chest discomfort. Examination revealed left sided mild hyper-resonance and decreased breath sounds. There is no history of chest trauma or invasive procedures. He is hemodynamically stable, with a SpO2 95% on room air. What is the best chest X-ray view to visualize this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Depressed hemidiaphragm on the contralateral side
explanationHtml:
In pneumothorax, depression of the hemidiaphragm occurs on the ipsilateral (affected) side.

Chest radiograph in pneumothorax shows the following features:

Ipsilateral:

  • A hyperlucent area (dark area without lung markings) is seen between the lung margin and chest wall
  • Inwardly shifted visceral pleural line (thin, sharp white line)
  • Depression of the diaphragm, rib cage expansion
  • Deep sulcus sign: Deep lateral costophrenic angle can be seen in a supine X-ray

Contralateral:

  • Features of mediastinal shift to the opposite side:
    • Tracheal deviation
    • Cardiac displacement

Depressed hemidiaphragm on the contralateral side
Mediastinal shift to the contralateral side
Collapse and volume loss of ipsilateral lung

question: All of the following features can be seen in patients with pneumothorax except:

explanationHtml:
The above M-mode ultrasound of the right lung shows a stratosphere or barcode sign specific for pneumothorax.

In a normal lung, M-mode ultrasound shows a sand-like (seashore) appearance due to normal lung sliding. In pneumothorax, lung sliding is lost and the normal sand-like appearance beneath the pleural line is replaced by parallel lines. This is termed the stratosphere or barcode sign, suggesting the presence of air in the pleural cavity.

The images below show the comparison between a normal lung and pneumothorax on M-mode ultrasound.


Supine chest radiography has low sensitivity for traumatic pneumothorax. Thoracic ultrasound has high sensitivity and specificity for the detection of small or occult pneumothorax in critical care patients.

Pleural effusion on ultrasound appears anechoic with an echogenic line at the fluid-lung interface if it is transudate. Exudative and hemorrhagic effusions may appear echogenic with pleural thickening. The fluid shows movement and changes in shape with breathing, along with the presence of septa and fibrous strands.

Consolidation on ultrasound appears hypoechoic with heterogeneous echotexture. If it is isoechoic with the liver and is referred to as lung hepatization.

Haemothorax, a common traumatic injury, appears as a complex echogenic pleural collection with internal echoes and septations on ultrasound.

question: A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with complaints of right-sided chest pain after a motor vehicle collision.  On performing an ultrasound the following was seen. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and radiograph showing a spinnaker sign is suggestive of pneumomediastinum.

Spinnaker sign (also called angel wing sign) is a radiographic sign seen in neonates with pneumomediastinum. Pneumomediastinum is the presence of extraluminal gas within the mediastinum. The pressure from the collected gas displaces the two lobes of the thymic tissue upward and laterally from its normal position. This results in large, wedge-shaped opacities on radiograph resembling the spinnaker headsails of a boat.


Other signs of pneumomediastinum are:

  • Ring around the artery sign - air around the pulmonary artery
  • Tubular artery sign - air adjacent to major aortic branches
  • Double bronchial wall sign - air adjacent to bronchus outlining the wall clearly
  • Continuous diaphragm sign - the diaphragm can be seen continuously across the midline then it is suggestive of free gas within the mediastinum.

The signs seen in pneumomediastiinum are shown below.


The spinnaker sail sign should be distinguished from a thymic sail sign which is a normal finding on a neonatal chest x-ray. It represents a physiologically enlarged thymus in a neonate.

question: A term neonate born by vacuum-assisted delivery developed mild respiratory distress 1 hour after birth. Arterial oxygen saturation remained > 95% without supplemental oxygen. Chest radiography performed 6 hours after birth is given below. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The lateral decubitus view is the best view to evaluate a small pleural effusion. It can identify as little as 10 ml of pleural fluid.

The image given below shows a lateral decubitus view showing pleural effusion - marking A shows fluid layering in the right pleural cavity. The amount of pleural fluid can be approximately quantified by measuring the distance A.

The minimal amount of fluid required to be detected on X-ray imaging for pleural effusion:

  • Lateral (erect) view: 75 ml pleural fluid
  • Erect PA view: 200 ml pleural fluid
  • Lateral decubitus view: >10 ml pleural fluid

Features of chest radiograph in pleural effusion:

  • Blunting of costophrenic angles
  • Ellis-S curve – This is a radiological illusion and occurs as a medial radiological density due to the presence of partially aerated lung between the anterior and posterior fluid layers, whereas laterally the density is higher due to the presence of fluid only. The actual fluid level is horizontal
  • Opaque hemithorax in massive effusion

The image below is a chest X-ray PA view showing pleural effusion with Ellis-S curve.

The best investigation for minimal pleural effusion is USG, which can identify as little as 3 to 5 mL of fluid.

question: A patient with pneumonia complains of shortness of breath. A small pleural effusion is suspected. What is the best chest X-ray view to evaluate this patient?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario and X-ray is suggestive of loculated pleural effusion.

The chest X-ray shows loculated pleural effusion that tracks along the lateral chest wall and the costophrenic angle (causing blunting).

Loculated pleural effusion is trapped pleural fluid that forms due to adhesions from chronic inflammation or infection. It appears as a localized pleural-based lentiform or dome-shaped opacity with smooth margins that displaces adjacent lung. Associated with empyema, hemothorax, tuberculosis, or CHF (vanishing tumor).

A pleural lesion can be differentiated from a parenchymal lesion by the angle it makes with the chest wall. Pleural lesions make an obtuse angle with the chest wall (such as loculated effusion, pleural plaques, mesothelioma) whereas parenchymal lesions make an acute angle with the chest wall (e.g., lung masses, consolidation, abscesses).

Pneumothorax presents with hyperlucency and absent lung markings without any pleural-based opacity on chest X-ray.

Lobar consolidation presents as airspace opacities that make an acute angle with the chest wall. It occupies an entire lobe with air bronchograms visible within it.

Pulmonary infarct appears as a wedge-shaped, pleural-based opacity (Hampton hump), with its apex pointing toward the hilum, associated with pulmonary embolism, distinguished from loculated effusion by its wedge morphology and clinical context.

Shown below is an image of hampton hump in pulmonary infarct.

question: A 30-year-old man presented with a history of fever and chest pain for the last 7 days. A chest X-ray was done. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
A split pleura sign is seen in empyema.

Empyema is defined as a collection of pus in the pleural cavity. It is usually associated with pneumonia but may also develop after thoracic surgery or trauma.

A hallmark feature of empyema on CT imaging is the split pleura sign, where the parietal and visceral pleura show enhancement. This sign is considered the most sensitive and specific indicator of empyema on CT, helping to distinguish it from peripheral lung abscess.

CT scan showing split pleura sign:


A peripheral lung abscess appears as a round or oval cavity with thick, irregular walls making an acute angle with the chest wall. An air-fluid level is often seen within the cavity. The split pleura sign is absent.

Image below shows a peripheral lung absces on axial CT oh the chest.

question: Split pleura sign is seen in:

explanationHtml:
Air bronchograms are not seen in pleural effusion.

In pleural effusion, there is a homogenous opacity with absent broncho-vascular markings, obliteration of costophrenic angle, and no air bronchograms.

Air bronchogram is defined as a pattern of air-filled bronchi (dark) on a background of opacified lung (grey/white).

It is almost always caused by a pathological airspace/alveolar process, in which something other than air fills the alveoli. Air bronchograms will not be visible if the bronchi themselves are opacified (e.g. by fluid) and thus indicate patent proximal airways.

Air bronchograms can be seen with several conditions:

  • Pulmonary consolidation
  • Pulmonary oedema
  • Hyaline membrane disease
  • Non-obstructive atelectasis
  • Severe interstitial lung disease
  • Neoplasms: adenocarcinoma
  • Pulmonary lymphoma
  • Pulmonary infarct
  • Pulmonary haemorrhage

The given radiograph shows peribronchial thickening and the air bronchogram sign:

CT showing consolidation with air bronchograms:

question: In which of the following conditions will you not see an air bronchogram?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, pleural calcification is least likely to be seen in sarcoidosis.

The calcification commonly seen in sarcoidosis, lymph node calcification, typically showing eggshell or stippled calcification.

Conditions showing pleural calcification:

  • Asbestosis
  • Haemothorax
  • Pyothorax/empyema
  • Tuberculosis
  • Previous surgery
  • Radiation therapy

Asbestos-related pleural plaques are bilateral and discrete, delicate plaques located on the parietal pleura, commonly at the diaphragm, axillae, and 3 and 9 o'clock positions. Whereas pleural plaques from other causes (e.g., post-empyema, hemothorax) are usually unilateral, dense, coarse, irregular sheets on the visceral pleura, located at the posterior lung bases and posterior chest wall.

The chest radiograph below shows extensive calcification of the pleura.

question: In which of the following conditions is pleural calcification least likely to be seen?

correctAnswer: D. Hydropneumothorax - Rupture of hydatid cyst
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of shortness of breath and chest discomfort with the chest X-ray showing a straight horizontal air-fluid line, suggests the most probable diagnosis to be Hydropneumothorax. One of the causes of hydropneumothorax is rupture of hydatid cyst.

Hydropneumothorax can occur due to:

  • Thoracentesis
  • Rupture of a hydatid cyst
  • Thoracic trauma
  • Bronchopleural fistula (e.g., tuberculosis)
  • Oesophagopleural fistula

Pleural effusion is characterized by the presence of the meniscus sign and costophrenic angle blunting.

Congestive heart failure is associated with pleural effusion, not hydropneumothorax. The X-ray shows cardiomegaly, cephalisation, kerley B lines and bat-wing appearance.
