question: A 47-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of shortness of breath and chest discomfort. An erect chest X-ray was taken and is given below. What is the diagnosis, along with its potential cause?

explanationHtml:
The structure marked in the given CT thorax image is the superior vena cava.

The image below depicts all the major structures labelled in the CT thorax image:
question: Identify the structure marked in the CT scan shown below:

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is pericardial effusion. The given image shows a globular enlargement of the cardiac shadow, known as the "money bag" appearance.

Pericardial effusion is defined as accumulation of excess fluid exceeding 50 mL in the pericardial space. Common etiologies include heart failure, renal dysfunction, infections, malignancy, and myocardial infarction.

The investigation of choice is echocardiography. However, the following x-ray findings are also characteristic for pericardial effusion:

  • AP view - money bag or leather bottle-shaped heart
  • Lateral view – Oreo cookie sign (fluid is seen between two layers of fat)

In the following image, pericardial fluid (yellow asterisk) outlined by paracardial fat (blue arrows) and epicardial fat (orange arrows) is called the oreo cookie sign.
question: A 35-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of low-grade fever and progressive chest pain. Chest X-ray revealed the following. Considering the symptoms and imaging, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
All the options listed are radiographic signs of left atrial enlargement (LAE) on chest X-ray, except lateral displacement of the oesophagus. In LAE, the oesophagus is displaced posteriorly, seen on a lateral view barium swallow study.

Radiographic signs seen in LAE include:

  • Enlargement of left atrial appendage
  • Enlargement of the left atrial appendage along the upper left cardiac border, leading to straightening of the left heart border.
  • Posterior displacement of the oesophagus - seen on the lateral view of the barium swallow study.
  • Elevation of left main bronchus and widening of the carina.
  • Double density sign or double atrial shadow - the enlarged LA extends towards the right cardiac border, hence, both RA and LA borders can be seen distinctly over the right heart border (as shown below):


The causes of left atrial enlargement are as follows:

  • Congenital: Ventricular septal defect , Patent ductus arteriosus
  • Acquired: Mitral valvular disease, left ventricular failure, left atrial myxoma
question: All of the following are radiographic signs of left atrial enlargement on chest X-ray except:

explanationHtml:
The given chest X-ray shows an upturned cardiac apex in a patient with Tetralogy of Fallot, which is seen due to right ventricular hypertrophy.

The image below shows a boot-shaped heart seen in the Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). There is right ventricular hypertrophy seen as an upturned cardiac apex, along with a concave appearance of the pulmonary artery.

TOF is a cyanotic congenital heart condition and has four characteristic components: Ventricular septal defect, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (pulmonary stenosis), overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy (late feature).

Other radiographic features seen in TOF are:

  • Pulmonary oligaemia (due to pulmonary stenosis)
  • Normal-sized heart without heart failure
  • Right aortic arch (observed in approximately 25% of cases).
question: A 5-year-old male child presents with progressive breathlessness and cyanosis that worsens with physical activity. Chest X-ray is shown below. What is the cause of the classic appearance of heart seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The best description for the above condition is atrialization of the ventricle. Based on the clinical scenario and the X-ray showing a box-shaped cardiac silhouette caused by right atrial enlargement, this is typically seen in Ebstein's anomaly.

Ebstein anomaly is characterized by an abnormal tricuspid valve that is displaced downwards into the right ventricle. Hence, a part of the right ventricle is now located above the tricuspid valve. This is called atrialization of the ventricle. There can be associated tricuspid regurgitation with or without stenosis.

Maternal lithium intake during the first trimester has been associated with Ebstein anomaly.

X-ray findings depend on the degree to which the tricuspid valve is displaced downwards. The features are an enlarged right atrium which causes severe right-sided cardiomegaly, giving rise to a box-shaped cardiac shadow and pulmonary oligemia.

options.text: Right outflow tract obstruction with overriding of aorta
Abnormal pulmonary vein drainage into systemic venous circulation

question: A baby is brought to the clinic as he turns blue every time he cries. Chest X-ray reveals the following. Which of the following best describes the underlying condition?

explanationHtml:
The egg-on-string or egg-on-the-side appearance on chest X-ray is seen in transposition of great arteries (TGA). This appearance is due to altered cardiac contours as a result of cardiomegaly, as shown in the image below.

The heart appears egg-shaped due to cardiomegaly. The upper mediastinum becomes narrow because of reduced thymic shadow and the abnormal position of the transposed great vessels. This produces the classic egg-on-string appearance on chest X-ray.

In d-TGA, the aorta arises from the right ventricle, whereas the pulmonary trunk arises from the left ventricle. d-TGA is also called uncorrected TGA.
question: An infant is brought with poor feeding and lethargy. Chest X-ray reveals an egg-on-string appearance. Which of the following conditions is this finding most suggestive of?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is constrictive pericarditis. The given image shows calcified pericardium, called an egg-in-cup appearance. It is typically seen in constrictive pericarditis.

In constrictive pericarditis, there is fibrous or calcific constrictive thickening of the anterior and lateral pericardium that prevents normal diastolic filling of the heart. The resulting diastolic dysfunction leads to features of right heart failure. The thickness of the pericardium is best assessed on MRI.

Note: The egg-in-cup (or ball-on-tee) appearance is also a urographic finding seen in renal papillary necrosis.
question: A 61-year-old woman presented with chest pain and fatigue. The chest radiograph is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The correct answer is B. 1 - Tetralogy of Fallot, 2 - TAPVR.

In patient 1, cyanosis on exertion with squatting for relief is classic for TOF. Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance and venous return, increasing flow through the obstructed RV outflow tract.

The chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) due to right ventricular hypertrophy with a concavity in the region of the pulmonary artery, and the lung fields are oligaemic.


Patient 2, a neonate with cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen indicates cyanotic congenital heart disease. TAPVR is associated with total mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous blood flow within the heart, producing cyanosis.

The chest X-ray shows a figure-of-eight or snowman appearance due to the supracardiac shadow formed by the anomalous pulmonary veins draining via the left superior vena cava and innominate vein. The heart is enlarged with increased pulmonary vascularity.
question:
The X-rays of two patients are given below. Patient 1 is a 5-year-old boy with cyanosis and breathlessness worsening on exertion. He squats after physical activity for relief. Patient 2 is a 3-day-old neonate with severe cyanosis since birth, unresponsive to oxygen supplementation. What are the most likely diagnoses?

TGA: Transposition of great arteries

TAPVR: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return

TOF: Tetralogy of Fallot

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario and the image showing the figure of 3 sign point towards coarctation of aorta as the cause of hypertension in this patient.

The aorta having pre-stenotic dilatation, the narrowed segment at the coarctation site and post-stenotic dilatation gives the appearance of a 'figure of 3' sign. Left paramediastinal shadow is also seen. These findings are shown below.

Coarctation of aorta is a congenital heart defect characterized by the narrowing of the thoracic aorta near the insertion of the ductus arteriosus. It is associated with the bicuspid aortic valve, atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, mitral regurgitation and Turner syndrome. It is more common in males.

On barium swallow, the reverse figure 3 sign (also known as the E sign) is seen as the medial equivalent of the figure 3 sign seen on chest X-ray. It is formed by prestenotic dilatation of the ascending aorta, indentation of the coarctation site and post-stenotic dilatation of the descending aorta.

Notching of ribs (Roesler's sign) due to inferior rib erosion by dilated intercostal collateral vessels, is also seen in coarctation of aorta. It affects ribs 3/4 to 8. Ribs 1 and 2 are spared because their intercostal arteries arise from the costocervical trunk, above the coarctation.

Other chest X-ray features in coarctation of the aorta are dilated left subclavian artery, dilated ascending aorta.

Below is an image depicting rib notching.
question: A 30-year-old woman presents with persistent hypertension, chest pain and cramping in her legs, particularly during exertion. A chest radiograph was taken, which reveals the condition, as shown in the image below. What is the likely underlying cause of her hypertension?

explanationHtml:
The X-ray shows inferior rib notching. It is seen in coarctation of aorta (CoA).

Rib notching (Roesler sign) in CoA occurs due to erosion of the inferior margins of the ribs by dilated collateral intercostal vessels that bypass the coarctation. Ribs 1 and 2 are spared as they arise from the costocervical trunk. Ribs 4-8 are commonly notched.

Preductal coarctation does not produce rib notching.

Coarctation of aorta also shows a Figure of 3 or reverse 3 sign, which refers to an abnormality in the contour of the aorta, as shown below.


Causes for inferior rib notching (Roesler sign) are:

  • Unilateral:
    • Subclavian artery occlusion.
    • Coarctation of aorta involving left subclavian or anomalous right subclavian artery
  • Bilateral:
    • Coarctation of aorta, occlusion, aortitis
    • Takayasu’s disease and atheroma of subclavian artery
    • Pulmonary oligemia (ToF, pulmonary atresia, stenosis)
    • SVC or IVC obstruction
    • AV malformation
    • Neurofibromatosis type 1
question: A radiologist observes the following finding on a patient's  X-ray. Which condition is it seen in?

explanationHtml:
The described finding of central pulmonary artery dilatation with tapering of peripheral branches is called peripheral pruning, and is characteristic of pulmonary artery hypertension (PAH).

This means that the blood vessels appear cut off before they reach the outer 1/3 of the lung. Hence, the edge of the lung fields is darker than usual, and the central area is often whiter.

Plain radiographic findings in pulmonary artery hypertension include elevated cardiac apex due to right ventricular hypertrophy, enlarged right atrium, prominent pulmonary outflow tract, enlarged pulmonary arteries, and peripheral pruning.

The image below shows Chest X-ray findings in pulmonary hypertension:
question: A patient presents with progressive breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows dilatation of central pulmonary arteries with tapering of peripheral arterial branches. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for this finding?

correctAnswer: A. Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
explanationHtml:
Plethoric lung fields are seen in Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC). In this condition, pulmonary venous obstruction results in pulmonary arterial hypertension, resulting in plethoric lung fields.

Pulmonary plethora Pulmonary oligemia

Acyanotic

  • Ventricular septal defect
  • Atrial septal defect
  • Patent ductus arteriosus

Cyanotic

  • TAPVC

Cyanotic

  • Ebstein anomaly
  • Tetralogy of Fallot
  • Tricuspid atresia


Pulmonary plethora (increased pulmonary perfusion): In conditions with left-to-right shunting, oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs, increasing pulmonary blood flow. On chest X-ray, the hilar and intrapulmonary vessels look more prominent because they are overfilled.


Pulmonary oligaemia (decreased pulmonary perfusion): In conditions with obstruction to right-sided blood flow, less blood reaches the lungs. On chest X-ray, the vascular markings are reduced, so the lung fields appear more radiolucent. Image below shows oligemic lung fields in TOF.
question: Plethoric lung fields are seen in:

explanationHtml:
The given CT scan showing a double lumen and dilatation of the aorta is suggestive of an aortic dissection.

In this condition, blood enters the space below the intima of the aorta. This results in the formation of a true lumen and false lumen. The true lumen is often the smaller of the two because of being compressed by the false lumen, as shown below (2D MRI showing the dissection flap at peak systole and mid-diastole. The true lumen expands during systole and collapses during diastole due to pressure fluctuations from the false lumen).

Feature True Lumen False Lumen
Position Medial, smaller Lateral, larger
Enhancement Early, washes out Late or thrombosed
Behaviour May collapse Often dilates
Branch supply Coronaries, celiac, SMA, right renal Left renal artery
Signs — Cobweb sign, Beak sign


The cobweb sign refers to slender linear strands of incompletely sheared media within the false lumen.

The beak sign is a wedge of hematoma at the edge of the false lumen, forming an acute angle between the dissection flap and the outer aortic wall.
question: A 50-year-old patient has come with sudden onset of chest pain and his CT scan shows the following picture. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
CT Pulmonary angiography is the next best investigation for pulmonary embolism (PE) in a patient with low likelihood of PE and a positive D-dimer.

CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the investigation of choice for suspected PE as it directly demonstrates intraluminal filling defects in the pulmonary arteries.

Shown below is a CT angiography demonstrating multiple filling defects both at the bifurcation (saddle pulmonary embolism) and in the pulmonary arteries.


V/Q scan is a nuclear medicine test that assesses ventilation and perfusion in the lungs. It is reserved for patients with contraindications to iodinated contrast (e.g., contrast allergy, renal impairment) and preferred in pregnancy when chest X-ray is normal. If the chest X-ray is abnormal, underlying lung pathology reduces accuracy in V/Q scans. A V/Q mismatch (absent segmental perfusion with normal ventilation) indicates high probability (>95%) of PE.
question: A patient presented with breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. Clinical likelihood of pulmonary embolism was low based on Wells score and D-dimer was elevated. What is the next best investigation?

explanationHtml:
Contrast enhanced CT (CECT) is the initial investigation for aortic dissection as it is more widely available and takes a shorter time when compared to MRI.

The image below depicts CT chest showing Type A aortic dissection from the aortic root. (A) Axial view and (B) sagittal view. The arrows indicate the intimal flap.

MRI, though highly accurate for acute aortic disease evaluation, is usually confined to cases of severe renal insufficiency or when the use of iodinated contrast medium is absolutely contraindicated.

Trans-oesophageal ultrasound (TOE) is performed for bedside evaluation in patients too unstable for transportation.
question: What is the initial investigation for evaluating a patient suspected to have an aortic dissection?

explanationHtml:
In the above clinical scenario, chest pain and dyspnea after air travel most likely points to a diagnosis of pulmonary embolism. Westermark sign is seen in the given chest x-ray.

It is defined by a hyper-lucent area with decreased vascularity due to reduced blood supply to the involved part of the lung.

Even though characteristic signs are seen on chest x-ray, it is neither sensitive nor specific for pulmonary embolism. CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the investigation of choice in pulmonary embolism.
question: A 65-year-old man presents with complaints of sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. He had arrived from an international trip three days ago. A chest X-ray was done. What is this finding called?

explanationHtml:
The Doppler waveform of the venous blood flow in the lower limb distal to non occlusive chronic DVT is monophasic.

The normal venous waveform shows a variation (phasicity) secondary to respiration referred to as a respirophasic waveform. Loss of this phasic variation results in a monophasic waveform suggestive of venous obstruction. If there is incomplete obstruction of the vein lumen, there is usually loss of the phasic respiratory venous flow pattern, and a continuous flow wave may be observed that is minimally affected by augmentation.

The image given below shows the normal monophasic signal from a vein showing respiratory phasicity.
question: The Doppler waveform of the venous blood flow in the lower limb distal to non occlusive chronic DVT is _____.

explanationHtml:
The marked vessel is the common femoral vein, the largest structure forming the mickey mouse sign at the saphenofemoral junction.

The normal anatomy of the femoral vessels and great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction on USG is called the mickey mouse sign. The mickey mouse sign involves:

  • Common femoral artery
  • Common femoral vein
  • Great saphenous vein

The given images below show the mickey mouse sign (FV- femoral vein; FA- femoral artery; GSV- great saphenous vein).
question: The USG image below shows a transverse section of the lower limb vessels demonstrating a classic mickey mouse sign. Identify the marked vessel.

explanationHtml:
In the given echocardiogram, the arrow points to the tricuspid valve.

Transthoracic echocardiography is a first-line tool for structural and functional assessment of the heart. Two-dimensional echocardiography provides images of cardiac structures analogous to a thin slice through the heart, depicting the relationships of the RA, RV, LA, and LV.

Transthoracic echocardiography is performed with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position, with the probe placed at the cardiac apex for apical views.


In the apical four-chamber view, the apex is seen at the top and the atria at the bottom, with all four chambers visible simultaneously. The tricuspid valve is identified between the right atrium and right ventricle in this view, alongside the mitral valve on the left side.
question: In the given echocardiogram of a healthy individual, identify the valve marked.

explanationHtml:
The echocardiogram demonstrates a large pericardial effusion with a swinging heart, characteristic of cardiac tamponade, which shows electrical alternans on ECG.

In cardiac tamponade, echocardiography may show the heart oscillating within a large pericardial effusion, producing the classic swinging heart appearance. On ECG, due to the heart swinging toward and away from the chest wall leads with each beat, alternating high- and low-voltage QRS complexes are seen. This is called the characteristic electrical alternans appearance.


Clinically, cardiac tamponade presents with Beck's triad: muffled heart sounds, elevated JVP, and hypotension. On examination, the arterial pulse may show an exaggerated drop in systolic blood pressure (>10 mmHg) during inspiration, termed pulsus paradoxus.

On echocardiography, right atrial collapse in late diastole is the most sensitive echocardiographic sign of tamponade physiology, significant when it persists for more than one-third of the cardiac cycle. A dilated IVC with minimal respiratory variation further supports elevated right atrial pressure. Together, these findings confirm hemodynamically significant cardiac tamponade.

Apical echocardiogram demonstrating right atrial collapse in cardiac tamponade:


Echocardiography showing a large IVC with minimal changes with respiration:


Stratosphere sign is an M-mode finding in pneumothorax.

Pericardial knock is heard in constrictive pericarditis, not tamponade.

Pulsus bisferiens is seen in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) and aortic regurgitation.
question: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident with hemodynamic instability. Echocardiography findings are shown below. Which of the following findings is likely to be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache with CT revealing blood in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures point to the diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

The given image is that of a non-contrast CT (NCCT) and acute bleed appears hyperattenuating (bright). On NCCT, acute clotted blood measures 60–70 HU, appearing hyperattenuating relative to normal brain parenchyma (gray matter 35–40 HU, white matter 25–35 HU), which accounts for its bright appearance in the subarachnoid space.

In subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), blood enters the cerebrospinal fluid–filled subarachnoid space and accumulates, most prominently in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures. These sites are commonly involved because SAH usually results from rupture of berry aneurysms in the vessels of the Circle of Willis.

This leads to characteristic hyperdensity in these regions on CT imaging, often producing a typical basal “star-shaped” appearance.

The symptoms include sudden, severe headache, which may be associated with vomiting, decreased consciousness, and seizures. Neck stiffness may occur due to meningeal irritation.

The modified Fisher scale is a method for grading SAH as seen on non-contrast CT (NCCT). The Hunt and Hess scale describes the severity of SAH and is used as a predictor of survival.

question: A patient complains of neck stiffness and severe headache. The CT image shown below is suggestive of which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The most common site of hypertensive bleed in the brain is the basal ganglia marked as site 1 in the given image.

The most common cause of intracerebral haemorrhages is hypertension. Hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage most often involves the basal ganglia, particularly the putamen. Other common sites include the thalamus, pons, and cerebellum.

In the question image, the labeled sites correspond to the following anatomical structures:

  • Site 1: Putamen (most common site of hypertensive ICH)
  • Site 2: Cerebral cortex
  • Site 3: Posterior limb of internal capsule
  • Site 4: Thalamus (second most common site)

Following are the typical locations of ICH in order of decreasing frequency:

  • Basal ganglia haemorrhage (especially the putamen)
  • Thalamic haemorrhage
  • Pontine haemorrhage
  • Cerebellar haemorrhage

question: What is the most common site of hypertensive bleed in the brain?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is epidural hematoma.

The axial CT shows a bright (hyperdense), biconvex (lens-shaped) area, indicating an epidural hematoma, which is a collection of blood between the skull and the dura mater, usually caused by trauma. The characteristic shape is because the dura mater is tightly attached at the sutures, limiting the spread of blood. If the bleeding is severe, it can compress the brain and lead to herniation.

A swirl sign is seen in a brain hematoma, representing acute blood extravasation, showing fresh, unclotted blood with lower attenuation than the clotted blood (which is of a higher attenuation), highlighting the need for surgical intervention.

The following CT image depicts a swirl sign:

question: A patient is brought to casualty after falling from a balcony. Based on the CT scan finding provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The MRI SWI image shows multiple punctate blooming hypointense foci, suggestive of diffuse axonal injury (DWI).

The clinical scenario of a declining GCS score following a road traffic accident, combined with the given MRI demonstrating hypointense microhemorrhagic foci, suggests diffuse axonal injury.

Diffuse axonal injury is a severe form of traumatic brain injury caused by rotational acceleration/deceleration, leading to axonal shearing or disruption and forming microhemorrhages. Typically, these lesions are located at the grey-white matter junction in the corpus callosum and, in severe cases, the brainstem.

Diffuse axonal injury is characterized by multiple focal lesions with a characteristic distribution:

  • CT may be normal
  • MRI is the preferred modality for assessing suspected diffuse axonal injury. The most sensitive sequence is gradient-recalled echo (GRE) sequence or susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI), which shows haemorrhagic foci as hypointense blooming lesions.

The Susceptibility Weighted Imaging (SWI) is a form of MRI sequence that is very sensitive to microhemorrhages, and is the investigation of choice in diagnosing DAI when CT is normal. The image below shows DAI on the SWI sequence of MRI:

question:
A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency room following an RTA. His GCS progressively declines over hours. Based on the MRI SWI image shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?

RTA - Road traffic accident
SWI - Susceptibility-weighted imaging

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario and cerebral MR angiography image showing the "puff of smoke" appearance point to the diagnosis of Moyamoya disease.

Moyamoya disease is a rare, non-inflammatory, progressive, occlusive disease affecting the large intracranial arteries. In this condition, the lenticulostriate arteries form a rich collateral circulation around the occlusive lesions, creating the "puff of smoke" angiographic appearance, referred to as "moyamoya" in Japanese.

It exhibits a bimodal age distribution, with onset typically occurring in the first and fourth decades of life. The most common presentation is stroke or transient ischemic attacks (TIA), with the nature of these events differing by age group. In childhood, ischemic events are predominant, while hemorrhagic manifestations are frequent in adults.

question: A 9-year-old child presents with recurrent transient ischemic attacks and occasional headaches. MR angiography is done as shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given CT image demonstrates the Mount Fuji sign, a specific radiological finding of tension pneumocephalus.

This sign is characterised by bilateral compression and separation of the frontal lobes due to the trapped subdural and interhemispheric free air, which appears as non-attenuating collections resembling the peak of Mount Fuji.

Tension pneumocephalus is a rare, life-threatening condition most commonly caused by traumatic head injury. Other causes include skull base fractures, neurosurgical procedures, infections (meningitis, encephalitis, or brain abscess), brain tumours, or the use of nitrous oxide during anaesthesia.

The mass effect exerted by the subdural air compresses the underlying brain parenchyma, often resulting from a ball-valve mechanism causing one-way air entry into the subdural space, thus raising intracranial pressure (ICP), which leads to rapid clinical deterioration, such as worsening consciousness, necessitating urgent neurosurgical intervention to decompress the trapped air and prevent permanent brain damage.

The raised ICP and rapid neurological deterioration distinguish it from non-tension pneumocephalus, which lacks these changes.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Neurovascular Disorders, Trauma & Ct Brain
question: The CT scan of a patient who presented with deteriorating consciousness is shown below. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The best imaging modality for the early diagnosis of cerebral infarction is diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI).

Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) identifies areas of restricted diffusion of water molecules, making it more sensitive to early cellular changes than conventional MRI. The Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) map confirms true restriction by eliminating T2 shine-through. Together, they are used to detect conditions like acute stroke, tumors, and infections by highlighting how densely packed or restricted the cells are.

Acute infarct can be detected within minutes to early hours, when CT and routine MRI have low sensitivity.


Note: In case of suspected stroke, the preferred investigations are as follows:

  • Investigation of choice: NCCT
  • Gold standard investigation: MRI
  • Earliest detection of infarct: DWI

According to Stroke Guidelines, the initial investigation is non-contrast CT due to its rapid acquisition time, widespread availability, and cost-effectiveness. It helps quickly rule out haemorrhagic stroke and facilitates the timely administration of intravenous tPA in eligible patients.

Acute MCA territory infarct on NCCT is shown below:
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Neurovascular Disorders, Trauma & Ct Brain
question: What is the best imaging study for earliest diagnosis of cerebral infarct?

explanationHtml:
The empty delta sign is a characteristic finding of cerebral venous thrombosis (superior sagittal sinus thrombosis), seen on contrast-enhanced CT(CECT) or MRI. It appears as a triangular filling defect (clot) outlined by contrast. This sign is not observed on non-contrast imaging.

Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) is a condition where a blood clot forms in superficial or deep draining dural venous sinuses. The blockage raises brain pressure, causing headache, seizures, or confusion, and can lead to swelling or bleeding if untreated.

Cerebral venous thrombosis is commonly seen in hypercoagulable states such as:

  • Oral contraceptive pill use
  • Pregnancy and puerperium
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Dehydration
  • Intracranial infections.

It presents with headache (most common), seizures, intracranial hypertension, focal neurological deficits, and altered mental status.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is a septic thrombus formed in the cavernous sinus. It spreads from infection of the sinuses, teeth, ears, nose, and skin of the face. The contents of the cavernous venous sinus that may be affected include

  • Cavernous segment of the internal carotid artery
  • Perivascular sympathetic plexus
  • Abducens nerve (running through the Dorello’s canal)
  • oculomotor nerve, trochlear nerve, and the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve as part of the lateral wall.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Neurovascular Disorders, Trauma & Ct Brain
question: The empty delta sign is a radiological feature of which of the following conditions?

correctAnswer: B. Pseudoaneurysm of internal carotid artery
explanationHtml:
The given image is a digital subtraction angiogram (DSA), and it shows a pseudoaneurysm of the internal carotid artery.

A pseudoaneurysm (false aneurysm) refers to a contained rupture of the arterial wall, where blood escapes through a defect in the intima and media but is held by the adventitia or surrounding tissues, forming a sac. In contrast, a true aneurysm involves dilation of the artery with all three layers (intima, media, adventitia) intact but weakened.

It is identified by disruption of the normal vessel with formation of an outpouching that is contained by surrounding tissues rather than the true wall layers.

On imaging, it typically shows a narrow neck connecting the lumen to the sac, in contrast to the broad neck of a true aneurysm. Other features include irregularity of the wall, surrounding soft tissue stranding, or hemorrhage, especially in acute or subacute settings.

The right ICA injection anteroposterior view shows the neck of the pseudoaneurysm originating from the transverse segment of the cavernous portion of the ICA.


Carotico-cavernous fistula is characterized by the premature filling of the veins as shown in the image below:

Angiofibroma is characterised by a tumour blush. It is the radiological enhancement of a tumour that reveals opacification of the well-vascularized tumours.

Hemangioma can be differentiated from other vascular malformations by the presence of a well-circumscribed mass demonstrating intense tissue staining, usually in a lobular pattern.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Neurovascular Disorders, Trauma & Ct Brain
question: Based on the given image, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The NCCT image shows hyperdense foci in the region of the pineal gland and choroid plexuses (trigones), consistent with typical physiological calcification.

Physiological intracranial calcification is a common normal finding. Pineal calcification may be seen by around 20 years of age. Common sites include the pineal gland, choroid plexus, and basal ganglia.

Pineal calcification appears as a small, dense, midline calcific focus posterior to the third ventricle. It is symmetrical, sharply marginated, and clinically silent. Choroid plexus calcification is commonly seen in the trigones bilaterally. Basal ganglia calcification is usually seen as small punctate calcific foci in the globus pallidus and is more common with ageing, especially after about 30 years.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Neurovascular Disorders, Trauma & Ct Brain
question: A 35-year-old male undergoes NCCT head following polytrauma. An incidental finding is noted. What does this finding most likely represent?

explanationHtml:
Basal ganglia calcification is not a feature of hemochromatosis. The causes of pathological basal ganglia calcifications are :

  • Endocrinopathies: Hypoparathyroidism (primary or secondary), pseudohypoparathyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism
  • Vasculitis (e.g. SLE)
  • Mitochondrial disorders (e.g. Mitochondrial myopathy)
  • Infections: Brucellosis, TORCH, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), HIV
  • Other inherited disorders: Neuroferritinonpathy, Cockayne syndrome
  • Radiation
  • Chemotherapy
  • Carbon monoxide poisoning
  • Lead poisoning

The following image is a CT brain showing bilateral basal ganglia calcification:

question: Basal ganglia calcification can be seen on imaging of patients with all of the following conditions, except:

explanationHtml:
A neonate presenting with high-output cardiac failure and a large midline vascular structure on MRA is diagnostic of vein of Galen malformation (VGAM), which is caused due to persistent median prosencephalic vein (MPV).

VGAM is an arteriovenous fistula between intracranial arteries and the embryologic median prosencephalic vein, with distension of the MPV and downstream dural sinuses through a persistent falcine sinus. The resultant high-flow shunting leads to venous hypertension, communicating hydrocephalus, and high-output cardiac failure.

Two subtypes exist: choroidal, presenting in neonates with cardiac failure, and mural, presenting later with hydrocephalus. Even when hydrocephalus is present, the treatment of choice is endovascular embolization rather than CSF diversion.


Obstruction of the fourth ventricular outlets causes Dandy-Walker malformation, presenting with hydrocephalus and a cystic posterior fossa.


Herniation of cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum describes Chiari malformation.


Splitting of the arachnoid membrane results in an arachnoid cyst.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Neurovascular Disorders, Trauma & Ct Brain

options.text: Obstruction of the fourth ventricular outlets
Herniation of cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum

question: A 3-day-old neonate presents with high-output cardiac failure. His MRA brain is shown. What is the underlying anomaly responsible for this condition?

explanationHtml:
A cystic lesion in the suprasellar region with calcification is suggestive of craniopharyngioma.

Craniopharyngioma develops from embryologic remnants related to Rathke pouch. It is typically located around the sellar/suprasellar region, close to the pituitary stalk.

Craniopharyngiomas are classified into two types:

1. Adamantinomatous type: more common, seen in children (peak 5–15 years). It often presents as a large mixed cystic-solid suprasellar lesion with lobulated margins and internal septations. Calcification is present in ~90% of cases. The cystic part may appear bright on T1-weighted MRI because of proteinaceous contents. The enhancing portion represents the solid component.

Axial T1-weighted MRI (A) shows a large suprasellar mass with mixed cystic and solid contents. Axial CT (B) shows calcification within the mass.


2. Papillary type: less common, occurs in older adults (5th–6th decade), is solid for the most part, and calcifications are rare. It carries a better prognosis.

Contrast-enhanced CT (a) and sagittal T1-weighted MRI (b) show a solid-cystic suprasellar mass with posterior extension into the interpeduncular cistern.


Features favouring the adamantinomatous type over papillary type include pediatric age, T1 hyperintense cystic content, and calcification on CT.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: A cystic lesion in the suprasellar region with calcification is seen on the MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Lipoma of the corpus callosum shows bracket calcification on skull X-ray.

Intracranial lipomas are most commonly located in the midline and are commonly associated with congenital malformations such as agenesis/dysgenesis of the corpus callosum. Pericallosal lipomas are classified into the anteriorly located bulky tubulo-nodular type and the posteriorly located ribbon-like curvilinear type. Imaging is the mainstay in the diagnosis of intracranial lipoma.

The image below shows bracket calcification:

Tuberous sclerosis shows calcification of subependymal hamartomas in the wall of the ventricles.

Sturge-Weber syndrome shows tram track calcification.

Meningioma on X-ray shows calcification, hyperostosis and increased vascular markings; it is usually seen in the falx.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: Bracket calcification on skull X-Ray is seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The given MRI of the brain demonstrates a craniopharyngioma, which is a suprasellar tumour that arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch.

The two variants of craniopharyngioma are:

  • Adamantinomatous type (common in children): Predominantly solid with cystic components. Diagnostic features include compact lamellar keratin ("wet keratin") and areas of dystrophic calcification.
  • Papillary type (common in adults): Contains both solid sheets and papillae lined by well-differentiated non-keratinized squamous epithelium.

These tumours are usually large and heterogeneous, displaying solid and cystic components. The cysts contain a cholesterol-rich, thick brownish-yellow fluid that is compared to 'machine oil'.

Clinical features include headaches (most common), visual abnormalities - decreased acuity and bitemporal hemianopia, GH deficiency, growth failure, delayed sexual maturation due to pituitary hypofunction, and polyuria (central diabetes insipidus).

CT may show calcifications associated with the solid and cystic wall components, as shown in the image below:


MRI is the imaging modality of choice, with the cystic component appearing isointense to hyperintense
signal on T1 due to proteinaceous contents, hyperintense on T2, but may show variable signal. The solid component shows intense enhancement on T1. Given below is the MRI -T1 weighted image:


Craniopharyngiomas do not expand the pituitary fossa unless they become huge, which is a differentiating feature from pituitary macroadenomas.

Pituitary apoplexy is an acute clinical condition associated with the rapid expansion of the pituitary gland, which is evident on an MRI as enhancement around a non-enhancing infarcted centre.

Pituitary macroadenoma (with cystic degeneration or necrosis) shows indentation at the diaphragma sellae, giving rise to a snowman/figure of eight appearance/cottage loaf. Calcification is often absent. The image below shows the snowman appearance:


Rathke cleft cyst shows no solid or enhancing component on T1. Calcification is rare. It is unilocular, and the majority are completely or mostly intrasellar.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: What is the probable diagnosis based on the image of the scan given below?

explanationHtml:
The given axial T1 post-contrast MRI image shows the lesion involving the mid-falx cerebri and a hyperintense and homogeneously enhanced mass in the midline arising from the falx, suggestive of meningioma.

Meningiomas are extra-axial tumours, i.e., they arise outside the brain tissue. They develop from arachnoid cap (meningothelial) cells of the meninges and can occur anywhere along these coverings. They are more common in women, likely due to the presence of estrogen and progesterone receptors, and are associated with NF-2 gene mutation.

Typical meningiomas appear as dural-based masses isointense to grey matter on both T1 and T2 weighted imaging and demonstrate vivid contrast enhancement on both MRI and CT. CSF vascular cleft sign indicates that the mass is extra-axial. There is a cleft between the tumour and normal brain parenchyma.

The image below shows the CSF vascular cleft sign on a T2 weighted image:


Dural tail sign refers to tapering enhancement of the dura extending away from the base of the tumor on post-contrast MRI.

The image is an axial T1W spin-echo MRI of the brain with contrast enhancement showing dural tail (arrow) in meningioma.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: A 40-year-old woman presented with recurrent headaches. MRI shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Erosion is not an X-ray feature of meningioma.

Skull X-ray findings in meningioma are:

  • Local hyperostosis - Thickening of skull bone
  • Prominent frontal vascular markings - due to hypervascularity of the tumor
  • Calcification

The X-ray given below shows a calcified meningioma:
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: Which of the following findings would you not see on the skull X-ray of a patient with meningioma?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is glioblastoma. Post-contrast MRI in the case of glioblastoma multiforme demonstrates a large heterogeneous mass that crosses the corpus callosum into both frontal lobes.

They have a preferential spreading along the condensed white matter tracts, such as corticospinal tracts and the corpus callosum, and can give rise to the so-called 'butterfly glioma', involving the contralateral hemisphere. The term 'butterfly' refers to the symmetric wing-like extensions across the midline.

There is also evidence of a previous biopsy tract down to the lesion.

Glioblastoma is the second most common adult primary intracranial neoplasm. It carries the worst prognosis (WHO grade IV).
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: A 65-year-old man has been experiencing worsening headaches and new-onset seizures. MRI with contrast was done and is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the magnetic resonance (MR) spectroscopy showing a choline peak is diagnostic of glioma. NAA levels are decreased on MR spectroscopy in patients with glioma.

MR spectroscopy is a non-invasive means of obtaining metabolic information. The image below shows a normal MR spectroscopy.

Tuberculoma shows a lipid peak in MR spectroscopy.

In Canavan disease, there is a marked increase in N-acetyl aspartate. Its concentration decreases with insults to the brain such as a neoplasm, infarct, or abscess. N-acetyl aspartate (NAA), which is the most prominent resonance in a proton spectrum, is accepted as a normal neuronal functional marker.

Increased choline reflects increased membrane synthesis and/or an increased number of cells, as seen in lymphoma. However, lymphomas of the nervous system are very rare and seen in immunodeficient states like HIV.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: A 7-year-old girl presents with progressive ataxia and symptoms of increased intracranial tension, including headaches and vomiting. MR spectroscopy was acquired from the region of interest (ROI), marked by the red square. Based on the findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct match is1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c

Tumor Location
1. Acoustic schwannoma b. CP angle
2. Meningioma d. Parasagittal/convexity
3. Craniopharyngioma a. Suprasellar
4. Ependymoma c. Fourth ventricle

Vestibular schwannoma is the most frequent tumor of the cerebello-pontine angle. It develops from the vestibular component of the eighth cranial nerve. They classically show an "ice cream cone" appearance due to the intracanalicular component widening into a CP angle mass.

Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are characteristic of neurofibromatosis type 2.

CP angle tumours (Mnemonic- SAME ):

  • S: Schwannoma (8th nerve > 5th)
  • A: Aneurysm, arachnoid cyst
  • M: Meningioma, metastases
  • E: Epidermoid, ependymoma

The given image shows bilateral CP angle masses (vestibular schwannomas):


Meningiomas most commonly occur at parasagittal, falcine, and lateral convexity sites. They show a broad dural base, homogeneous enhancement, and a dural tail sign on MRI. Hyperostosis of adjacent bone may be seen.


Craniopharyngioma is the most common suprasellar tumor in children. It presents as a large, lobulated, cystic suprasellar mass with calcification in up to 90% of cases. Mixed solid-cystic morphology is typical.


Posterior fossa ependymomas arise as intraventricular masses that fill the fourth ventricle. A characteristic feature is their "plastic" nature, extension through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie into adjacent cisterns. Calcification and cysts are common.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question:
Match the following brain tumors with their most common location:

Tumor Location
1. Acoustic schwannoma a. Suprasellar
2. Meningioma b. CP angle
3. Craniopharyngioma c. Fourth ventricle
4. Ependymoma d. Parasagittal/convexity

explanationHtml:
The MRI shows bilateral enhancing masses at the cerebellopontine (CP) angles with extension into the internal auditory meati, the characteristic appearance of vestibular schwannomas. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are pathognomonic of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2).

Vestibular schwannomas arise from the superior vestibular division of the vestibulocochlear nerve. This tumour is the most common mass in the cerebellopontine(CP) angle. Its extracanalicular extension into the CP angle may create the "ice cream cone" appearance.

The presence of bilateral acoustic schwannoma is highly suggestive of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2). NF2 is associated with meningiomas and ependymomas in addition to schwannomas (MISME). Unlike NF1, cutaneous manifestations are rare.

MRI is the imaging modality of choice in assessing the possible vestibular schwannoma.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: The T1 weighted axial MRI of a patient presenting with bilateral hearing loss is shown below. Which of the following syndromes can be suspected in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Snowman appearance is seen in pituitary adenoma.

The image is a sagittal post-contrast MRI in a case of pituitary macroadenoma (>1 cm). Indentation at the diaphragma sellae gives rise to snowman/figure of eight appearance.

Pituitary adenoma is the most common tumor arising in the sellar region.

  • Pituitary microadenoma: < 1 cm in size
  • Pituitary macroadenoma: > 1 cm in size and usually extending superiorly.

Clinical features include bi-temporal hemianopia, headache, and vomiting. Skull X-ray finding is ballooning of the sella. MRI is the investigation of choice.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: Snowman or figure of eight appearance as shown in this MRI is seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The salt and pepper appearance is a highly sensitive and specific sign for head and neck paragangliomas.

Paragangliomas characteristically show a salt-and-pepper appearance on T1-weighted MRI due to high vascularity. The “pepper” represents multiple flow voids from high-flow intratumoral vessels, while the “salt” represents areas of slow flow or hemorrhage.

The given MRI axial T2 image shows punctate signal voids within the mass.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: In which of the following conditions is the 'salt and pepper' sign observed?

explanationHtml:
Expansion of the CSF space with contralateral cord displacement on MRI is seen in intradural extramedullary (IDEM) tumors.

Spinal tumors are classified by location into extradural (60%), intradural extramedullary (30%), and intramedullary (10%). MRI is the imaging technique of choice and helps distinguish compartments through direct visualization of the spinal cord and thecal sac.

IDEM tumors displace the cord to the opposite side, widening the ipsilateral CSF space. IDEM tumors include meningiomas, nerve sheath tumors (schwannomas, neurofibromas), and drop metastases.

Intramedullary tumors arise within the cord itself. Extradural tumors are the most common and may compress the cord or cauda equina from outside.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: MRI of a patient showed expansion of the CSF space with displacement of the spinal cord to the opposite side. This finding is seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Based on the given clinical scenario and radiologic finding, the most likely diagnosis is optic nerve sheath meningioma, a benign tumour arising from the arachnoid cap cells of the optic nerve sheath. It is most frequently seen in middle-aged women, with bilateral cases linked to neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF-2). Post-contrast CT or MRI show tram-track sign.

The post-contrast T1 weighted axial MRI image below shows a hypoattenuating optic nerve surrounded by the peripheral enhancement of the tumour(tram-track sign):


Optic nerve glioma is intrinsic to optic nerve, commonly seen in children, often associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1). It presents as fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve on imaging. The tram-track sign is useful in differentiating between optic nerve sheath meningioma and optic nerve gliomas.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: A 50 -year-old woman presents with a gradual loss of visual acuity in the right eye. A CT head post-contrast reveals thickening of the optic nerve-sheath complex with a tram-track appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The MRI brain showing a cyst with a dot sign (representing an eccentrically placed scolex within a parasitic cyst), is characteristic of the vesicular stage of neurocysticercosis.

Neurocysticercosis is the most common form of cysticercosis. This CNS infection typically occurs by ingestion of Taenia solium eggs through food or water contaminated with human faeces. The eggs hatch and develop into encysted larvae (cysticerci) in the brain and other tissues. It can affect the brain parenchyma, subarachnoid space and ventricles.

Clinically, it presents with seizures and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (headache, nausea, vomiting, vision changes), dizziness, ataxia, confusion or signs of meningeal irritation.

Parenchymal neurocysticercosis can be categorised into four stages -

  • Vesicular stage (viable larva) - thin-walled cyst, CSF-like signal, no enhancement, no oedema; scolex visible as eccentric hyperdense dot appearing as the "dot in hole" sign
  • Colloidal vesicular stage (degenerating larva) - cyst content becomes proteinaceous, appearing T1 and FLAIR hyperintense, ring enhancement with perilesional oedema
  • Granular nodular stage (dead larva, collapsing cyst) - thick enhancing walls with progressive surrounding oedema
  • Calcified nodular stage (inactive disease) - punctate calcification on CT with no enhancement, no oedema
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: An MRI brain performed during evaluation of an intracranial lesion demonstrates the following finding. What is the stage of the lesion?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, only primary CNS lymphoma may present as a solid homogeneous lesion without ring enhancement in a normal immunocompetent person.

The other conditions given — tuberculoma, toxoplasmosis, and brain abscess — all of these classically present as ring-enhancing lesions on imaging.

In India, neurocysticercosis and tuberculomas are the commonest causes of a ring-enhancing lesion on brain imaging.

Ring-enhancing brain lesions can be caused by the following conditions:

  • Neurocysticercosis
  • Tuberculoma
  • Cerebral abscess
  • Metastasis
  • Toxoplasmosis
  • Subacute infarct /hemorrhage/contusion
  • Demyelination (incomplete ring)
  • Tumefactive demyelinating lesion (incomplete ring)
  • Radiation necrosis
  • Postoperative change

The image below shows ring enhancement in brain abscess:


Note: Primary CNS lymphoma can show ring enhancement in immunocompromised or HIV-positive individuals. However, the other options — tuberculoma, toxoplasmosis, and brain abscess — classically present with ring enhancement, making lymphoma the best answer.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: Which of the following may not present with a ring-enhancing lesion on imaging?

explanationHtml:
The given MRI shows the cortical ribbon sign, which is seen in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). This sign refers to the ribbon-like signal hyperintensity of cerebral cortical gyri.

CJD is a human prion disease caused by conversion of normal cellular prion protein, PrPC, into the abnormal misfolded isoform, PrPSc, which accumulates in the brain. Clinically, it is characterised by rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, akinetic mutism, and cerebellar or visual disturbances.

Brain MRI is an important diagnostic tool in CJD. It may show hyperintensity of the cortex, basal ganglia, and/or thalamus on DWI/FLAIR sequences. The pattern of cortical hyperintensity is called cortical ribboning.

Subtypes of CJD and imaging features:

  • Sporadic CJD (sCJD): Most common form, accounts for ~85% of human prion disease cases
  • Variant CJD (vCJD): Linked to exposure to BSE/tainted beef. It tends to affect younger patients and often begins with psychiatric symptoms
  • Familial CJD (fCJD): Genetic prion disease due to PRNP mutation
  • Iatrogenic (iCJD): Caused by prion-contaminated materials in medical procedures

EEG shows characteristic periodic triphasic or polyphasic sharp wave complexes seen as spikes or spike-wave patterns (image below). CSF is predominantly normal but may show a positive assay for 14-3-3 protein.

Management is mainly supportive, as the disease is usually fatal within a year of the onset of symptoms.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: The given MRI finding is seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Craniopharyngiomas, ependymomas, oligodendrogliomas, and chordomas are associated with calcification.

Commonly calcified lesions are:

  • Oligodendrogliomas (90%)
  • Choroid plexus tumours
  • Ependymoma
  • Central neurocytoma
  • Meningioma
  • Craniopharyngioma
  • Teratoma
  • Chordoma

Commonly hemorrhagic lesions include:

  • Glioblastoma multiforme (grade 4 glioma)
  • Oligodendroglioma
  • Metastases: Melanoma, lung, and breast
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question:
Patients with which of the following conditions are likely to have calcified lesions on CT head?

  1. Craniopharyngioma
  2. Ependymoma
  3. Chordoma
  4. Glioblastoma multiforme
  5. Oligodendroglioma

explanationHtml:
The given clinical presentation of seizures, along with the above MRI findings of leptomeningeal enhancement and cortical atrophy, indicates a diagnosis of Sturge-Weber syndrome.

Sturge-Weber syndrome is a neurocutaneous disorder that is characterised by unilateral capillary malformation at the region of trigeminal supply known as port wine stain or nevus flammeus, ipsilateral diffuse cavernous hemangioma of the choroid and ipsilateral leptomeningeal hemangiomatosis, which causes seizures and intellectual disability.

MRI findings in Sturge-Weber syndrome include a pial angioma, which appears as diffuse pial enhancement of variable thickness. Other associated findings include enlargement of the choroid plexus on the same side and dilated transmedullary veins connecting the superficial and deep cerebral venous systems.

Image below shows a patient with Sturge-Weber syndrome with left facial port-wine stain and T1 post-contrast MRI demonstrating leptomeningeal enhancement (red arrows) and enlarged deep draining veins (yellow arrows).


The tram-track sign in the brain refers to the parallel calcification of the cerebral cortex best seen on CT (shown below):
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: The MRI of a patient who presented with seizures is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical triad of epilepsy, hypopigmented macules (ash-leaf spots), and facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) is classic for tuberous sclerosis. The CT image confirms the diagnosis by showing calcified subependymal hamartomatous nodules.

Classic radiological features of tuberous sclerosis include calcified subependymal nodules along the lateral ventricles, cortical tubers (increased T2/FLAIR signal), white matter radial migration lines, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) at the foramen of Monro that shows progressive growth and association with hydrocephalus. Extracranial findings include cardiac rhabdomyomas and renal angiomyolipomas.

The image given below shows calcified subependymal hamartomatous nodules:
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Cns Tumors, Infections & Neurocutaneous Syndromes
question: A 12-year-old boy with a history of infantile spasms presents with seizures. On examination, hypopigmented macules and facial angiofibromas were present. CT image is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The combination of bilateral renal cysts and a cerebellar cystic lesion with an enhancing mural nodule (hemangioblastoma) is classic for Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL).

Hemangioblastomas are tumours of vascular origin and occur in both patients with Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease and sporadically. On imaging, hemangioblastomas appear as a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule, which can mimic pilocytic astrocytoma (seen in NF1). However, the clinical context of bilateral renal cysts points to VHL rather than NF1.

Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease characterises the development of numerous benign and malignant tumours in different organs. It is associated with a mutation in the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3 (VHL has 3 letters: chromosome 3). They are WHO grade I tumours that can occur in the central nervous system.

Features of VHL include:

    • Multiple bilateral renal cysts and renal cell carcinoma (affects the majority of patients)
    • Pheochromocytoma
    • CNS hemangioblastoma - cerebellar and spinal
    • Retinal haemangioblastoma
    • Choroid plexus papilloma


Neurofibromatosis is an autosomal-dominant neurocutaneous syndrome of 2 types:

    • NF1 (neurofibromatosis 1) is also called Von Recklinghausen disease. It involves the NF1 gene on chromosome 17. It is an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by multiple café-au-lait macules and associated cutaneous neurofibromas.
    • In NF2, common findings include bilateral vestibular schwannomas and other nervous system tumors such as meningiomas, gliomas, schwannomas, and neurofibromas. Posterior subcapsular lenticular opacities may also be seen.

On MRI, extracanalicular extension of vestibular schwannomas into the cerebellopontine angle can lead to an "ice cream cone" appearance, as shown below:

Tuberous sclerosis is a multi-system neurocutaneous syndrome caused by the mutation of genes coding for hamartin (chromosome 9) and tuberin (chromosome 16), which leads to the formation of angiomyolipomas, cysts in kidneys, multiple hamartomas, giant cell astrocytomas, and cortical tubers. Skin manifestation includes facial angiofibroma (adenoma sebaceum), shagreen patch and confetti skin lesions. It can also be associated with renal angiomyolipoma and cardiac rhabdomyoma.

The CT image given below shows calcified subependymal hamartomatous nodules:

Sturge Weber syndrome is a neurocutaneous disorder(phakomatoses) that is characterized by unilateral capillary malformation at the region of trigeminal supply known as port wine stain or nevus flammeus, ipsilateral diffuse cavernous hemangioma of the choroid and ipsilateral leptomeningeal hemangiomatosis, which causes seizures and intellectual disability.

In Sturge-Weber syndrome, associated MRI findings may include enlargement of the ipsilateral choroid plexus and prominent transmedullary veins linking the superficial and deep venous drainage systems.

MRI shows leptomeningeal enhancement and CT shows intracranial calcification. The tram-track sign in the brain refers to the parallel calcification of the cerebral cortex.

question: A 45-year-old man with known bilateral renal cysts presents with headache and imbalance. MRI brain is shown below. Which syndrome is classically associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
The coronal T1-weighted MRI shows bilateral caudate nuclei atrophy with compensatory lateral ventricular dilatation (boxcar ventricles), consistent with Huntington’s disease.

Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by the expansion of CAG repeats in the HTT gene on chromosome 4.

It commonly presents with a combination of movement abnormalities, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Mri Brain In Neurodegenerative & Other Cns Disorders
question: A 50-year-old male presented with cognitive deficit, involuntary hand and finger movements, and muscle incoordination. The MRI image is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The axial FLAIR MRI shows the face of the giant panda sign, characterized by hypointensity of the superior colliculus with hyperintensity of the tegmentum and normal substantia nigra, consistent with Wilson’s disease.

Wilson’s disease is a rare, autosomal recessive disorder characterized by excessive deposition of free copper in tissues. It is due to a loss of function mutation of the ATP7B gene. It is also known as hepatolenticular degenerative disease.

MRI brain in advanced disease with neurological manifestations can show the following:

  • Giant panda face sign: Hypointense superior colliculus (chin and mouth of panda), the hyperintense area around the tegmentum of the midbrain (eyes of panda), and normal substantia nigra (ears of panda).
  • Bright claustrum sign: Thin rim of a hyperintense area in the claustrum with normal putamen.
  • Mercedes-Benz/trident sign: Hyperintense pons trisected by a hypointense line.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Mri Brain In Neurodegenerative & Other Cns Disorders
question: A 25-year-old man presented with personality changes, abnormal movements, jaundice and pruritus. MRI of the brain is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The diagnosis is multiple sclerosis.

In the given scenario, the symptoms of tingling and numbness of both limbs, along with the brain MRI showing ovoid hyperintense demyelinating plaques with their long axis perpendicular to the ventricular and callosal surface, known as Dawson fingers, characteristic of multiple sclerosis (MS).

MS is an autoimmune disease that primarily affects the white matter of the central nervous system, causing inflammation, demyelination, axonal damage and neurodegeneration. It predominantly affects women aged 20-40 years and typically follows a relapsing-remitting course, although progressive forms can also occur. The clinical presentation varies depending on the affected location, with common symptoms including paresthesia, visual disturbances (such as optic neuritis), motor weakness and ataxia. Dawson fingers are best visualized on FLAIR imaging and represent demyelination and oligodendrocyte loss, accompanied by astroglial scarring.

The following MRI image depicts Dawson fingers arranged at right angles along medullary veins (callososeptal location).
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Mri Brain In Neurodegenerative & Other Cns Disorders
question: A 35-year-old woman presented with tingling and numbness of upper and lower limb extremities. The MRI image is shown below. What is the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Multiple system atrophy type C
explanationHtml:
The hot cross bun sign on MRI is seen in patients with Multiple System Atrophy type C (MSA-C).

The hot cross bun sign is characterised by cruciform pontine hyperintensity due to selective neuronal loss of the transverse pontocerebellar fibres, which is most commonly observed in patients with MSA-C.

Multiple system atrophy (a type of synucleinopathy) is a neurodegenerative disorder with varying degrees of involvement of the basal ganglia and the olivopontocerebellar complex. Autonomic dysfunction is more severe and generalised, often presenting as orthostatic hypotension. MSA has been divided clinically into two forms according to the dominant non-autonomic symptoms:

  • MSA-C: Predominance of cerebellar symptoms (olivopontocerebellar atrophy)
  • MSA-P: Predominance of Parkinsonian signs and symptoms (striatonigral degeneration)

MRI is a valuable diagnostic adjunct, often revealing cerebellar and brainstem atrophy causing pontine hot cross bun sign.

The axial T2-weighted image at the level of middle cerebellar peduncles below shows the hot cross bun sign:

Multiple system atrophy-parkinsonian type (MSA-P) is characterised by atypical parkinsonism that is symmetrical and predominantly axial. MRI typically reveals hyperintensities along the lateral aspect of the putamina, and T2-weighted imaging may demonstrate hypointensity in the striatum due to iron deposition. Although not exclusive to MSA, the hot cross bun sign is more commonly seen in MSA-C than in MSA-P.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is an atypical Parkinsonian disorder. It classically causes slow eye movements, difficulty opening the eyelids, and limitation of vertical gaze, especially impaired downward gaze.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Mri Brain In Neurodegenerative & Other Cns Disorders
question: The hot cross bun sign on MRI would be seen in patients with which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The trident sign is an axial T2-weighted MRI finding seen in central pontine myelinolysis, the pontine variant of osmotic demyelination syndrome.

This condition typically follows rapid correction of severe hyponatremia. It causes non-inflammatory myelin injury in the central part of the pons.

On T2W MRI, the central pontine lesion appears hyperintense in a trident-like configuration. The peripheral regions of pons and corticospinal pathways are remain relatively preserved. The lesion is usually dark on T1 and may show restricted diffusion, appearing bright on DWI and dark on ADC.

Clinical features may include quadriparesis, bulbar weakness, dysarthria, and pseudobulbar palsy.

question: The trident sign on axial T2-weighted MRI is seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The loss of the swallow tail sign supports the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease.

The swallow tail sign describes the normal axial imaging appearance of nigrosome-1 within the substantia nigra on a high-resolution T2/SWI weighted MRI.


In Parkinson’s disease, loss of non-iron-containing neurons in the dorsolateral substantia nigra eliminates the signal split, causing absence of the swallow tail sign on SWI.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Mri Brain In Neurodegenerative & Other Cns Disorders
question: During MRI brain scan of a patient, the radiologist notices the absence of swallow tail appearance. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The likely diagnosis is Alexander's disease. The T2-weighted MRI findings show hyperintensity in the frontal white matter with bilateral symmetrical involvement, pointing towards Alexander disease.

Alexander disease is a type of dysmyelinating disease that typically progresses posteriorly to involve the parietal white matter and internal and external capsules, often accompanied by the formation of cysts.

Dysmyelinating diseases, or leukodystrophies, are inherited neurodegenerative disorders that affect the integrity of myelin in the brain and peripheral nerves.

Other examples of dysmyelinating diseases include:

  • Metachromatic leukodystrophy:
    • Late infantile (most common), juvenile, and adult types.
    • Symmetric confluent areas of T2 hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter.
    • Radiating T2-hypointense lines through the demyelinated deep white matter represent the sparing of the perivascular white matter. This results in the tigroid and leopard skin patterns when imaged in the long axis or cross-section, respectively.
  • X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy: Affects the white matter of the central nervous system, adrenal cortex, and testes.
  • Canavan disease: Spongiform leukodystrophy. Involvement of the subcortical U fibers, thalamus, and globus pallidus with relative sparing of the internal capsules and putamen. MR spectroscopy shows increase in NAA.
  • MELAS Syndrome: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes.

The following image shows the areas of hyperintensities noted in each of these conditions:

question: A T2 weighted MRI was done for a child who presented with delayed milestones. It showed hyperintensity in frontal white matter with bilateral and symmetrical involvement. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The eye of the tiger sign can be seen in Hallervorden-Spatz syndrome.

The 'eye of the tiger' sign on the T2-weighted MRI appears as bilateral symmetrical hyperintense signals in global pallidus (due to gliosis and spongiosis), surrounded by hypointense areas (due to abnormal accumulation of iron).

Hallervorden-Spatz syndrome or Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) is an autosomal recessive disorder causing involuntary spasticity and progressive dementia. It is a subset of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA).

It is also seen in Progressive supranuclear palsy, early-onset levodopa-responsive Parkinsonism, and cortical-basal ganglionic degeneration.

The image below depicts the eye of the tiger sign on T2-weighted MRI:

question: Eye of tiger sign on MRI is seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
This patient's clinical features and T2W MRI of the brain showing periventricular ovoid hyperintense lesions oriented perpendicular to lateral ventricles, called Dawson's fingers, are characteristic of multiple sclerosis.

Multiple sclerosis(MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system characterized by inflammation, multiple demyelinating plaques, and relapsing and remitting symptoms.

Common features include visual disturbances (optic neuritis), limb weakness, spasticity, paresthesia, and bladder dysfunction.

MRI is the investigation of choice. The classic finding is Dawson’s fingers, which refer to periventricular ovoid plaques oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles along medullary veins, best seen on sagittal FLAIR. Plaques are also seen in the corpus callosum, juxtacortical white matter, infratentorial region, optic pathway, and spinal cord. Active plaques enhance with gadolinium; chronic plaques may appear as T1 black holes.

Spinal cord lesions are typically present at multiple spine levels, are short-segment, cervical, and involve less than half the cord cross-section.


Moyamoya disease shows a "puff of smoke" appearance on the MR angiography findings as shown in the image below:


Metachromatic leukodystrophy shows tigroid and leopard skin patterns on T2-weighted MRI, as shown below:


Progressive supranuclear palsy shows a hummingbird sign on MRI, as shown below:

question: A 30-year-old woman has been experiencing intermittent visual disturbances and episodes of difficulty walking over the past few months. Neurological examination reveals spasticity in the lower limbs and hyperreflexia. T2W MRI of the brain shows periventricular ovoid hyperintense lesions oriented perpendicular to lateral ventricles. Which of the radiological findings is most characteristic of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The axial T1-weighted MRI reveals a molar tooth sign at the superior cerebellar peduncle level. This, combined with the clinical presentation, indicates Joubert syndrome.

This condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. It is characterized by cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and manifests with hypotonia, tachypnea, abnormal eye movements, developmental delay, and ataxia.

The molar tooth sign results from abnormal development of the midbrain, with a deep interpeduncular fossa and thick, horizontally oriented superior cerebellar peduncles that fail to cross normally.

On axial MRI, this configuration gives the midbrain the appearance of a molar tooth. The fourth ventricle may also appear abnormally shaped, resembling a bat wing.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Mri Brain In Neurodegenerative & Other Cns Disorders
question: A mother brought her 7-month-old infant with concerns of abnormal eye movements and developmental delay. MRI was done and is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given case of a neonate with the image of T1 weighted MRI showing a figure of eight appearance, which is diagnostic of lissencephaly.

Lissencephaly is a neuronal migration disorder occurring between the 8th and 14th weeks of gestation.It leads to absent or poorly developed gyri and sulci, a thickened cortex, and shallow, widened Sylvian fissures, producing the characteristic imaging appearance. Associated anomalies may include agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum or septum pellucidum.

The following image shows the figure of eight sign of lissencephaly:


Holoprosencephaly is a developmental disorder of the brain that results from the defective formation of the prosencephalon and inadequate induction of forebrain structures. The pancake brain sign represents the appearance of the cerebral parenchyma in the case of alobar holoprosencephaly.


The presence of unilateral or bilateral clefts within the cerebral hemispheres that connect the outer surface of the brain with the lateral ventricles due to an abnormality of morphogenesis is called schizencephaly.


Porencephaly is an extremely rare cephalic disorder involving encephalomalacia. It is a neurological disorder of the central nervous system characterized by cysts or cavities within the cerebral hemisphere.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Mri Brain In Neurodegenerative & Other Cns Disorders
question: A neonate presents with seizures, poor feeding, and hypotonia. The MRI brain is shown below. Identify the congenital brain anomaly.

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is Dandy-Walker malformation.

The CT image shows a large cystic area that occupies the posterior aspect of the posterior fossa, communicating directly with the fourth ventricle. No normal vermis can be identified, with a small vermian remnant appearing displaced and rotated superiorly.

In Dandy-Walker malformation, the posterior fossa is enlarged. The lateral venous sinuses and tentorium are positioned higher than normal. The CT findings, along with the clinical features, are consistent with Dandy-Walker malformation.


Arnold Chiari malformation occurs due to the displacement of the brainstem and cerebellum downwards through the foramen magnum.
Chiari I malformation is characterised by herniation of the cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum. It is seen in adults, often associated with syringomyelia.

The image of Arnold Chiari malformation type 1 is given below:


Chiari II malformation is characterised by herniation of the cerebellar vermis, brainstem, and fourth ventricle through the foramen magnum. It is seen in infants, almost always associated with myelomeningocele.


The MR angiography in the vein of Galen malformation shows an enlarged midline venous structure, with multiple arteriovenous communications leading to aneurysmal dilatation. The image below shows the malformation:


Joubert syndrome is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder. The 'molar tooth sign', which refers to the prominence of superior cerebellar peduncles at the midbrain-hindbrain junction on axial MRI of the brain, is a pathognomonic finding in this condition. The image given below shows the molar tooth sign.

question: A mother brings her 2-month-old infant with complaints of irritability and seizures. On examination, the infant has a bulging fontanelle and macrocephaly.MRI was done, which shows the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The best plane for measurement of the volume of the hippocampus is the coronal plane, angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus in MRI, which is represented by the image marked B.

Coronal MRI is taken perpendicular to the long axis of the temporal horn can be used to measure:

  • Volume of hippocampus - measured in Alzheimer's disease and mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
  • Medial temporal lobe atrophy (MTA)
