question: Which of the following is the best plane for the measurement of volume of hippocampus?

explanationHtml:
The brain MRI shows Dawson fingers, which are characteristic of multiple sclerosis. Spinal cord lesions in MS are typically short-segment, peripheral/eccentric, and involve less than half of the cord cross-sectional area. They are most commonly seen in the cervical cord.

Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system characterised by inflammation, multiple demyelinating plaques, and relapsing and remitting symptoms. Dawson fingers are findings on brain MRI showing ovoid hyperintense lesions perpendicular to the ventricular surface, corresponding to areas of demyelination.

Sagittal T2 MRI showing short-segment peripheral cord lesion in MS:


In Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD), spinal cord lesions are longitudinally extensive (>3 segments), central in location, and involve more than half of the cord cross-sectional area. They may show T1 hypointensity. NMOSD is associated with anti-AQP4 antibodies.

Sagittal T2 MRI showing longitudinally extensive central cord lesion (>3 segments) in NMOSD:


In acute transverse myelitis, lesions involve more than two-thirds of the cord cross-section with cord swelling. ATM presents with weakness, sensory loss, and autonomic dysfunction, and may be linked to infections or autoimmune conditions. Transverse myelitis may be idiopathic or may occur as part of inflammatory demyelinating disorders such as NMOSD.

Sagittal MRI showing a swollen T2-hyperintense cord lesion.:


Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is a monophasic condition that usually follows an infection. Cord lesions are large and confluent, extend over multiple segments, cause cord swelling, and can involve grey matter, white matter, or both. Brain MRI in ADEM shows large, patchy, poorly marginated white matter lesions with frequent thalamic and basal ganglia involvement, unlike MS where periventricular lesions are seen.

Sagittal MRI of spine (left) and brain (right) showing large confluent lesion in a patient with ADEM after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
lessonTitle: Neuroimaging Mri Brain In Neurodegenerative & Other Cns Disorders
question: A 35-year-old woman presents with tingling and numbness in the upper and lower limbs. Her brain MRI is shown below. What is the expected characteristic pattern of spinal cord involvement in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical features and x-ray showing a J-shaped sella and a thickened calvaria are suggestive of Hurler syndrome.

Mucopolysaccharidoses show a group of skeletal changes called dysostosis multiplex. The radiological features of dysostosis multiplex include:

  • Broad, poorly modelled tubular bones -anterolateral ribs, medial clavicles
  • Localized bone narrowing in posterior ribs, proximal metacarpals, and iliac bases
  • Elongated, J-shaped sella turcica; possible scaphocephalic skull
  • Thoracolumbar gibbus (kyphosis)
  • Inferior projection of anterior vertebral bodies
  • Increased convexity of vertebral endplates


Hurler syndrome is also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I). It occurs due to a defect in α-L iduronidase, leading to the accumulation of heparan sulphate and dermatan sulphate. Apart from the skeletal abnormalities, the patients show clinical features like corneal clouding, intellectual disability, coarse facial features, visceromegaly .

Sanfilippo syndrome (MPS III) is primarily a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, with absent corneal clouding.

Gaucher’s disease presents with hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bone crises, while the cornea remains clear and the pattern of skeletal involvement differs from that seen in mucopolysaccharidoses.

Morquio syndrome (MPS IV) is characterized by marked skeletal dysplasia, including short-trunk dwarfism, with intelligence generally preserved. Corneal clouding may occur but is usually mild.
question: An 18-month-old child is brought to the pediatrician with the history of distension of abdomen and delayed mental development. On examination, the cornea is cloudy and radiograph of the skull is given below. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The structure marked in the image is the internal auditory canal.

The IAM carries five structures: facial nerve, nervus intermedius, cochlear nerve, superior vestibular nerve, and inferior vestibular nerve. It is divided by a horizontal ridge (falciform crest) into upper and lower parts.

In the superior compartment, the facial nerve and nervus intermedius lie anteriorly, and the superior vestibular nerve lies posteriorly. They are separated by Bill’s bar.

In the inferior compartment, the cochlear nerve lies anteriorly and the inferior vestibular nerve posteriorly.


Vestibular schwannoma arises in the IAM and extends into the cerebellopontine angle, producing the classic ice-cream cone appearance on MRI.

External auditory canal (EAC) is an S-shaped, 24mm long. Outer third is cartilaginous and contains hair, ceruminous glands, and fissures of Santorini. Inner two-thirds is bony and contains no glands, narrows at the isthmus and may have foramen of Huschke anteriorly.

The vestibular aqueduct is a bony canal that extends from the vestibule (specifically the medial wall near the saccule) to the posterior cranial fossa, housing the endolymphatic duct and terminating in the endolymphatic sac.

The various structures of the petrous bone visible on a CT are shown below:
question: Identify the structure marked by the arrow in the image given below.

explanationHtml:
The position of the head, as shown in the image, is placed to obtain a Waters' view X-ray of paranasal sinuses.

Waters' view (also known as the Occipitomental view or nose-chin position) is a radiographic view, where an X-ray beam is angled at 37° to the orbitomeatal line. The rays are passed from behind the head and are perpendicular to the radiographic plate.

The maxillary sinus is viewed best in this view. Frontal and ethmoidal sinuses can also be visualised. The sphenoid sinus can be seen in the Waters' view with an open mouth.
question: A patient is made to place his head in a position as shown in the image. Which of the following X-ray views is obtained?

explanationHtml:
Lyre sign is seen on a carotid angiogram in the presence of a carotid body tumor.

Carotid body tumors are mostly benign tumors located at the common carotid bifurcation. On the carotid angiogram, they appear as enhancing lesions that splay and displace the internal and external carotid arteries. The splaying of ECA-ICA is called Lyre's sign, as shown below:


Carotid body tumors are neurogenic tumors or paragangliomas arising from the chemoreceptor cells of the carotid bulb, hence called chemodectoma. Familial carotid body tumors are linked to mutations involving the SDH gene. The pathophysiology is believed to be chronic hypoxia in high-altitude states that stimulates tumorigenesis, which is why the tumor is commonly seen in individuals from hilly areas.

Clinical features are a painless, slow-growing, pulsatile lateral neck mass in the 5th decade, firm in consistency moves from side to side but not up to down. The tonsil may be displaced medially. A bruit may be associated with the tumor.

The image below shows the musical instrument Lyre, after which this sign is named -
question: Lyre sign is seen in:

explanationHtml:
The CT shows Phelps sign (erosion of the bony plate between the carotid canal and jugular fossa) which is seen in glomus jugulare.

Glomus tumors are the commonest benign tumors involving the middle ear.

Glomus jugulare develops from the jugular bulb and can extend into the hypotympanum and jugular foramen. When affected, the lower cranial nerves (IX to XII) may cause neurological deficits.

On CT, the tumour presents as a soft-tissue mass centred on the jugular bulb, frequently expanding the pars vasorum of the jugular foramen and extending superiorly into the hypotympanum and middle ear cavity. They cause irregular bone erosion around the jugular fossa. Phelp's sign refers to erosion of the carotico-jugular spine, causing the carotid canal and jugular bulb to appear to merge.

On CECT, the tumor shows intense contrast enhancement due to their extremely vascular nature. The internal jugular vein is frequently involved and the mass may narrow or obstruct the IJV at the jugular bulb causing the vein to show changes suggestive of thrombosis on CT and MRI.

question: A 55-year-old man presents with vertigo and pulsatile tinnitus. The CT temporal bone is shown below. What is the radiological sign seen, and the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given image is that of Caldwell's view.

Caldwell view is obtained with the nose and forehead placed against the image receptor, and the X-ray beam angled 15–20° caudally. It is mainly used to assess the frontal sinus.
question: Identify the X-ray view in the given image:

explanationHtml:
The given manometry findings are suggestive of distal esophageal spasm. Corkscrew esophagus is the most likely finding on a barium swallow study in this condition.

In distal esophageal spasm, the manometry demonstrates normal to strong esophageal contractions (DCI > 450 mmHg·s·cm) with normal lower esophageal sphincter relaxation (normal IRP) and preserved coordinated peristalsis.

The image below shows the corkscrew appearance.

Although DES may present as a corkscrew or rosary bead esophagus on barium swallow, manometry remains the gold standard for diagnosis. On manometry, these contractions are repetitive, simultaneous, and of high amplitude, but normal peristalsis is preserved between the episodes with normal LES relaxation.

Diffuse esophageal spasm (DES) is a hypermotility disorder caused by spontaneous, abnormal contractions seen primarily affecting the distal two-thirds of the esophagus, with normal deglutitive lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation. This condition is seen most often in females.

Patients typically present with dysphagia for both solids and liquids, retrosternal non-cardiac chest pain, and symptoms such as heartburn, regurgitation, and the sensation of food being stuck in the throat.

question:
A 52-year-old woman presents with intermittent chest pain and dysphagia to both solids and liquids. High-resolution esophageal manometry reports are as follows. What is the most likely finding on a barium swallow study?

Distal Contractile Integral (DCI) > 450 mmHg·s·cm

Normal Integrated Relaxation Pressure (IRP)

Preserved peristalsis

correctAnswer: A. 1- Normal esophageal motility, 2 - Achalasia cardia type I
explanationHtml:
The manometry findings are consistent with 1- Normal esophageal motility; 2- Achalasia cardia type I.

Esophageal manometry is displayed as a colour-coded plot, where the X-axis represents time and the Y-axis represents the distance from the upper esophageal sphincter (UES). Pressure changes are mapped using a colour spectrum from low to high pressure.

At rest, both the UES and lower esophageal sphincter (LES) maintain baseline tone to prevent air entry and reflux, shown as intermediate pressure colours. The scale typically ranges from blue (no pressure), green (low), yellow, orange, red, to purple (highest pressure).

During a normal swallow, the UES relaxes first, appearing as a blue zone. A coordinated peristaltic wave then propagates down the esophagus, seen as a sequential rise in pressure (green to red), reflecting smooth bolus transit through space and time.

When the bolus reaches the LES, it relaxes (blue), allowing entry into the stomach; this represents normal peristaltic activity.

The image below shows the normal esophageal manometry.

Achalasia cardia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the absence of esophageal peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) in response to swallowing.

The different types of Achalasia as defined by the Chicago Classification are:

Type I achalasia (classic): Median IRP >15 mmHg with 100% failed peristalsis, premature contractions with DCI <450 mmHg·s·cm. No panesophageal pressurization or spastic activity is seen.

The image below shows Type I achalasia (Classic achalasia). It shows an absence of peristaltic colour progression along the esophagus, appearing largely uniform without the normal sequential green-to-red wave, reflecting complete failure of peristalsis.

Type II achalasia: Median IRP >15 mmHg with 100% failed peristalsis and panesophageal pressurization in ≥20% of swallows.

The image below shows Type II achalasia. It shows a diffuse, simultaneous rise in pressure across the esophageal body, seen as a uniform panesophageal colour band rather than a propagated wave, indicating pressurization throughout the esophagus.

Type III achalasia (spastic achalasia): Median IRP >15 mmHg with absent normal peristalsis and premature/spastic distal contractions in ≥20% of swallows, with DCI >450 mmHg·s·cm.

The image below shows Type III achalasia (spastic achalasia). It shows intermittent, non-propagated high-pressure segments appearing as irregular red/purple spikes at different points in time and space, reflecting spastic distal contractions without normal peristaltic coordination.

question: The following high-resolution esophageal manometry tracings are shown below. Which of the following best identifies the manometric tracings?

explanationHtml:
A patient with the given history and barium swallow findings of irregular narrowing and mucosal destruction are suggestive of carcinoma of the esophagus.

Esophageal carcinoma is more common in men, with tobacco use and alcohol being the strongest risk factors. The squamous cell carcinoma variant usually affects the upper 2/3rd, and the adenocarcinoma variant usually affects the lower 1/3rd of the esophagus. Clinical features include progressive dysphagia (most common), regurgitation of food, vomiting, odynophagia and weight loss.

On barium swallow, carcinoma of the oesophagus presents with irregular narrowing and ulceration with shouldered margins of the oesophagus. Flexible endoscopy with biopsy is preferred for confirmation of diagnosis. Contrast-enhanced CT and PET can be used to assess distant metastasis. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) is the investigation of choice to assess tumor invasion and lymph node metastasis.

Below is an image of a double contrast barium swallow in a patient with esophageal carcinoma, showing irregular narrowing distally with shouldered margins.

Diffuse esophageal spasm results in the corkscrew appearance of the esophagus on barium study.

Esophageal leiomyoma appears as a smooth, semilunar filling defect on barium swallow. it is seen as a discrete ovoid mass that is well outlined by barium.

Esophageal webs occur in the upper and middle esophagus as a thin membrane that can be identified by the translucent part on contrast radiology.

question: A 56-year-old female patient presented with progressive dysphagia for solids, loss of weight, and loss of appetite. A barium swallow done is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario, along with a barium swallow demonstrating an esophageal web in the upper esophagus, is suggestive of Plummer-Vinson syndrome.

Plummer–Vinson syndrome (also called Paterson–Brown–Kelly syndrome) classically occurs in middle-aged women with iron-deficiency anemia and is characterized by the triad of:

  • Dysphagia
  • Iron-deficiency anemia
  • Upper esophageal (post-cricoid) webs

It is clinically important because it is a premalignant condition associated with an increased risk of post-cricoid hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

The image below shows the triad of Plummer–Vinson syndrome.

Esophageal webs appear as thin mucosal projections inside the esophagus, formed by a core of fibrovascular tissue covered by epithelium. They are usually limited to the proximal esophagus and may cause obstruction. They are associated with:

  • Plummer–Vinson syndrome
  • GERD (Gastroesophageal reflux disease)
  • GVHD (Graft versus host disease)
  • Bullous diseases of the skin

The image below depicts a barium swallow showing a concentric web in the upper esophagus on a lateral view.

Whereas Schatzki’s ring is a thin submucosal circumferential ring in the lower esophagus at the squamocolumnar junction. It is often associated with a hiatal hernia. The patient develops intermittent swallowing difficulty associated with the rapid consumption of coarse meals.

The image below is a barium study showing the Schatzki ring located at the gastroesophageal junction, suggestive of hiatus hernia.

question: A young woman presented to the OPD with dysphagia and regurgitation of food. She was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia 6 months ago. A barium swallow was done and is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The mucosal ring at the squamocolumnar junction of the distal esophagus is a B-ring.

Distal esophageal rings are frequent findings on barium contrast X-ray studies. They are of two types:

  • B-ring - It occurs at the squamocolumnar junction or gastroesophageal junction. It is lined with squamous epithelium above and columnar epithelium below.
  • A-ring - It occurs above the B-ring, i.e., a few centimetres proximal to the gastroesophageal junction. It represents a physiological contraction of esophageal smooth muscle covered by mucosa. A-rings are usually asymptomatic (option B).

Schatzki ring, also called Schatzki-Gary ring, is a symptomatic narrow B-ring occurring in the distal esophagus. It is usually associated with a hiatus hernia.

The image below is a barium study showing the Schatzki ring located at the gastroesophageal junction.

Esophageal webs usually occur in the upper (post-cricoid) esophagus as thin, eccentric, semi-circumferential membranes. They consist of fibrovascular tissue covered by epithelium.

The barium swallow image below demonstrates an esophageal web in a patient with Plummer–Vinson syndrome, seen as a thin translucent membrane within the esophagus.

Esophageal stricture is a persistent narrowing of the esophagus, commonly caused by corrosives (most common), peptic injury, foreign body, surgery, radiotherapy, congenital factors, tuberculosis, or drugs (e.g., tetracycline).

The image below shows the esophageal stricture.

question: The mucosal ring at the squamocolumnar junction of the distal esophagus is ______.

explanationHtml:
The diagnosis is Zenker diverticulum, and the study shown is a barium swallow.

On a barium swallow, a Zenker diverticulum appears as a midline posterior outpouching from the distal pharynx at the pharyngoesophageal junction, typically at the C5–C6 level. The pouch may be transient and is best seen during swallowing, especially on the lateral view.

The barium swallow image given below shows the Zenker's diverticulum.

Barium sulfate is the preferred contrast for evaluating Zenker's diverticulum. Because it is often associated with gastroesophageal reflux and hiatal hernia, the distal esophagus should also be assessed.

It is caused by herniation of the mucosa and submucosa through the space between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus. This space is known as Killian's triangle, which is a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor in the posterior pharyngeal wall.

It is a pulsion diverticulum, formed due to increased intraluminal pressure forcing the mucosa and submucosa to herniate.

Note: Killian-Jamieson diverticulum is an outpouching from the lateral wall of the upper cervical esophagus.

The Cervical X-ray AP view given below shows the Killian–Jamieson diverticulum.

explanationHtml:
The given image is a barium swallow X-ray showing a feline esophagus suggestive of reflux esophagitis.

The feline esophagus is also known as esophageal shiver. These folds are 1-2 mm thick and run horizontally around the entire circumference of the esophageal lumen. It is thought to be due to the contraction of the muscularis mucosae of the esophagus. This results in the shortening of the esophagus and the bunching up of the mucosa in the lumen.

The appearance is almost always associated with active gastroesophageal reflux. The findings are transient, seen following reflux and not during swallowing. The appearance is confined to the distal two-thirds of the thoracic esophagus.

It can also be seen in hiatus hernia and eosinophilic esophagitis. Here, the folds are permanent and associated with strictures.

question: Which of the following investigations is shown in the radiograph?

explanationHtml:
The given barium meal study is showing string sign and mushroom sign is suggestive of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS).

Congenital (infantile) hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a condition caused by hypertrophy of the circular pyloric muscles of the stomach, leading to gastric outlet obstruction. It typically presents between 2 and 6 weeks of age with progressive, forceful, non-bilious vomiting immediately after feeding. This results in hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis due to the loss of fluid, hydrogen, and chloride ions.

On examination, a firm, movable, olive-shaped mass is palpable in the epigastrium, often accompanied by visible gastric peristalsis. Ultrasound is the investigation of choice for this condition.

Barium study signs in Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis:

  • String sign – Thin streak of barium passing through a narrowed pyloric canal
  • Double/triple track sign – Crowding of mucosal folds within the pyloric canal
  • Diamond sign (Twining recess) – Transient triangular cleft in the mid-pyloric canal with apex pointing inferiorly
  • Beak sign – Tapering streak of barium directed toward the pylorus due to antral impression
  • Mushroom / Kirklin / Umbrella sign – Indentation of the base of the duodenal bulb by the hypertrophied pylorus
  • Caterpillar sign – Visible gastric hyperperistaltic waves
  • Shoulder sign – Rounded indentation caused by the hypertrophied pyloric muscle

Given below is the barium meal study showing the string sign and the mushroom sign:

Ultrasonographic (USG) signs in Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis:

  • Cervix sign – Hypertrophied pylorus resembling the uterine cervix
  • Antral nipple sign – Redundant pyloric mucosa protruding into the gastric antrum

USG findings are shown below.

question: Given below is a barium meal study of a child. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The depth of the gastric carcinoma is assessed by endoluminal ultrasound.

Endoluminal ultrasonography allows visualization of the stomach wall as five distinct layers, which enables accurate evaluation of tumour penetration depth.

Endoluminal ultrasonography and laparoscopic ultrasonography outperform other available imaging methods in evaluating the extent of gastric cancer before surgery.

The image below shows an endoluminal ultrasound.

Abdominal ultrasound is less effective in identifying gastric pathologies. Barium meal radiology is now used less frequently due to advances in more sensitive diagnostic tools like endoscopy and CT imaging with oral contrast, replacing contrast radiology in investigating gastric malignancies.

Preoperative staging is performed with contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the abdomen and pelvis. The most important prognostic indicators in gastric cancer are lymph node involvement and depth of tumor invasion. However, computed tomography is inferior to endoluminal ultrasonography for assessing the depth of local tumour invasion in gastric carcinoma.

Laparoscopy is routine in the assessment of gastric cancer. However, the main limitation is in the evaluation of posterior extension, where CT and endoluminal ultrasound can provide this information.

explanationHtml:
The given abdominal x-ray of the neonate shows the double bubble sign, which is suggestive of duodenal atresia.

On abdominal X-ray, the double bubble sign represents the dilatation of the stomach and proximal duodenum. This can often be detected prenatally via ultrasound, but if missed, neonates typically present with bilious vomiting shortly after birth, as the obstruction is usually distal to the ampulla of Vater.

Causes of the double bubble sign are congenital obstructions like duodenal atresia (associated with Down syndrome), midgut volvulus, and external compression of the duodenum.

Duodenal atresia is the blockade of the duodenum due to the failure of recanalisation during embryonic development from its solid cord stage, leaving the duodenum partially or completely obstructed. It is often associated with trisomy 21/Down syndrome, prematurity, maternal polyhydramnios, cardiac malformations, and malformations of the hepatobiliary system.

question:
An abdominal x-ray of a neonate admitted to NICU is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?

NICU- Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

explanationHtml:
The above X-ray clearly shows the presence of subdiaphragmatic free gas in the right upper quadrant, indicating pneumoperitoneum.

Pneumoperitoneum refers to the presence of free gas within the peritoneal cavity outside the gastrointestinal tract. The most common cause is perforation of a hollow viscus. Gastric and duodenal perforations may occur in longstanding peptic ulcer disease, while intestinal perforations can result from ischemia, inflammation, diverticular disease, or obstruction.

Other causes include iatrogenic procedures, penetrating trauma, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and peritoneal dialysis.

Signs of pneumoperitoneum:

  • Bowel-related signs
    • Double wall sign/Rigler's sign/gas-relief sign- visualization of air on both the inner and outer aspects of the bowel wall
    • Telltale triangle sign/triangle sign - presence of a triangular-shaped pocket of air trapped between three adjacent bowel loops
  • Peritoneal ligament-related signs
    • Football sign- Large-volume pneumoperitoneum creates a football-shaped lucency across the abdomen
    • Falciform ligament sign- Free peritoneal air renders the falciform ligament visible on radiographs
    • Lateral umbilical ligament sign/inverted "V" sign- Air outlines the lateral umbilical ligament
    • Urachus sign - Air outlines the urachus
  • Right upper quadrant signs
    • Fissure for ligamentum teres sign- Air outlines the ligamentum teres
    • Hepatic edge sign- Cigar-shaped free-air pocket in the subhepatic region. It tracks superomedially following the contours of the liver
    • Lucent liver sign - Reduction of hepatic radiodensity due to accumulation of free gas anterior to the liver
    • Morison's pouch sign / Doge cap sign - Triangular/ crescentic gas lucency bound by the 11th rib
    • Periportal free gas sign
  • Diaphragmatic/Subphrenic signs
    • Cupola sign (supine radiograph)- free air beneath the central tendon of the diaphragm
    • Continuous diaphragm sign (erect radiograph)- air outlines the central diaphragm beneath the heart, making it visible across the midline

The X-Ray given below demonstrates the continuous diaphragm sign.

Free intraperitoneal gas is also detectable under the hemidiaphragm on an erect chest X-ray, as given below.

The CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis shows free intraperitoneal gas, which is suggestive of pneumoperitoneum.

question: From the X-ray given, pick out the probable diagnosis:

explanationHtml:
The given radiograph in a patient with pneumoperitoneum depicts Cupola sign.

Cupola sign refers to dependent air that rises within the abdominal cavity of the supine patient to accumulate underneath the central tendon of the diaphragm in the midline. It is seen as lucency overlying the lower thoracic vertebral bodies. The superior border is well-defined, but the inferior margin is not.

In the below radiograph, the arrows are pointing to the Cupola sign seen in the pneumoperitoneum.

Signs of pneumoperitoneum:

  • Bowel-related signs
    • Double-wall sign/Rigler's sign/gas-relief sign
    • Telltale triangle sign/triangle sign - A triangle of gas formed between three loops of the bowel or between the abdominal wall and two loops of the bowel.
  • Peritoneal ligament-related signs
    • Football sign
    • Falciform ligament sign
    • Lateral umbilical ligament sign/inverted "V" sign - Air outlines the lateral umbilical ligament
    • Urachus sign - Air outlines the urachus
  • Right upper quadrant signs
    • Cupola sign
    • Fissure for ligamentum teres sign- Air outlines the ligamentum teres
    • Hepatic edge sign - Cigar-shaped free-air pocket in the subhepatic region. It tracks superomedially following the contours of the liver
    • Lucent liver sign - Reduction of hepatic radiodensity due to accumulation of free gas anterior to the liver
    • Morison's pouch sign/Doge cap sign - Triangular/ crescentic gas lucency bound by the 11th rib
    • Periportal free gas sign.

The image below shows various signs seen in pneumoperitoneum.

question: The radiograph of a patient suspected to have pneumoperitoneum is shown below. Which of the following signs is seen here?

explanationHtml:
The given X-ray shows air under the diaphragm, indicative of pneumoperitoneum, which is not caused by acute intestinal obstruction.

Causes of pneumoperitoneum include:

  • Bowel perforation:
    • Gastric and posterior duodenal perforations in long-standing cases of peptic ulcers, ischemic bowel, and necrotizing enterocolitis
    • Small bowel perforation secondary to trauma or penetrating injuries
  • Post-surgery/laparoscopy
  • Causes other than perforation are:
    • Chilaiditi syndrome - the intestine is seen between the liver and diaphragm, giving a false impression of free air (pseudopneumoperitoneum)
    • Sub-phrenic abscess
    • Postoperatively, air may be present in the abdomen for up to 7 days

An intestinal obstruction would show multiple dilated loops on X-ray with possible air-fluid levels. Only when the obstruction becomes severe, and there is a perforation, does pneumoperitoneum occur.

The image given below is an abdominal radiograph showing multiple dilated loops with air-fluid levels suggestive of intestinal obstruction.

The image below shows Chilaiditi’s sign, characterized by the presence of gas at the right colic angle interposed between the liver and the right hemidiaphragm, as seen in Chilaiditi’s syndrome.
lessonTitle: Gi Imaging Upper Gi Disorders & Pneumoperitoneum
question: All of the following could be the cause of the following X-ray finding except:

explanationHtml:
The given chest X-ray image depicts Chilaiditi sign, characterized by the anterior interposition of the colon between the liver and the right hemidiaphragm, which can mimic air under the diaphragm, leading to pseudo-pneumoperitoneum.

Chilaiditi sign is typically an incidental finding on imaging and is most often asymptomatic. However, when associated with symptoms such as abdominal pain and distension, it is referred to as Chilaiditi syndrome.

An erect X-ray showing this sign may mislead clinicians into suspecting pneumoperitoneum, prompting unnecessary urgent surgical intervention, which is not required. To differentiate Chilaiditi syndrome from true pneumoperitoneum, a contrast-enhanced CT or a left lateral decubitus radiograph can be performed.

In the left lateral decubitus view, distended colonic loops with haustral markings will be visible, showing that the air is within the bowel and not in the peritoneal cavity.

Other conditions with the Chilaiditi sign are curvilinear pulmonary collapse, distended viscus, omental fat, and apposition of gas-distended bowel loops mimicking the double-wall sign.

Below is the chest X-ray and CT showing the presence of bowel loops under the diaphragm.

The CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis shows free intraperitoneal gas which is suggestive of pneumoperitoneum. The presence of free intra-abdominal gas almost always indicates perforation of a hollow viscus. Free intraperitoneal gas is also detectable under the hemidiaphragm on an erect chest X-ray as given below.

The existence of extraluminal gas within the mediastinum is referred to as pneumomediastinum. Gas may originate from the peritoneal cavity, lungs, trachea, central bronchi, oesophagus, or peritoneal cavity and travel to the neck or abdomen via the mediastinum. Spinnaker sign (also called angel wing sign) is a radiographic sign seen in neonates with pneumomediastinum.

The pressure from the collected gas displaces the two lobes of the thymic tissue upward and laterally from its normal position. This results in large, wedge-shaped opacities on radiograph resembling the spinnaker headsails of a boat. Other signs of pneumomediastinum are the V sign of Naclerio and continuous diaphragm sign.

Below is a chest X-ray showing spinnaker sign and CT showing the presence of pneumomediastinum.

question: Given below is an X-ray of a patient. What is the probable diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Left lateral decubitus abdomen X-ray with horizontal beam
explanationHtml:
Among the given options, the left lateral decubitus X-ray of the abdomen is the best view to visualize the pneumoperitoneum.

As little as 1 mL of free gas can be detected on a plain radiograph. Hence the best views to visualize pneumoperitoneum:

  • Erect chest X-ray – the first, most important, and useful view showing air beneath the diaphragm.
  • Left lateral decubitus abdominal image – In the left lateral decubitus position, the intra-abdominal viscera most prone to perforation (stomach and duodenum, caecum, sigmoid colon, and gallbladder) are located in a position favouring the rise of air to the right flank, and no superimposed gastric air bubble or splenic flexure air is present to be confused with extra-alimentary air.

CT abdomen is the most sensitive imaging technique to detect minimal pneumoperitoneum.

question: Identify the investigation from the given image?

explanationHtml:
The given ultrasound abdomen depicts the pseudokidney sign suggestive of intussusception.

Intussusception occurs when a portion of the bowel is telescoped into an adjacent segment. The most common location of intussusception is ileocolic. Clinically, it presents with cramping abdominal pain, palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass, and passage of red currant jelly stools.

A plain X-ray may reveal a meniscus-like appearance, where a soft tissue shadow is seen outlined against adjacent air-filled bowel loops. The target sign of intestinal intussusception, also known as the doughnut sign or bull's eye sign, is a diagnostic feature observed on abdominal ultrasound.

This appearance is due to concentric alternating echogenic and hypoechogenic bands. The echogenic bands are formed by the mucosa and muscularis, and the hypoechoic bands are formed by the submucosa.

Other ultrasound signs of intussusception include:

  • Pseudokidney sign - This is seen in the longitudinal section of the bowel. The edematous bowel resembles renal parenchyma, and the mesentery, which is dragged into the intussusception, resembles renal hilum
  • Crescent in a doughnut sign - A bright, curved, crescent-shaped echogenic area representing mesenteric fat that is drawn into the intussuscepted segment of bowel

The images below show USG films depicting the target sign and pseudo-kidney sign, respectively.
question: You are performing an ultrasound abdomen and notice the below finding. Which of the following conditions is it associated with?

explanationHtml:
Based on the given clinical scenario and the target sign observed on ultrasonography, intussusception is the likely diagnosis.

A barium enema study in this condition is likely to show a coiled spring appearance, caused by the barium outlining the lumen of the intussusceptum and the surrounding intraluminal space.

The images given below are the barium enema study showing a coiled spring appearance.

Raspberry thorn appearance is not an established radiological sign in any known clinical context. Rose thorn appearance on barium study is seen in Crohn's disease. Saw tooth appearance on barium enema is seen in colonic diverticulosis.
question: An infant was brought to the casualty with an incessant cry, abdominal distension, and a history of passing blood-stained stools. Target sign was noted in the right hypochondrium on ultrasonography. What would you expect to see in the barium enema study?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with the corkscrew sign seen in the upper gastrointestinal contrast study is suggestive of midgut volvulus.

Midgut volvulus is a complication of malrotation of the bowel and may result in proximal bowel obstruction. It can occur at any age, but it is commonly seen in the first few months of life. The baby presents with bilious vomiting, abdominal pain, and failure to thrive.

The images given below are from an upper gastrointestinal contrast study showing the following findings:

  • A - It describes the spiralling of the duodenum and jejunum around the mesenteric vessels, suggestive of a corkscrew appearance
  • B - An incomplete duodenal obstruction and dilation of the first and second portions of the duodenum are seen.
question: A neonate presented with bilious vomiting. Initial ultrasound of the abdomen demonstrated a whirlpool sign. A subsequent upper gastrointestinal contrast study was performed, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given CT abdomen depicts a swirling appearance of the mesentery and superior mesenteric vein around the superior mesenteric artery, known as the 'whirlpool sign' or 'whirl sign', seen in patients with midgut volvulus.

The whirlpool sign is seen when a structure twists upon itself. It is most commonly described in the abdomen, where the bowel rotates around its mesentery, with the superior mesenteric vein (SMV) wrapping in a clockwise spiral around the superior mesenteric artery (SMA).

The whirlpool sign is seen in several settings:

  • malrotation complicated by midgut volvulus
  • caecal volvulus
  • sigmoid volvulus
  • closed-loop bowel obstruction
  • ovarian torsion

The marked CECT image below shows the whirlpool sign.
question: Which of the following conditions is associated with the finding given in the CT abdomen?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of a patient developing persistent diarrhoea following prolonged antibiotic therapy for pneumonia is suggestive of pseudomembranous colitis. The Accordion sign is seen in pseudomembranous colitis.

Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) is commonly caused by the disruption of the commensal colonic microflora due to prolonged antimicrobial use, especially antibiotics like cephalosporins, ampicillin, clindamycin, and fluoroquinolones. The more severe form of CDI is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC).

Toxigenic Clostridium difficile produces toxin A (an enterotoxin) and toxin B (a cytotoxin), damaging the epithelial-cell barrier function and causing diarrhoea and pseudomembrane formation, which initially appear as small whitish-yellow plaques and later coalesce to involve the entire colon wall. The patient also presents with fever, abdominal pain, and leukocytosis.

On CT imaging, the accordion sign, also referred to as the concertina sign, may be seen. These terms refer to a harmonica-like musical instrument. The thickened edematous bowel resembles the folds of an accordion. The hyperaemic-enhancing mucosa stretches over the thickened submucosal folds, producing this appearance. This is also seen when the contrast gets trapped between oedematous haustral folds and pseudomembranes of the colon.

The accordion sign is typical for pseudomembranous colitis, but can also be seen in:

  • ischemic colitis
  • AIDS-related colitis
  • severe edema from cirrhosis

The CT image below depicts the accordion sign:
question: A patient on prolonged antibiotic therapy for pneumonia develops persistent diarrhoea. Stool examination is positive for toxins A and B. Which of the following findings is most likely seen on CT abdomen and pelvis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of a 64-year-old man with severe abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and obstipation, along with the radiograph showing the coffee bean sign with reduced haustral markings, is likely to be sigmoid volvulus.

The coffee bean sign can be seen in both sigmoid and cecal volvulus. A sigmoid volvulus can be differentiated from a cecal volvulus by the swirl sign, the location of the obstructed loop, and anatomical appendages.

Haustrations Lost Present

Primary Management Endoscopic decompression (sigmoidoscopy/flatus tube) Usually requires resection or caecopexy

Paralytic ileus results from impaired neuromuscular activity of the bowel, which disrupts the normal propagation of peristaltic movements. It is most commonly seen after abdominal surgery such as laparotomy. Computed tomography is considered more reliable in distinguishing a dynamic ileus from mechanical intestinal obstruction.

The image given below is an X-ray of the paralytic ileus showing gas-filled loops of the intestine with multiple fluid levels.

Colonic diverticula are generally considered false diverticula, in which the inner lining of the bowel protrudes outward through weak points in the muscular wall. The given barium enema study shows a saw-tooth appearance due to barium-filled outpouchings, suggestive of colonic diverticulosis.
question: A 64-year-old man is rushed to the ER with severe abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and obstipation. His erect X-ray abdomen is as shown. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
In the given clinical scenario, an elderly man presenting with constipation, along with a barium enema image showing the "bird of prey" sign, is highly suggestive of sigmoid volvulus.

On barium enema, this radiological feature demonstrates a progressive narrowing of the sigmoid colon at the site of twisting, forming a hooked beak-like appearance.

Sigmoid volvulus is a cause of large bowel obstruction and occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on the sigmoid mesocolon. Symptoms include constipation, abdominal bloating, nausea, and/or vomiting. The onset may be acute or chronic. It occurs more commonly in patients with chronic constipation.

The image below shows the factors predisposing to sigmoid volvulus.

X-ray of the abdomen shows a large, dilated loop of the colon, often with a few air-fluid levels. Specific signs include the coffee bean sign/bent inner tube sign, Frimann-Dahl sign(three dense lines converge towards the site of obstruction), and the absence of rectal gas. CT may reveal a large gas-filled loop without haustral markings, forming a closed-loop obstruction

The radiological signs associated with sigmoid volvulus are shown below.
question: An elderly man presents with constipation. A barium enema study is shown in the image below. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The artery marked by the red arrow is the superior mesenteric artery (SMA).

The presence of liver, spleen, and the upper pole of the left kidney in the given axial section indicates the L1 plane where the SMA originates, which arises approximately 1 cm below the celiac trunk. The left renal vein courses between the abdominal aorta and the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, as demonstrated in the CT image below.

The CT also depicts nutcracker syndrome, a left renal vein entrapment syndrome characterized by extrinsic compression of the left renal vein (LRV), most commonly between the abdominal aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. This syndrome is one of the proposed reasons why left-sided varicoceles are more common than right-sided ones.


The superior mesenteric artery is the second major branch of the abdominal aorta. The SMA supplies the midgut, extending from the ampullary region of the second part of the duodenum to the splenic flexure of the large intestine.

The relations of the superior mesenteric artery are as follows:

Anterior:

  • Splenic vein
  • Neck of the pancreas
  • Pylorus of the stomach

Posterior:

  • Uncinate process of the pancreas
  • Third (horizontal) part of the duodenum
  • Left renal vein
question: Identify the artery marked by the red arrow.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with the lead pipe appearance of the colon in the barium study, is suggestive of ulcerative colitis.

On barium studies, the lead pipe appearance refers to the complete loss of haustral markings in the affected section of the colon, which appears smooth-walled and cylindrical, resulting from chronic inflammation.

In the given double contrast barium enema, the descending and sigmoid colon are featureless with loss of haustra, while the ascending and transverse colon and terminal ileum appear normal.

Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease resulting in superficial erosions confined to the mucosa and submucosa of the colon. It starts from the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous manner. Clinical features include abdominal pain, diarrhea (often with blood), rectal bleeding, tenesmus, and passage of mucus.
question: A 24-year-old woman presents with chronic bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. A barium enema was done and is as shown. What is her likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with the CT abdomen showing the comb sign, is suggestive of Crohn's disease.

The comb sign refers to the hypervascular appearance of the mesentery seen in active Crohn's disease, caused by engorgement of the vasa recta.

Fibrofatty proliferation and perivascular inflammation accentuate these distended mesenteric vessels, producing parallel linear densities along the mesenteric border of the affected small bowel. These resemble the teeth of a comb, giving rise to the term comb sign.
question: A young man presented with weight loss, and recurrent episodes of non-bloody diarrhea for the past 6 months. CT abdomen was done and is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with the barium study findings, is suggestive of ileocecal tuberculosis. The given image shows dilated proximal ileum, narrowed terminal ileum and ileocecal junction, and shrunken cecum.

The ileocecal junction is the commonest site of tuberculosis in the gastrointestinal tract. Other sites involved in the abdomen are the liver, spleen, and peritoneum.

Barium meal follow-through study findings in ileocecal tuberculosis are:

  • Dilatation of the proximal ileum
  • Narrowed terminal ileum (string sign) and ileocecal junction
  • Gooseneck ileus – ileum hanging from the pulled-up cecum
  • The ileocecal angle becomes obtuse
  • The cecum appears shrunken and pulled up away from the right iliac fossa
  • Conical cecum
  • Fleischner sign

On barium enema, ileocecal tuberculosis typically shows narrowing of the terminal ileum, thickening and gaping of the ileocecal valve, and a contracted, hypermotile cecum. In contrast, carcinoma of the colon classically produces an “apple-core” appearance due to an annular constricting lesion.
question: A 30-year-old woman presented with a low-grade fever associated with loss of appetite and weight loss. A barium meal follow-through was done and is as shown. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The Fleischner sign observed in barium studies of ileocecal tuberculosis describes a widely gaping, thickened, patulous ileocecal valve alongside a narrowed and ulcerated terminal ileum.

Intestinal tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (often secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis) or by Mycobacterium bovis (as a primary GI infection), most commonly affects the ileocecal junction. Symptoms include cough, evening rise in temperature, weight loss, malaise, abdominal pain with distension, and intermittent diarrhea. On palpation, the abdomen has a soft, yielding consistency, and a palpable swelling may be detected in the right iliac fossa.

The provided single-contrast barium enema image shows the Fleischner sign, narrowing of the terminal ileum with fine contour irregularities, contracted cecum, and a widely patent ileocecal valve- characteristic of ileocecal tuberculosis.

Note: Fleischner sign could also refer to a prominent central pulmonary artery seen in pulmonary embolism or pulmonary hypertension.
question: Which of the following signs is seen on barium studies in patients with ileocecal tuberculosis?

explanationHtml:
String sign is not seen in ulcerative colitis.

String sign refers to the thin, string-like appearance of a severely narrowed bowel loop on radiographic imaging. This narrowing occurs due to spasms, edema, inflammation, or ulceration.

It is commonly seen in

  • Crohn’s disease (string sign of Kantor),
  • Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
  • Ileocaecal tuberculosis

question: String sign on radiological imaging is seen in all of the following conditions except?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with the given image showing the 'apple core appearance' in barium enema, is suggestive of carcinoma of the colon.

Apple core sign/napkin ring sign describes a short segment of irregular circumferential stricture involving the large bowel. It has shoulder margins resembling an apple core. The appearance is classically described in contrast enema studies and is almost always due to a stenosing annular colon carcinoma.

Colon carcinoma typically arises in patients above the age of 50 years. It arises from the adenomatous polyps after the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, influenced by environmental factors. Most colon cancers occur in the left colon.

The clinical features of colon carcinoma include a change in bowel habits or rectal bleeding in cases of left-sided colon tumors and iron deficiency anemia or a mass in proximal lesions of the colon.

Colonoscopy is the preferred investigation for suspected colorectal cancer. Barium enema may show a persistent irregular narrowing of the colon with an “apple-core” appearance. CT virtual colonography has largely replaced barium enema due to better lesion detection and lower invasiveness, though biopsy still requires endoscopy. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is standard for assessing disease extent.

The image below shows the apple-core sign:

Whereas, the string sign in ileocecal tuberculosis is due to long-segment smooth concentric narrowing of the terminal ileum caused by inflammatory fibrosis, producing a thin “string-like” passage of contrast.
question: A 59-year-old man is being evaluated for a change in bowel habits associated with abdominal discomfort. A barium enema study was done and is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis of this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given barium enema study is showing a saw tooth appearance suggestive of colonic diverticulosis. Both single and double-contrast barium enemas are able to demonstrate diverticula as barium-filled outpouchings.

Colonic diverticula are almost all false diverticula i.e., mucosa herniating through a defect in the muscularis and covered by overlying serosa (where present). This herniation typically occurs where nutrient arteries enter the colon, and therefore, are more common on the mesenteric side of the colon. Colonic diverticula are most common in the sigmoid colon and, to a lesser extent, in the descending colon.

Given below is the barium enema study of colonic diverticulosis, the arrows are pointing to the barium-filled outpouching suggestive of diverticula.
question: A barium enema study of a patient is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with the barium enema, showing a narrowed rectum and a cone-shaped transition zone leading to a proximally dilated ganglionated bowel, together suggest Hirschsprung disease.

Hirschsprung disease is characterized by aganglionosis (absence of ganglion cells) in the distal colon and rectum. This may occur due to the failure of neuroblasts in neural crest cells to migrate into bowel segments or the degeneration of already migrated neuroblasts. Hence, functional obstruction develops due to a spasm in the denervated colon.

The barium enema demonstrates a sudden transition in caliber from the narrow aganglionic distal segment to the dilated proximal bowel, along with reversal of the rectosigmoid ratio (rectosigmoid ratio <1, measured as the widest width of the rectum relative to the sigmoid colon), findings characteristic of Hirschsprung disease.

Typical features include delayed passage of meconium within the first two days of life, progressive abdominal swelling, vomiting, and constipation. In some cases, severe bowel inflammation may occur and can be life-threatening. A strong association is also seen with Down syndrome.

It demonstrates a narrowed distal segment without normal nerve supply, a tapered transitional area, and an enlarged bowel segment proximal to the obstruction. A full-thickness rectal biopsy is the gold standard investigation.

The image below shows dilated ganglionic and contracted aganglionic segments in Hirschsprung disease:
question: A 7-week-old infant presents with abdominal distension and delayed passage of meconium. A barium enema study is performed, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
A newborn presenting with respiratory distress shortly after birth, along with the chest X-ray showing bowel loops in the thoracic cavity, is suggestive of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).

During normal fetal development, the pleuroperitoneal cavities become separated by 8–10 weeks of gestation. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) arises when the pleuroperitoneal canal fails to close properly, allowing abdominal organs to herniate into the thoracic cavity.

This intrusion restricts lung growth and function, leading to pulmonary hypoplasia, which is the primary cause of mortality. The most common form of CDH is a Bochdalek hernia, typically occurring on the left side.

Chest X-ray findings in congenital diaphragmatic hernia include:

  • Bowel loops in the thorax
  • Indistinct diaphragm with opacification of part of or all the hemithorax (typically left-sided)
  • Deviation of lines such as the endotracheal tube, nasogastric tube, umbilical arterial and venous catheters.

The X-ray given below shows the congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

Given below is the chest radiograph of a Bochdalek hernia.

Given below is the chest radiograph of Morgagni hernia.

Note: Bag and mask ventilation is to be avoided in the management of this baby. Bag and mask ventilation may increase abdominal distension and limit the expansion of the hypoplastic lungs.
question: A newborn presented with severe respiratory distress soon after birth. A chest X-ray was done and is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The CT shows Mercedes-Benz sign, characteristic of cholelithiasis.

Mercedes–Benz sign (triradiate sign), is seen when a gallstone contains central radiolucent gas, which has a negative HU. The fissures may be tri-radiate or bi-radiate (seagull sign). These fissures appear dark on CT or radiographs, giving the sign its characteristic appearance.

Gallbladder stones are the most common gallbladder condition and frequently an incidental finding. When symptomatic, patients present with dull, persistent RUQ pain radiating to the back, with nausea and vomiting. The episodes are typically triggered after meals due to CCK-mediated gallbladder contraction. Episodes are recurrent and self-limiting.

Only about 10% of gallstones are radiopaque. Ultrasonography (USG) is the most accurate initial imaging modality of choice for the diagnosis of gallbladder stones. These stones appear as echogenic foci producing acoustic shadows. The sensitivity of USG for gallstones is >95%.

The CT image below depicts the Mercedes-Benz sign:

The image below shows ultrasonography of the gall bladder with cholelithiasis.
question: A patient underwent contrast CT abdomen for evaluation of small bowel pathology. The following incidental finding was noted. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with the CT showing gas within the wall of the gallbladder, is suggestive of emphysematous cholecystitis.

Emphysematous cholecystitis is a rare and severe form of acute cholecystitis, characterized by gas formation within the gallbladder wall or lumen due to necrosis. This condition often stems from ischemia or gangrene of the gallbladder, followed by infection with gas-forming bacteria such as Clostridium welchii, C. perfringens, and occasionally aerobes like Escherichia coli.

It predominantly affects elderly males and diabetic patients. Patients typically present with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and a low-grade fever, with crepitus detectable on physical examination.

CT is demonstrates intramural / intraluminal gas better than ultrasound, which may give a false-negative result.

Due to a high mortality rate associated with complications like gangrene and perforation, emergency cholecystectomy and antibiotics are essential for management.

explanationHtml:
Double-barrel sign is seen in CBD obstruction. It causes dilatation of CBD with increased lumen size which becomes comparable to the portal vein. This gives the appearance of a double-barrel.

question: Abdominal USG in a patient with pruritic jaundice revealed the double-barrel sign. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given ERCP shows a linear filling defect characteristic of a worm in the biliary tree. One of the commonly found worms in the biliary tree is Ascaris.

The given Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangio Pancreaticography (ERCP) below shows a linear filling defect characteristic of a worm in the biliary tree. The worm may also be seen as parallel filling defects - railway track sign. The same image has been marked with arrows to help appreciate the presence of this worm in the bile duct.


Choledocholithiasis or common bile duct stones are classified based on their point of origin. Choledocholithiasis is mostly clinically silent but may present with biliary colic and even obstructive jaundice. The following ERCP image shows a round filling defect (marked with an arrow) within the common bile duct, indicative of choledocholithiasis.

ERCP or MRCP offers detailed visualization of the ductal systems and pancreatic stones. Upstream ductal dilatation suggests a hydrostatic obstruction, with main pancreatic duct stones producing a more pronounced upstream dilatation compared to the stones in side branches of the duct.

Bile duct strictures are areas where the intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary ductal system narrows. The constriction blocks the usual forward flow of bile, leading to widening upstream and causing serious health issues due to the effects of bile duct blockage. Below is an ERCP showing the presence of a distal bile duct stricture.
question: The given finding on ERCP is characteristic of:

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario along with the triangular cord sign on the USG is suggestive of biliary atresia.

The triangular cord sign represents the fibrous ductal remnant of the extrahepatic bile duct in biliary atresia. It is usually seen as an echogenicity along the anterior wall of the right portal vein. In the above image, the arrow represents the fibrous atretic plate at the porta hepatis.

Biliary atresia may also be termed as noncystic obliterative cholangiopathy. It is a disease of the intra and extrahepatic bile ducts of unknown etiology.

The classification of biliary atresia with the regions involved is as follows:

Type I - Common bile duct
Type IIa - Common hepatic duct
Type IIb - Common bile duct, hepatic duct, cystic duct.
Type III (most common type) - Common bile duct, hepatic duct, cystic duct; no anastomosable ducts at porta hepatis.

Clinical features include persistent jaundice, clay-colored stools, and hepatomegaly. Untreated newborns will show signs of liver cirrhosis and failure (ascites, portal hypertension, and failure to thrive).

Laboratory evaluation will show elevated levels of direct and indirect bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase. Ultrasound will show hypoplastic or absent gallbladder and the triangular cord sign. The definitive diagnosis is by intraoperative cholangiography. Preoperative percutaneous transhepatic cholecystocholangiography combined with liver biopsy in cholestatic infants has a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity of 93% for diagnosing biliary atresia.
question: A neonate was admitted to the NICU with persistent jaundice. A USG abdomen was done and is shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and comet-tail artefact on USG is seen in adenomyomatosis of the gallbladder.

Adenomyomatous hyperplasia of the gall bladder (cholecystitis glandularis proliferans) involves proliferation of the gallbladder epithelium and smooth muscle, resulting in wall thickening. The mucosa forms small intramural outpouchings known as Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses. The most common location is in the fundus of the gall bladder, and the sinuses often contain stones.

On ultrasound, gallbladder adenomyomatosis may appear as focal or diffuse thickening of the gallbladder wall. Small intramural cystic spaces can produce bright echoes and characteristic comet-tail or ring-down artefacts. The comet-tail artefact is caused by the cholesterol crystals trapped within the Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses, causing reverberation (a large number of reflected waves).
question: Abdominal USG in a 50-year-old male with right upper quadrant abdominal pain revealed the comet tail artefact. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Colon cut-off sign is an abdominal radiographic sign which can be associated with acute pancreatitis.

The colon cut-off sign refers to the abrupt termination of the gas filling of the colon on the left side. The inflammation of acute pancreatitis may extend to the phrenicocolic ligament via the transverse mesocolon, causing a functional spasm of the splenic flexure, resulting in the colon cut-off sign. Though originally described in abdominal radiographs, this sign has also been demonstrated in contrast enema and computed tomography.

Acute pancreatitis is a condition characterized by inflammatory damage to the pancreas, presenting clinically with epigastric pain radiating to the back, which is relieved by bending forward, nausea, and vomiting. Some may also present with signs of bleeding into the fascial planes, such as Cullen’s sign, Grey Turner’s sign, Fox sign, and Bryant’s sign (discolouration of the scrotum).

Radiological signs in acute pancreatitis include colon cut-off sign, preserved renal halo sign, and sentinel loop sign (upper abdomen).
question: Which of the following abdominal X-ray signs is associated with acute pancreatitis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario with elevated serum amylase and lipase suggests acute pancreatitis. Grey Turner's sign, seen in this condition, is a clinical sign, not a radiological finding, characterized by flank discolouration due to retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis can present clinically with certain named signs like Cullen’s sign, Grey Turner’s sign, Fox sign, and Bryant’s sign (discolouration of the scrotum).

Radiological signs in acute pancreatitis include the colon cut-off sign, the renal halo sign, and the sentinel loop sign (upper abdomen).

Note: The sentinel loop sign may aid in localizing the source of inflammation. For example, the sentinel loop sign in the right lower quadrant may be due to appendicitis.
question: A patient with chronic alcoholism presented with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. His lab reports showed elevated serum amylase and lipase levels. Which of the following signs is unlikely to be seen in the radiograph of this patient?

explanationHtml:
The investigation of choice to assess prognosis in patients with acute pancreatitis is CECT. It is used to calculate the modified CT severity index.

Plain erect chest x-ray and abdominal radiographs are not diagnostic of acute pancreatitis and can only be used to rule out certain differentials. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) is the imaging investigation of choice. Various scoring systems are used to grade the severity of acute pancreatitis based on blood investigations and radiographic findings.

Below is an axial CECT image showing an inflamed pancreas with peripancreatic inflammatory fat stranding:


The optimal time for the performance of contrast-enhanced CT imaging in cases of acute pancreatitis is more than 72 hours from the onset of symptoms. In the first 72 hours, CT may underestimate the extent of necrosis. CT scan in pancreatitis is indicated in patients with severe acute pancreatitis, organ failure, sepsis, and patients with clinical deterioration despite treatment.

MRI is preferred over CT in children and pregnancy to avoid ionizing radiation.
question: What is the investigation of choice to assess the prognosis of patients with acute pancreatitis?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a double duct sign and dilatation of pancreatic duct side branches (arrows), suggesting pancreatic head carcinoma.

The double duct sign refers to the presence of simultaneous dilatation of the common bile duct and pancreatic ducts. Being an anatomical sign, it can be seen on all modalities that can visualise the region, including MRI, CT, ultrasound, MRCP, and ERCP.

Causes of the double duct sign are:

  • Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas and ampullary carcinoma constitute the most common causes.
  • Other malignant causes are cholangiocarcinoma of the distal common bile duct, lymphoma, or metastasis.
  • Chronic pancreatitis and ampullary stenosis are a few of the benign conditions which can also cause this.

In contrast, double-barrel sign is seen in CBD obstruction. It causes dilatation of CBD with increased lumen size which becomes comparable to the portal vein. This gives the appearance of a double-barrel.
question: The CT findings of a patient being evaluated for anorexia and jaundice are shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with the barium study showing an enlarged duodenal loop with 'reversed 3 sign' of Frostberg is suggestive of carcinoma head of the pancreas.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas arise most commonly in the head of the gland. Pancreatic carcinoma presents with varied symptoms, commonly including weight loss and anorexia, which may or may not be accompanied by abdominal pain. Tumours in the pancreatic head often cause early bile duct obstruction, leading to jaundice.

Frostberg's inverted 3 sign is a sign seen on a barium examination. There is effacement and distortion of the mucosal pattern on the medial wall of the second part of the duodenum due to focal mass and local edema. This sign classically indicates carcinoma of the head of the pancreas and duodenal carcinoma but has also been described in benign conditions such as chronic pancreatitis and duodenal ulcers.

Antral pad sign may also be seen in barium studies in patients with carcinoma head of the pancreas. Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiogram shows a characteristic 'gloved finger' obstruction of the intrapancreatic common bile duct, which is pathognomonic for carcinoma of the pancreatic head.

The image of a barium meal showing an inverted 3 sign is given below.
question: A 54-year-old man presents with abdominal pain, anorexia, and weight loss. A barium study was performed and is as shown. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The honey-comb appearance of cysts with central stellate calcification on the CT abdomen is seen in serous cystadenoma of the pancreas.

CT findings of serous cystadenoma of the pancreas:

  • Typically demonstrates a microcystic, lobulated mass in the pancreatic head sometimes described as a 'honey-comb'.
  • A characteristic enhancing central scar may be present which can show associated stellate calcification (present in ~20% of cases)

The images given below are the CT abdomen showing sunburst calcification suggestive of serous cystadenoma of the pancreas.
question: Which of the following conditions is associated with a honey-comb appearance  with central stellate calcification on CT abdomen?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the CT showing a central dot sign suggest Caroli's disease.

The central dot sign of Caroli’s disease is a central enhancing fibrovascular bundle containing a portal vein surrounded by a focally dilated intrahepatic bile duct cyst.

Shown below is an Axial CECT of the abdomen showing multiple cystic dilatations of the intrahepatic bile ducts. The arrows point to the central dot sign (enhancing portal radicles surrounded by dilated bile duct cysts).

Caroli disease is a congenital biliary disorder in which segmental intrahepatic bile ducts show multiple cystic dilatations. It is also classified as a type V choledochal cyst, according to Todani classification. They present with a triad of jaundice, a palpable upper quadrant mass, and abdominal pain.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI/MRCP) is the investigation of choice, revealing the anatomy of the ducts. CT delineates the extent of the intra- or extrahepatic dilatation. ERCP defines the distal biliary tree. CT findings in Caroli disease are characterised by multiple hypodense rounded areas that are inseparable from the dilated intrahepatic bile ducts and central dot sign.

Given below is axial T2-weighted MRI of the abdomen showing multiple T2-hyperintense cystic dilatations of the intrahepatic bile ducts in Caroli's disease.
question: A 10-year old boy presented with jaundice and right upper abdominal pain. An abdominal CT was done and is as shown. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Kehr's sign is a clinical finding seen in splenic rupture and not a radiographic finding.

Kehr's sign refers to referred pain in the tip of the left shoulder when firm pressure is applied over the left upper quadrant. This is commonly due to diaphragmatic irritation resulting from blood accumulation beneath the left diaphragm in cases of suspected splenic rupture. It is also elicited by raising the left leg.

The spleen is the visceral organ most commonly injured in blunt trauma abdomen. Severely ill patients may present with hypovolemic shock manifesting as tachycardia, hypotension, and pallor. Splenic injury can be subtle clinically. Rupture may even occur after trivial trauma or minor triggers, especially in spontaneous or pathological cases.

Signs of splenic rupture on plain X-ray are obliteration of splenic outline, loss of psoas shadow, elevation of left hemidiaphragm and fracture of lower ribs on left side. The investigation of choice in blunt trauma abdomen is CECT.

A splenic laceration appears on CT as a linear tear in the spleen. It is often associated with bleeding into the abdomen.

The image below is a CT abdomen showing a hematoma in the spleen due to splenic laceration.

The image given below is a CECT abdomen shows a hematoma in the spleen due to splenic laceration.
question: Which of the following signs is unlikely to be seen in the radiograph of a patient suspected to have splenic rupture?

explanationHtml:
The LI-RADS category LR-4 denotes Probably HCC.

Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) is a comprehensive system used to assess the probability of HCC in all high-risk patients with cirrhosis, and non-cirrhotic patients with Hepatitis B infection. It cannot be applied to patients <18 years and those with cirrhosis due to congenital and vascular causes.

LI-RADS category Definition Management
LR-NC Negative / Non categorizable
LR-1 Definitely benign Continued routine surveillance
LR-2 Probably benign
LR-3 Intermediate risk Variable follow-up
LR-4 Probably HCC Close follow-up, additional imaging, biopsy, or treatment
LR-5 Definitely HCC Treatment without biopsy, radiologic T-staging
LR-TIV Definitely a tumour, invading vein
LR-M Probably malignancy but not specific for HCC Close follow-up, additional imaging, biopsy, or treatment
LR-Treated Treated observation Close follow-up to assess treatment response.


The LIRADS score is determined based on the following factors:

  • Arterial phase hyperenhancement
  • Observed size
  • Enhancing capsule
  • Nonperipheral washout of contrast, and
  • Threshold growth > 50% in 6 months

A chronic hepatitis B positive patient is being evaluated for hepatocellular carcinoma using multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT. According to the LI-RADS CT classification, the scan is reported as LR-4. Which of the following corresponds to this category?

explanationHtml:
The marked structure in the MRCP image is that of common hepatic duct.

MRCP is a non-invasive test used to visualise the intra and extrahepatic biliary tree and pancreatic ductal system. By acquiring images using heavily T2-weighted sequences, this technique uses the fluid present in the biliary and pancreatic ducts as an intrinsic contrast medium.
question: Given below is an MRCP image of a patient with biliary stones. Identify the marked structure.

explanationHtml:
The given image shows enhancement of the portal vein along with liver parenchyma, appearing hyperdense (bright). This is characteristic of the portal venous phase.

Contrast-enhanced CT involves injection of an intravenous contrast agent into a peripheral vein, it sequentially opacifies the hepatic arteries, portal vein, and hepatic veins.

CECT involves injecting contrast into a peripheral vein. It then travels through the liver's blood vessels in sequence:

  • Arterial phase (30 sec): Hepatic artery is enhanced
  • Portal venous phase (60 sec): Liver parenchyma and portal veins enhance
  • Delayed/venous phase (3-5 min): Hepatic veins get enhanced

The liver receives 75% of its blood from the portal vein and 25% from the hepatic artery. This dual supply determines which structures get enhanced in each phase.

The image below is CECT of the liver, showing the appearance across various phases.

The image below shows the delayed venous phase
question: A 50-year-old man underwent a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen. Identify the phase of contrast enhancement depicted in this image.

explanationHtml:
The clinical history of recurrent epigastric pain with X-ray showing pancreatic calcifications at L1-L2 level is characteristic of chronic pancreatitis. All of the mentioned findings are expected in chronic pancreatitis except double-duct sign which is seen in pancreatic head malignancy, not chronic pancreatitis.

Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disease causing irreversible destruction of pancreatic tissue, with the most common cause being alcohol. In the later stages, exocrine insufficiency leads to steatorrhoea and endocrine insufficiency results in diabetes mellitus.

On CT, diagnosis requires at least three of four findings for high specificity: parenchymal calcifications, intraductal calcifications, parenchymal atrophy, and cystic lesions.

Image below shows axial and coronal CT showing pancreatic calcifications in chronic pancreatitis.


On MRCP, irregular dilatation of the main pancreatic duct and side branches with multifocal strictures produces the classic chain-of-lakes appearance.
The duct-penetrating sign (main duct traversing an inflammatory mass without complete obstruction) helps differentiate focal chronic pancreatitis from adenocarcinoma, which completely obstructs the duct.

The image below shows chain-of-lakes appearance on MRCP:
question: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with recurrent epigastric pain. X-ray of the abdomen is shown below. All of the following radiological features are expected in this condition except?

explanationHtml:
The clinical history of an obese multiparous woman with postprandial RUQ pain radiating to the shoulder (fat-female-forty-fertile) points to cholelithiasis. The image shows a wall-echo-shadow sign, with 1 pointing to the echogenic gallstone and 2 pointing to the shadow of the gallstone.


Cholelithiasis is commonly seen in women. Over 70% of the gallstones are composed of cholesterol, while the pigment gallstones, composed of calcium carbonate, constitute most of the remaining 30%.

Ultrasound is the best test for gallbladder stones, which are mobile, dependent echogenic foci in the gallbladder lumen that produce acoustic shadowing. Stones move with positional change unless impacted

Wall-echo-shadow (WES) sign in USG is produced due to a well-defined echogenic gall bladder wall (W), overlying the echoes (E) from gallstones, and prominent posterior acoustic shadowing (S) that is seen behind the stones.

Wall – A bright (hyperechoic) line representing the gall bladder wall

Echo – A second bright line from the surface of gallstones inside the gallbladder

Shadow – A dark area posterior to the stones. Dense stones block ultrasound waves, preventing transmission beyond them.
question: A 42-year-old obese multiparous woman presents with recurrent postprandial right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder for 3 months. Her ultrasound is shown below. Identify the labelled structures.

correctAnswer: C. Central stellate scar with calcifications
explanationHtml:
Fibrolamellar HCC characteristically shows a well-circumscribed mass with a central stellate scar with calcifications on CECT.

Fibrolamellar HCC (FL-HCC) is a rare, well-circumscribed variant of hepatocellular carcinoma that presents in a younger population and characteristically shows neurotensin positivity. Unlike conventional hepatocellular carcinoma, FL-HCC occurs without preexisting cirrhosis and rarely presents with raised AFP levels.

On CECT, it presents as a well-circumscribed mass with heterogeneous arterial enhancement. Characteristic features on CECT include a central scar showing persistent enhancement on delayed phase, commonly with calcifications.

MRI shows the central scar as hypointense on T2-weighted imaging (unlike focal nodular hyperplasia, where it is hyperintense).


Multiple hypovascular lesions on the portal venous (parenchymal) phase are characteristic of metastasis. Most primaries arise from the colon, stomach, and breast.

The following image depicts multiple hypovascular liver metastases:


Arterial phase hyperenhancement with washout in the portal venous or delayed phase is seen in hepatocellular carcinoma, as the tumour derives its blood supply from hepatic arteries.

The image below is CECT of HCC, showing a lesion isodense on pre-contrast (a), with non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement (b, arrow), non-peripheral washout on portal venous (c) and delayed phase with enhancing capsule(d) :


On CECT, a peripheral enhancing rim with fluid density is characteristic of a liver abscess. This typically demonstrates wall enhancement during the arterial phase, followed by progressive washout. The presence of the Double Target sign and the cluster sign together is highly suggestive of a pyogenic abscess.

The image showing double target sign is given below:


Note:

Both FNH and fibrolamellar HCC show a central stellate scar, but they can be differentiated on MRI. In FNH, the central scar is hyperintense on T2W MRI and calcifications are rare. In fibrolamellar HCC, the central scar is hypointense on T2W MRI, and calcifications are common.
