Washout in the portal venous or delayed phase
Peripheral enhancing rim with fluid density

question: A 24-year-old man with solitary hepatic mass was diagnosed with fibrolamellar HCC. What is the characteristic CECT finding in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Hepatic hemangioma demonstrates the light bulb sign on T2-weighted MRI.

Hepatic hemangiomas are composed of large, blood-filled vascular spaces. This fluid content gives very high signal intensity on T2-weighted MRI, appearing markedly hyperintense and resembling a bright light source. This is the light bulb sign. On T1-weighted MRI, hemangiomas usually appear hypointense and therefore do not demonstrate the bright "light bulb" appearance.

The image below illustrates the characteristic light bulb sign on T2W-MRI observed in hepatic hemangioma.


Hepatic hemangiomas are the most common benign liver lesions. They typically present as well-defined, solitary masses, often in the right lobe of the liver. They are typically incidental findings, as they are usually asymptomatic.

CECT demonstrates nodular enhancement in the peripheral region. Contrast then gradually progresses inward on the portal venous and delayed images, producing the characteristic centripetal fill-in pattern.


Ultrasonography characteristically shows a homogeneously hyperechoic mass.
question: Which of the following modalities demonstrates the "light bulb sign" seen in hepatic hemangiomas?

explanationHtml:
An incidental liver lesion with a T2-hyperintense central scar in a young woman on OCPs is characteristic of focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH).

Focal Nodular Hyperplasia (FNH) is the most common benign hepatic tumor in young women (20–50 years). It arises from a congenital vascular malformation and contains abnormal bile ducts. Unlike hepatic adenoma, FNH retains hepatobiliary contrast and has no malignant potential. The central stellate scar is characteristic.

On T2W-MRI, the lesion is isointense, scar hyperintense (bright). Arterial phase shows intense homogeneous enhancement (scar non-enhancing). In delayed phase, the scar enhances. Hepatobiliary phase shows contrast retention.

NOTE: Both FNH and fibrolamellar HCC show a central stellate scar.

  • FNH: Central fibrovascular scar appears hyperintense (bright) on T2W MRI. Calcifications are rare.
  • Fibrolamellar HCC: Central fibrous scar appears hypointense (dark) on T2W MRI. Punctate calcifications in >50% of cases.

USG or CT-guided biopsy is recommended to differentiate the two.

Hepatic adenoma is strongly associated with oral contraceptive use. Unlike FNH, it has no functioning bile ducts, so it does not retain hepatobiliary contrast. It can hemorrhage and has 1–5% malignant potential.

On MRI, adenoma shows homogeneous arterial enhancement with washout in the portal/delayed phase and no uptake in the hepatobiliary phase.


Hemangioma is the most common benign hepatic tumor overall. On T2, it appears markedly hyperintense, exceeding splenic signal (light bulb sign). In the arterial phase, it shows peripheral nodular enhancement, followed by centripetal fill-in in the portal/delayed phases. In the hepatobiliary phase, there is no uptake.


Hepatic abscess appears as an ill-defined hypodense lesion with rim enhancement on contrast CT. On MRI, it is T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense. As it liquefies, the center shows debris with an irregular wall. Clinically presents with fever, RUQ pain, and raised inflammatory markers. Image is shown below:
question: A 35-year-old woman on oral contraceptives presents with an incidentally detected liver lesion. T2-weighted MRI findings are shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The intravenous urogram demonstrates inferolateral displacement of the opacified lower-pole collecting system due to an obstructed, non-opacified upper pole. This characteristic appearance is known as the “drooping lily sign” and is typically seen in patients with a duplicated collecting system.

In such cases, complete obstruction of the upper pole collecting system prevents it from opacifying, while the normally draining lower pole remains visible. The resulting downward and outward displacement of the lower pole creates the classic drooping lily appearance.

The image below shows the drooping lily sign.

A duplicated collecting system is a common congenital anomaly of the urinary tract that occurs due to the division of the ureter as it ascends upwards from the bladder to the renal parenchyma during the embryological period of life. Thus, the person might have two collecting systems for one kidney.

There are 2 types of duplication:

  • Incomplete duplication (Y ureter) occurs when a single ureteric bud bifurcates after arising from the mesonephric duct, resulting in two proximal ureteric limbs that join distally to form a single ureter before entering the bladder
  • Complete duplication develops when two distinct ureteric buds originate separately from the mesonephric duct during embryogenesis

In adults, the condition generally remains without any symptoms. Whereas pediatric cases are frequently linked with vesico-ureteric reflux. Females are more commonly affected. Voiding is normal, but prolonged dribbling of urine is seen.

Duplex collecting systems may also be complicated by vesicoureteric reflux, obstruction, or ureterocoele. When the upper pole ureter is obstructed, the lower pole collecting system appears displaced and stretched on imaging, creating the "drooping lily" sign observed in intravenous urography.

The Weigert-Meyer law describes the relationship of the upper and lower renal moieties in duplicated collecting systems to their drainage. When there are abnormalities associated with the duplication of the collecting systems,

  • The upper pole ureter inserts more medially and inferiorly, and is more likely to be obstructed (often associated with ureterocele), leading to dilatation and scarring
  • The lower pole ureter enters the bladder in a more lateral position and possesses a relatively short intramural course, it has an increased tendency for vesicoureteric reflux.

The illustration given below shows the Weigert-Meyer law.
question: During the evaluation of a patient with recurrent UTIs, the following urographic finding was observed. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The ball on tee sign is seen in renal papillary necrosis, not ball and socket.

Renal papillary necrosis refers to ischemic necrosis of the renal papillae. It can be acute or chronic. Calyceal or ureteral obstruction by sloughed papillae manifests with flank pain, haematuria, and renal impairment.

The image given below shows the following signs of renal papillary necrosis.

The common causes include analgesic abuse (phenacetin, NSAIDs, paracetamol: especially in combination), diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease, pyelonephritis (especially in children), and obstruction.
question:
Which of the following is not an IVU finding in patients with renal papillary necrosis?

IVU- Intravenous Urography

explanationHtml:
The clinical presentation, together with CT findings of an enlarged kidney containing areas of parenchymal necrosis and mottled gas collections, is highly suggestive of left-sided emphysematous pyelonephritis.

Emphysematous pyelonephritis is a severe, acute, necrotising infection of the kidney caused by gas-producing organisms. It predominantly affects diabetic patients who are particularly susceptible due to their hyperglycaemic state, which promotes bacterial growth and fermentation.

The most common causative organism is Escherichia coli, which ferments sugar to produce carbon dioxide, leading to gas accumulation within renal parenchyma or perinephric tissues. Less commonly, organisms like Klebsiella and Proteus species can also cause this condition.

The CT images below show intrarenal parenchymal gas suggestive of emphysematous pyelonephritis.

Almost all patients present with fever, vomiting, and flank pain. Patients frequently present with sepsis and ketoacidosis. If not treated early, it may lead to fulminant sepsis and is associated with high mortality.

The diagnosis is primarily established radiographically, with a CT scan being the investigation of choice in identifying the extent of the emphysematous process and guiding management.
question: A diabetic patient presents with acute onset fever and dysuria. Urinalysis reveals plenty of leukocytes with glycosuria. A CT scan of the abdomen is performed, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
explanationHtml:
The given MR nephrogram shows linear bands of contrast extending from the medulla of the kidney towards the cortex of the kidney, called a striated nephrogram. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) does not show a striated nephrogram.

Whereas, Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) shows a striated nephrogram.

A striated nephrogram is usually seen in:

  • Medullary sponge kidney (MSK)
  • Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD)
  • Acute papillary necrosis
  • Acute pyelonephritis
  • Renal tuberculosis
question: The MR nephrogram of a patient with loin pain is given below. All of the following can be included in the differential diagnoses except:

explanationHtml:
The findings are suggestive of an acute ureteric obstruction presenting as a dense, persistent nephrogram, where contrast remains in the kidney longer than expected.

In the given scenario, there is a delayed visualization of the left kidney, with contrast persisting beyond 10 minutes, while it has already cleared from the right kidney. Retention of intravenous contrast within the renal parenchyma for more than 3 minutes is defined as a dense, persistent nephrogram and is most commonly associated with acute ureteric obstruction.

The image below demonstrates a persistent nephrogram on the left side, with no contrast within the left pyelum and ureter.
question: A patient is undergoing a nephrogram. Two minutes after administering the contrast, both kidneys are visualized. After 10 minutes of contrast administration, only the left kidney is visualized. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Among the above options, the earliest radiographic finding in genitourinary tuberculosis on intravenous pyelography is the presence of moth-eaten calyces.

Moth-eaten calyces refer to the ragged, feathery calyceal outline due to irregular erosions of the calyx. This appearance is due to necrotizing papillitis, which further progresses to form medullary cavities that eventually communicate with the collecting system.

Genitourinary tuberculosis is caused by the dissemination of the organism through the bloodstream and is thus always a secondary TB. There is either reinfection or reactivation of old TB. It can affect the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, prostate, seminal vesicles, epididymis, and vas deferens.

Lesions caused by tuberculosis in the kidney include:

  • Papillary ulcer - the earliest lesion.
  • Pyonephrosis - caused by multiple scattered papillary ulcers undergoing caseous necrosis, which later become filled with pus.
  • Perinephric abscess - by extension of pyonephrosis or tuberculous renal abscess.
  • Pseudocalculi - occur when calcium gets deposited in a papillary ulcer healed with fibrosis.
  • Ghost calyces - caused by the destruction of the calyces.
  • Putty/cement kidney: Amorphous dystrophic calcification eventually involves the entire kidney (seen in X-ray and CT).

The illustration below shows the lesions caused by tuberculosis in the urinary tract, followed by an Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP) depicting moth-eaten calyces.

The intravenous urogram shown below demonstrates multiple infundibular stenoses involving the left kidney.

The given image shows the signs of renal papillary necrosis.
question: Among the following options, which is the earliest radiographic finding seen in patients with genitourinary tuberculosis?

explanationHtml:
Sterile pyuria in a patient with a history of tuberculosis raises suspicion of renal tuberculosis. The most sensitive imaging modality for diagnosing renal tuberculosis is CT urography.

Renal tuberculosis occurs due to hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, making it a secondary infection. There is either reinfection or reactivation of old TB. It is more common in males and typically presents with symptoms such as increased urinary frequency, polyuria, dysuria, hematuria, loin pain/suprapubic pain, and sterile pyuria.

In sterile pyuria, urine appears pale and opalescent due to the presence of pus cells. Renal TB is a cause of sterile pyuria. Diagnosis can be established through a tuberculin test or by analyzing at least 3 consecutive early-morning urine samples for acid-fast bacilli using Ziehl–Neelsen staining, followed by culture.

The most sensitive imaging modality in renal tuberculosis is CT urography/pyelography. NCCT is the preferred means of visualizing renal calcifications.

CT findings in renal tuberculosis may present in different stages:

  • Early stage:
    • Single or multiple areas of papillary necrosis
    • Irregular dilatation of the calyces (uneven caliectasis)
  • Advanced stage:
    • Multiple strictures occurring throughout the collecting system
    • Localized or diffuse hydronephrosis
    • Thickening and enhancement of the wall of the collecting system
    • Reduced enhancement of the renal parenchyma due to direct renal involvement
  • End-stage:
    • Progressive hydronephrosis results in very thin parenchyma, mimicking multiple thin-walled cysts
    • Diffuse dystrophic calcification of the destroyed kidney gives rise to the characteristic "putty kidney", as shown below:
question: A 59-year-old man was referred for abdominal pain and sterile pyuria. He was diagnosed with tuberculosis 10 years ago but was non-adherent to treatment. What is the most sensitive imaging modality for his current presentation?

explanationHtml:
The given X-ray shows coarse amorphous calcifications of both kidneys suggestive of medullary nephrocalcinosis. Alport's syndrome causes cortical nephrocalcinosis.

Nephrocalcinosis refers to the presence of calcification in the renal parenchyma, with most cases affecting the medulla and the remaining occurring in the cortex. On plain radiographs, cortical nephrocalcinosis and medullary nephrocalcinosis can produce punctate calcific opacities in the corresponding cortical and medullary zones of both kidneys.

Causes of medullary nephrocalcinosis include:

  • Distal renal tubular acidosis
  • Medullary sponge kidney
  • Hypercalcemia - including sarcoidosis
  • Hyperparathyroidism
  • Hyperoxaluria

Causes of cortical nephrocalcinosis include:

  • Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)
  • Graft rejection
  • Acute cortical necrosis
  • Chronic glomerulonephritis
  • Alport syndrome
question: A 29-year-old man presented with bilateral vague loin discomfort. Plain X-ray KUB was done. All of the following can cause this finding except:

explanationHtml:
The likely diagnosis is fibromuscular dysplasia(FMD).

The given renal angiographic image depicts the 'string of beads' sign, characterised by alternating areas of stenosis and small aneurysms in the renal arteries. This appearance is typical of FMD, a renovascular cause of secondary hypertension.

Fibromuscular dysplasia is a segmental, non-atheromatous, dysplastic type of angiopathy characterised by focal irregular thickening in medium and large muscular arteries predominantly affecting females. The most common subtype is medial fibroplasia.

The typical presentation is in the young person, commonly females, with new-onset hypertension. The most common sites of involvement in decreasing order of frequency are as follows: Renal arteries > carotid arteries > peripheral (limb) arteries - most commonly iliac arteries.
question: The renal angiographic picture of a patient is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given X-ray KUB image shows a markedly contracted bladder wall with reduced capacity, called a thimble bladder, which is a late complication of genitourinary tuberculosis.

Tuberculous cystitis results in fibrosis and stiffening of the entire urinary bladder, leading to an inability to expand and a significant reduction in bladder capacity, as depicted in the figure. The medical term for this feature on the intravenous urogram is a thimble bladder.

Genitourinary tuberculosis results from hematogenous spread of the pathogen and therefore represents a secondary form of infection. It may arise due to either reactivation of a dormant focus or a new reinfection. It can affect the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, prostate, seminal vesicles, epididymis, and vas deferens.

Lesions caused by tuberculosis in the kidney include:

  • Papillary ulcer - the earliest lesion
  • Pyonephrosis - caused by multiple scattered papillary ulcers undergoing caseous necrosis, which later become filled with pus
  • Perinephric abscess - by extension of pyonephrosis or tuberculous renal abscess
  • Pseudocalculi - occur when calcium gets deposited in a papillary ulcer healed with fibrosis
  • Ghost calyces - caused by the destruction of the calyces
  • Putty/cement kidney - calcification, which eventually involves the entire kidney

Ureteric lesions seen in genitourinary tuberculosis include Kerr’s kink (kinking of the ureteropelvic junction), stricture, beaded ureter, and shortening of the ureter. Other features of bladder TB include:

  • Golf hole ureteric orifice - This is due to fibrosis, causing the rigid, withdrawn, dilated ureteric orifice to look like a golf hole (cystoscopic finding).
  • Stippled calcifications

Schistosomiasis of the bladder begins with nodular wall thickening and progresses to a contracted, fibrotic bladder with calcifications. Cystoscopy shows pseudotubercles and “sandy patches,” and late disease increases the risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

Neurogenic bladder occurs due to defects anywhere in the pathway of the micturition reflex, e.g., spinal cord trauma, diabetes. It presents with urgency or urge incontinence.
question: Which of the listed conditions is characterized by the post-contrast appearance shown in the given image?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario and the CT-KUB, which demonstrates extensive bladder wall calcification resembling a fetal skull, are highly suggestive of Schistosomiasis.

Schistosoma haematobium primarily causes genito-urinary schistosomiasis. The adult worms live in the veins of the urinary bladder. Chronic schistosomiasis presents as painless terminal hematuria, dysuria, and proteinuria. Fibrosis may cause obstructive uropathies like hydronephrosis and hydroureter.

The radiographic features are as follows:

  • Acute phase - nodular bladder wall thickening
  • Chronic phase:
    • Contracted fibrotic, thick-walled bladder.
    • Curvilinear calcifications due to large numbers of calcified eggs in the bladder wall.
    • Complication - squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), presenting as a mass.

The CT-KUB shown below shows the calcified bladder resembling a fetal skull, suggestive of Schistosomiasis.

In bladder tuberculosis, chronic fibrosis and scarring may shrink the bladder into a small-capacity “thimble bladder.” The intravenous urogram shown below demonstrates a thimble bladder.

Pine cone or Christmas tree appearance, in which the bladder is elongated and pointed with a thickened trabeculated wall, is seen in cases of neurogenic bladder. The intravenous urogram shown below demonstrates the "pine cone" or "Christmas tree" appearance.

Cystourethroscopy is the mainstay for the diagnosis of bladder carcinoma. It is performed on patients with hematuria. The most common radiological sign is an interruption of the normal flow of contrast on intravenous urography (IVU). Non-contrast CT, MRI, and ultrasonography are used for the immediate management of patients with gross painless haematuria.
question: A 45-year-old man with lower urinary tract symptoms was lost to follow-up. Two months later, he returned with worsening symptoms, and repeat CT-KUB imaging revealed a densely calcified bladder resembling a fetal skull. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The likely diagnosis is neurogenic bladder. The given cystogram shows an elongated and pointed bladder with a thickened trabeculated wall, called a Christmas tree or pine cone bladder. This is seen in patients with severe neurogenic bladder and increased sphincter tone.

Neurogenic bladder is a term applied to a dysfunctional urinary bladder that results from an injury to the central or peripheral nerves that control and regulate urination. It causes detrusor sphincter dyssynergia. Neurogenic bladder typically occurs due to suprasacral lesions (above S2-S4) or apical lesions (in and around S2-S4).

Pine cone bladder is not pathognomonic of a neurogenic bladder. It may also be seen in patients with lesions anywhere along the sacral reflex arc. Occasionally, it is also seen in non-neurogenic bladder neck obstruction.

Tuberculous cystitis results in fibrosis and stiffening of the entire urinary bladder, leading to an inability to expand and a significant reduction in bladder capacity, as depicted in the image below. The medical term for this feature on a micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) is "thimble bladder".

Bladder carcinoma causes mucosal and muscular disruption of the bladder wall. Cystourethroscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis in patients presenting with hematuria, and intravenous urography commonly shows a filling defect.

Schistosomiasis of the bladder, caused by Schistosoma haematobium, presents with nodular bladder wall thickening in the acute stage and a contracted, calcified bladder in chronic disease. Cystoscopy may show nodules, pseudotubercles, ulcers, or sandy patches, and long-standing disease can progress to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

The CT-KUB image below shows calcification of the bladder wall.
question: The cystographic evaluation of a woman with recurrent urinary tract infection is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a pear-shaped bladder. A neurogenic bladder does not cause a pear-shaped bladder.

A pear-shaped bladder refers to a deformation in which the normally round or ovoid bladder is externally compressed, causing it to take on a pear-like appearance. This shape may appear either inverted (often described as a “teardrop bladder”) or upright, depending on the direction and distribution of the surrounding pelvic tissue exerting pressure on the bladder.

The causes of the pear-shaped bladder include pelvic abscess, pelvic lipomatosis, pelvic hematoma, and symmetrical pelvic lymphadenopathy.

Neurogenic bladder results in a Christmas tree, fir tree, or pine cone appearance, where the urinary bladder becomes elongated with a pointed shape and a thickened trabeculated wall, as depicted below:
question: In a patient with the following cystogram finding, which of the following would you not suspect?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a right-sided fishhook or S-shaped appearance of the ureter, where the right ureter hooks behind the inferior vena cava (IVC), as seen in the retrocaval ureter.

Circumcaval or retrocaval ureter is a developmental anomaly of the inferior vena cava (IVC). It is due to the abnormal development of the right supracardinal system. A persistent right posterior cardinal vein ends up passing in front of the ureter. The anomaly always occurs on the right side, as this is the side of the normal IVC.

The GIF demonstrates the characteristic fishhook (S-shaped) configuration of the ureter.

Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) is a condition with a retrograde urinary flow from the bladder to the ureter and kidney. It is usually congenital. VUR can cause urinary stasis and lead to urinary tract infection (UTI). It also predisposes to pyelonephritis, which can lead to renal scarring due to parenchymal inflammation. This is known as reflux nephropathy. A micturating cystogram is used to confirm the VUR.

The image below demonstrates unilateral vesicoureteric reflux.

Note: Bilateral fishhook or J-shaped or hockey stick ureters describe the course of the distal ureter in patients with significant benign prostatic hypertrophy (BPH).
question: A child with recurrent UTIs is suspected to have a congenital renal anomaly. The following picture is seen on IV urography. Based on these findings, which of the following would you suspect?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario with recurrent UTIs and hydronephrosis on USG is suggestive of vesicoureteric reflux (VUR). The investigation of choice in this condition is a voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) or micturating cystourethrogram (MCU).

VUR refers to an abnormal urine flow from the bladder to the ureters and occurs in young children. This reflux predisposes to pyelonephritis by allowing the entry of bacteria into the usually sterile upper tract. As such, the diagnosis is first suspected after a UTI in a very young child or recurrent UTIs. USG may reveal abnormalities like hydronephrosis and dilated ureters. VCUG must be performed in such children before the age of 6 years to look for:

  • Presence and grade of VUR.
  • Whether reflux occurs during micturition or bladder filling.
  • Presence of associated anatomical anomalies.

The grading of VUR is based on the height of reflux up the ureters and the degree of dilatation of the ureters, as shown below.

The MCU image given below shows grade V vesicoureteric reflux.

The 99mTc-DTPA scan is used to assess glomerular filtration rate, as the tracer is eliminated solely through filtration without undergoing tubular handling. It also helps in determining split renal function and overall renal functional status.

The investigation of choice for ureteropelvic junction obstruction is a 99mTc-Mercaptoacetyl-triglycine (MAG3) scan. 99mTc-MAG3 is the most commonly used isotope in dynamic renography. Its uptake reflects the tubular function.

The 99mTc-DMSA scan is used for the assessment of the renal cortex as it binds to the sulfhydryl groups in proximal tubules with longer retention than other agents. It allows for a better assessment of differential renal function. It is used for the evaluation of the renal structure and morphology, detection of renal scarring in reflux nephropathy and pyelonephritis, and evaluation of renal anatomical abnormalities.
question: A 2-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of fever with recurrent urinary tract infections. He suffered 4 episodes over the past 9 months and had been hospitalized twice. An ultrasound revealed bilateral hydronephrosis with dilatation of the ureters. What is the investigation of choice in this child?

explanationHtml:
The given voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) shows a unilateral grade 4 vesicoureteric reflux (VUR). The investigation of choice to evaluate for renal scarring in reflux nephropathy is the Tc-99m DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan.

It is used in renal imaging to evaluate renal structure and morphology, particularly in paediatric imaging for the detection of scarring and pyelonephritis. DMSA is an ideal agent for the assessment of the renal cortex as it binds within the proximal tubules of the cortex with longer retention than other agents.

It allows a better assessment of differential renal function. It is a static scan as opposed to dynamic DTPA or MAG3 scans. Other common renal scans include:

  • Tc-99m DTPA (diethylene-triamine-pentaacetate) - used for direct measurement of GFR as it is cleared only via glomeruli with no tubular excretion (option B).
  • Tc-99m MAG3 (mercaptoacetyltriglycine) - excreted through the renal route via both glomeruli infiltration and tubular excretion. Hence, in pediatric patients and patients with poor renal function, this test is considered superior to a DTPA scan. (option C).
  • In renovascular hypertension, captopril DTPA is used for screening and the gold standard investigation is renal angiography.
  • Tc-99m pertechnetate - used for the investigation of gastrointestinal tract haemorrhage from Meckle's diverticulum.

The following image shows a DMSA scan of a patient with renal failure with reduced uptake in both kidneys.
question: The following spot film was taken while performing a voiding cystourethrogram for a 2-year-old girl. Which of the following investigations will be useful for the evaluation of renal scarring in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The ultrasound demonstrates the “keyhole sign,” characterised by dilatation of the proximal urethra and a thick-walled urinary bladder. This finding is highly suggestive of posterior urethral valves (PUV).

Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of severe obstructive uropathy in children. The valves are membranes that have a small posterior slit within them, which typically lie just distal to the verumontanum. They function as flap valves and are obstructive to antegrade urinary flow.

Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound, which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis above a distended bladder in the fetus, along with oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia. If the diagnosis is not made antenatally, then babies typically present with urinary infections in the neonatal period or with uremia and renal failure. Clinically, a poor urinary stream, dribbling, and palpable bladder (due to diverticula) can be present.

The diagnosis is best made during the micturition phase of VCUG in lateral or oblique views so that the posterior urethra can be imaged adequately. The following findings are seen:

  • Dilatation and elongation of the posterior urethra - the equivalent of the ultrasonographic keyhole sign (as shown in the image below).
  • Linear radiolucent band corresponding to the valve - seen occasionally.
  • Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) - seen in 50% of patients.
  • Bladder trabeculation/ diverticula.
question: A neonate is being evaluated for urinary abnormalities. Ultrasonography reveals the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) or micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) is the best imaging technique for diagnosing posterior urethral valves.

Posterior urethral valves result from the formation of a thick, valve-like membrane from a tissue of Wolffian duct origin (failure of regression of the mesonephric duct). This membrane courses obliquely from the verumontanum to the most distal portion of the prostatic urethra. They act as flap valves and are obstructive to antegrade urinary flow.

Ultrasound (USG) is the primary initial screening tool. PUVs are often discovered on antenatal maternal ultrasound (revealing bilateral hydronephrosis and a distended bladder) or early postnatal ultrasound. A classic sonographic finding is the "keyhole sign" (a thickened, distended bladder coupled with a dilated posterior urethra).

However, the diagnosis is best made during the micturition phase of VCUG in lateral or oblique views so that the posterior urethra can be imaged adequately. The following findings are seen:

  • Dilatation and elongation of the posterior urethra - the equivalent of the ultrasonographic keyhole sign (as shown in the image below).
  • Linear radiolucent band corresponding to the valve - seen occasionally.
  • Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) - seen in 50% of patients.
  • Bladder trabeculation/ diverticula.
question:
What is the investigation of choice for evaluating posterior urethral valves in a newborn male?

MCU - MIcturating cystourethrography; Tc DTPA - Tecnetitium-99m Diethylenetriamine Pentaacetate; DMSA - Dimercaptosuccinic acid

correctAnswer: C. Transitional cell carcinoma of ureter
explanationHtml:
The given retrograde ureterogram shows focal dilatation of the ureter caused by an intraluminal mass, producing the classic “goblet” or “champagne glass” sign. This appearance is most commonly associated with transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter.

Transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter may produce localized asymmetric or ring-like mural thickening. On imaging, it may be seen as a persistent filling defect or uneven ureteric narrowing, with abrupt margins at the proximal end. This gives the typical goblet sign, also called the champagne glass sign.

This sign occurs due to luminal dilatation distal to the tumour, caused by the slow-growing tumour expanding the ureteral lumen. Additional features include hydronephrosis, with or without hydroureter, and, in advanced cases, absent renal function due to chronic obstruction.

This sign indicates the pathology is chronic, permitting the lesion to be accommodated in the ureter. Other causes of goblet sign include metastatic disease in the ureter and endometriosis involving the ureter.
question: A 48-year-old woman underwent retrograde ureterography as part of an evaluation for intermittent loin pain and dysuria. The following finding is seen. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The diagnosis is renal angiomyolipoma. The given CT image shows well-circumscribed lesions with low attenuation (hypodense) that indicate fatty tissue, suggesting renal angiomyolipoma.

Angiomyolipomas (AMLs) are benign tumours that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. It is commonly seen in adults between 30 and 50 years of age, with a female predilection. AMLs predominantly affect the kidneys, though they can occur in other sites such as the liver (a common extra-renal location) and, less frequently, in the ovary, fallopian tube, spermatic cord, palate, and colon.

Histologically, angiomyolipomas consist of perivascular epitheloid cells with varying proportions of vascular, immature smooth muscle cells, and fat cells. Patients with AMLs present with flank pain, a palpable mass, hematuria, recurrent urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure.

Angiomyolipomas usually cause hypertension, but in the case of rupture leading to retroperitoneal haemorrhage, it will result in hypotension. Larger tumours increase the risk of complications, such as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, which can manifest as sudden-onset abdominal or flank pain, along with symptoms like nausea, vomiting, and hypotension.

Everolimus is used for the treatment of angiomyolipomas. Treatment should be considered for asymptomatic, growing AMLs measuring >3 cm in diameter. Angiomyolipomas do not normally require surgery unless life-threatening bleeding is present.

Renal cyst is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions need evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification is used for renal cysts. Cysts appear as hypodense lesions (greyish) with a thin wall, with or without septations.

CT image showing a simple renal cyst:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common malignant tumour of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Parapelvic cysts are small congenital lymphatic lesions located within the renal sinus, situated between the calyceal infundibula. They may exert pressure on and displace the calyceal system. On ultrasonography, they often resemble hydronephrosis because both present as hypoechoic areas within the renal sinus.

However, unlike hydronephrosis, parapelvic cysts do not communicate with the collecting system.
question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with severe back pain, vomiting, and hypotension. CT findings are given below. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
According to the Bosniak classification, this lesion is best categorized as Bosniak IIF.

Bosniak IIF lesions show multiple (≥4) thin septa with smooth minimal wall thickening up to 3 mm, measurable enhancement, and may show calcification. Nodules are not present. These are indeterminate lesions requiring follow-up.

The Bosniak classification system is used for the classification of renal cystic masses based on characteristics seen on contrast-enhanced CT. It helps predict malignancy risk and formulate a management plan.

  • Bosniak I: Simple cyst with thin wall (≤2 mm), no septa or calcification. No enhancing nodule
  • Bosniak II: Thin wall (≤2 mm), thin septa (≤2 mm), few septa (≤3), may have calcification. No enhancing solid nodule
  • Bosniak IIF: Multiple (≥4) thin septa with smooth minimal thickening (~≤3 mm), may show enhancement and calcification. No enhancing solid nodule
  • Bosniak III: Thick (≥4 mm), irregular or smooth but enhancing walls/septa. No enhancing solid nodule
  • Bosniak IV: Enhancing cystic mass with a definite enhancing soft-tissue nodule

The table below shows the malignancy risk associated with each type of cyst.

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario of sudden scrotal pain while playing is suspicious for testicular torsion; the investigation of choice is Doppler ultrasonography. It indicates reduced or absent blood flow to the testes.

In testicular torsion, twisting of the spermatic cord compromises the arterial supply to the testis. The twist occurs within the tunica vaginalis, producing the bell-clapper appearance and causing ischemic injury to the testis and epididymis. It is typically seen in adolescence. Patients usually present with acute scrotal pain and swelling, often accompanied by vomiting.

A high-riding, swollen, and tender testis with a tender twisted cord can often be palpated above it, along with an erythematous scrotum and absent cremasteric reflex on the affected side.

A Doppler ultrasound may be taken to assess the blood supply, but surgical exploration is still indicated as a clinical decision. Color Doppler ultrasonography demonstrates markedly reduced or absent arterial perfusion within the affected testis when compared with the opposite side.

Doppler studies have improved the ultrasonographic evaluation of testicular torsion with the presence of the whirlpool sign within the spermatic cord, which represents the twisted cord and is analogous to the twisted ovarian pedicle seen in ovarian torsion.

If torsion is clinically suspected, urgent scrotal exploration should be done without delay. A transverse scrotal incision is taken, and if the testis appears viable, repeat torsion is avoided by performing orchiopexy. The testis is secured to the scrotal septum using three permanent sutures placed through the tunica albuginea to minimize the risk of recurrent torsion.
question: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the ER with left-sided scrotal pain and nausea. It developed suddenly 30 minutes ago while playing football. On examination, the left scrotum is reddish with mild tenderness, and the testis is in horizontal lie. What is the investigation of choice?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of bilateral pedal edema in an elderly patient with left-sided renal cell carcinoma is suspicious for tumor extension into the left renal vein and inferior vena cava (IVC). The investigation of choice to assess the vascular extent of the tumor thrombus is MRI.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is beneficial for assessing vascular invasion, particularly of the renal vein and IVC. It aids in differentiating between benign and malignant thrombus. However, it does not provide a significant advantage over CT in staging nodal disease.

Renal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney that usually presents in the elderly. Cigarette smoking and hypertension are major associated risk factors. The classic triad of presentation is with flank pain, macroscopic haematuria, and a palpable flank mass. Advanced cases can also present with bilateral lower limb edema.

Triphasic contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis and staging of RCC (image given below). On CT, small lesions enhance homogeneously, whereas larger lesions have irregular enhancement due to areas of necrosis.

CT imaging further helps evaluate the functional status of the contralateral kidney, the extent of spread from the primary lesion, regional nodal involvement, adrenal gland abnormalities, and the presence of metastatic deposits within the abdomen.

Intravenous urography is no longer suitable for detecting renal masses, particularly if they occur centrally; cross-sectional imaging studies are more appropriate for investigating suspected renal masses.

FDG-Positron Emission Tomography (PET) has limited utility in the initial diagnosis and staging of renal cell carcinoma. This is due to the low fluorodeoxyglucose uptake by these tumors, which can make lesions difficult to detect. However, FDG-PET proves valuable in postoperative surveillance, identifying recurrence or metastases, and monitoring the effectiveness of targeted therapies.

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of renal calculi, and the investigation of choice is non-contrast CT (NCCT).

NCCT is useful as it has a greater sensitivity to tissue attenuation and, hence, can pick up stones that may appear radiolucent on plain X-rays.

A non-contrast CT scan is the imaging modality of choice for suspected urinary tract calculi. It is the most sensitive and gold-standard test for detecting stones as it is quick, detects most types of calculi, and can be performed with low radiation doses. A history of nephrolithiasis with new-onset flank pain should prompt immediate evaluation with non-contrast CT. The radiographic features depend on the stone composition.

Renal calculi are more common in males, with 90% of stones being radiopaque. Clinically, patients present with severe pain located over the renal angle, often radiating to the groin. The pain may be accompanied by vomiting due to pyloric spasm, as well as hematuria, nausea, fever, and, in some cases, symptoms of pyuria.

The following types of renal calculi may appear radiolucent on plain X-ray: Uric acid, Indinavir and pure matrix stones (may have radiodense rim or centre). On CT, most stones are usually opaque. However, indinavir and pure matrix stones appear radiolucent even on CT.

The following X-ray KUB image shows a staghorn calculus (struvite).
question: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department with complaints of severe, right-sided, colicky flank pain that radiates to his groin. He has a history of recurrent kidney stones. What is the investigation of choice?

explanationHtml:
Retroperitoneal fibrosis is the likely diagnosis.

The given IVP in a patient with persistent flank pain demonstrates medial deviation of both ureters. This occurs due to fibrous tissue deposition in the retroperitoneum, typically at the lumbosacral level, producing the characteristic “narrow-waisted” or “maiden waist” appearance. This imaging feature is classic for retroperitoneal fibrosis.

Retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF) is a chronic, nonspecific inflammatory process of the fibro-fatty tissue in the retroperitoneum, with the idiopathic type being the most common, accounting for about 70% of the cases. Patients typically present with persistent flank pain or back pain.

Progressive fibrotic thickening can compress the ureters, leading to bilateral hydronephrosis and, if untreated, renal failure. Aside from idiopathic causes, other causes of RPF include drug-induced factors ( e.g., methysergide, beta-blockers), advanced malignancy, radiation exposure, trauma, and chronic infections.

Diagnosis of RPF relies primarily on imaging studies. Intravenous urography shows a characteristic triad of medial deviation of the middle one-third of the ureters, producing a maiden waist sign, hydroureteronephrosis, and extrinsic compression of the ureters by the fibrotic process. CT and MRI are also useful in radiographic evaluation of RPF.
question:
The IVP of a patient with persistent flank pain is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

IVP- Intravenous Pyelogram

explanationHtml:
The given intravenous pyelography (IVP) depicts the cobra head or adder head deformity or spring onion sign seen in bilateral ureterocele.

These signs refer to a dilated, contrast-filled distal ureter surrounded by a thin rim of the ureteric wall and bladder mucosa. The GIF below illustrates the classic “cobra head” appearance.

Ureterocoele is a cystic enlargement of the intramural portion of the ureter, more commonly seen in females than males. It is thought to be caused by ureteric orifice atresia. They are similar to ectopic ureters, which typically drain the upper pole of the kidney and are associated with dysplastic or non-functional renal tissue.

If they present clinically, ureteroceles often manifest with urinary tract infections (UTIs) in children, while in adults, they are more likely to present with stones in the lower ureter. Ureteroceles can enlarge and obstruct the bladder neck or the contralateral ureteric orifice.

The classic sign of a ureterocele on intravenous urography is a ‘cobra head’, ‘adder head’, or 'spring onion sign'. On ultrasonography, it can be seen as a fluid-filled cystic mass in the bladder.

The treatment of simple ureteroceles is surgical excision with re-implantation of the ureter.
question: The following appearance in IVP is caused by:

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario is suggestive of a molar pregnancy. A transvaginal ultrasound is the most sensitive initial investigation for diagnosing this condition.

The snowstorm appearance on USG, combined with a raised hCG and a uterus larger than the date of pregnancy, leads to the diagnosis of a complete hydatidiform mole.

The transvaginal ultrasound image below demonstrates the characteristic “snowstorm” appearance of a molar pregnancy.

Molar pregnancy is of two types:

  • Complete mole appears as an echogenic uterine mass with numerous anechoic cystic spaces but without a fetus or amnionic sac. The appearance is described as a 'snowstorm' appearance. Theca lutein cysts may be seen in the ovary.
  • In partial mole, the fetus is present along with molar components.

The patient presents with a characteristic history of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or spotting, and vomiting during the first trimester. Also, there may be a history of passing grape-like vesicles vaginally.

Suction and evacuation is the treatment of choice. Serum hCG levels are checked within 48 hours of evacuation and are used as a baseline for future comparisons. It is then checked every week until it normalizes, which usually takes 4 to 8 weeks. After the hCG values return to normal, a regular follow-up is done monthly for 6 months.

explanationHtml:
The given MRI image shows agenesis of the corpus callosum.

Agenesis of the corpus callosum resulting from abnormal development of midline prosencephalic structures. It can be associated with other cerebral malformations such as heterotopias, polymicrogyria, or pachygyria (broad, thickened gyri).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice for evaluation, as it clearly delineates the anatomical features. Typical findings include widely spaced frontal horns of the lateral ventricles and an abnormally elevated third ventricle interposed between them.

On axial CT or MRI, the widely separated lateral ventricles and intervening Probst bundles create a characteristic "racing car" (Formula One car) appearance. The widely spaced frontal horns resemble the front tyres, while the dilated trigones (colpocephaly) represent the rear tyres.

The image given below shows the racing car sign in corpus callosal agenesis.

Marchiafava - Bignami disease is a rare condition characterized by demyelination of the corpus callosum most often in patients with chronic alcoholism. The MRI image in this condition shows the sandwich sign.

Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an autosomal-recessive disease that results from a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase A. Symmetric confluent areas of T2 hyperintensity are seen in the periventricular white matter. Radiating T2 hypointense lines through the demyelinated deep white matter represent the sparing of the perivascular white matter. This results in the tigroid and leopard skin patterns when imaged in the long axis or cross-section, respectively. Subcortical U-fibers are spared.

Wilson disease is characterized by the “face of the giant panda” sign. It is seen on axial FLAIR/T2 images of the midbrain and is characterized by hypointensity of the superior colliculus (forming the “chin and mouth”), hyperintensity in the tegmentum (forming the “eyes”), and preserved signal intensity of the substantia nigra (forming the “ears”).
question: Antenatal USG in a primigravida revealed fetal hydrocephalus. Postnatal MRI of the infant is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The frog-eye sign in the ultrasound is suggestive of anencephaly.

Anencephaly is an open defect in the calvaria and skin that results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. It is one of the earliest detectable congenital defects, detectable as early as 10 to 11 weeks of gestation. Screening for anencephaly reveals elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) levels.

Diagnosis is confirmed by sonography. The following are the radiological signs seen in anencephaly:

  • Frog eye sign - Absence of cranial calvaria, causing prominent orbits, thereby resembling the face of a frog.
  • Shower cap sign - The absence of the cranium could lead to the protrusion of a disorganised mass of brain tissue. This resembles a shower cap, giving rise to a characteristic triangular facial appearance.

The images given below show an open calvarium on antenatal ultrasound and a 'shower cap' sign.

Eye of tiger sign is the MRI finding seen in Hallervorden-Spatz syndrome, a rare autosomal recessive neurogenerative disorder, showing decreased T2 signal in globus pallidus and substania nigra.

The blob sign is seen in tubal ectopic pregnancy, and the T sign is seen in twin pregnancy.
question: A 30-year-old female with a history of anencephaly in a previous child is scheduled to undergo a screening ultrasound to rule out anencephaly in her current pregnancy. Which among the following findings confirms the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The pelvic ultrasound in a 35-year-old woman shows the 'T-sign' seen in a monochorionic twin pregnancy.

In monochorionic pregnancy, the chorion does not extend between the layers of the intertwin membrane. Thus, the inter-twin membrane comes to an abrupt halt in a T-configuration at the edge of the amniotic sac.

In contrast, in a dichorionic pregnancy, the sonographic image depicts a 'twin-peak' sign or the 'lambda sign" as the chorion is present between the intertwin membrane. A triangular portion of the placenta is seen inserted between the amniochorion layers.

The type of twin pregnancy is best diagnosed by transabdominal ultrasound at 11-14 weeks of gestation as the chorion and amnion are not yet fused. At 11-14 weeks, the intervening membranes are clearly visualized at the site of insertion of the amniotic membrane into the placenta. If not visualised transabdominally, transvaginal ultrasound is done.

Sonographic assessment is done by observing the following:

Monochorionicity Dichorionicity
Placental mass 1 2
Presence of intervening membrane T sign twin peak/ lambda/ delta sign
Thickness of intervening membrane <2mm ≥ 2mm
question: The pelvic ultrasound of a 35-year-old woman is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given image demonstrates transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS), which is carried out on an empty bladder. The bladder should be empty for transvaginal USG to allow visualisation of other structures.

A protective sheath (often a condom) is used over the probe before the TVS transducer is inserted into the vagina. It provides higher-resolution images compared to transabdominal USG because of the proximity to the pelvic organs. During a transabdominal ultrasound, the bladder should be full to create a good echo window.

Clinical Applications of TVS:

  • Early pregnancy
  • Lower uterine segment evaluation in late pregnancy
  • Endometrial thickness can be measured
  • Ectopic, pelvic masses
  • Obese patients
  • Follicular and endometrial studies
  • Doppler examination of pelvic organs
  • Interventional procedures

explanationHtml:
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the best investigation to identify congenital uterine anomalies.

MRI provides excellent visualization of the uterus by clearly delineating both the internal zonal anatomy and the external fundal contour. This level of detail is particularly important for differentiating major anomalies, such as a septate versus a bicornuate uterus. It is non-invasive and therefore highly preferred in clinical practice.

In addition, MRI allows a comprehensive assessment of the entire pelvic region. This helps identify any associated anomalies often linked with Müllerian defects, enhancing diagnostic accuracy and sensitivity in detecting uterine malformations.

Conventional ultrasonography is the primary initial investigation. However, not all anomalies can be accurately detected or classified, particularly when differentiating anomalies such as a septate uterus from a bicornuate uterus using traditional 2D ultrasound techniques.

MRI is considered the best investigation because it is superior to conventional ultrasonography for the evaluation of congenital uterine (Müllerian) anomalies. Computed Tomography and X-ray are not preferred, and in case of suspected pregnancy, they are avoided.

Hysterosalpingography is also performed. However, it cannot differentiate between a septate and bicornuate uterus, as only the uterine interior is visualized, resulting in similar images on HSG.
question: A young girl with primary amenorrhea is being evaluated for the presence of a congenital uterine anomaly. Which of the following is the best investigation to identify the anomaly?

explanationHtml:
The arrow shown in the given transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) points to the gestational sac, which is the earliest sonographic evidence of pregnancy. It may typically be visualised by 4-5 weeks of gestation.

Visualization of a yolk sac inside the gestational sac, typically seen as a highly echogenic circular structure surrounding a dark central area, establishes that the pregnancy is situated within the uterine cavity. It is typically visible by the middle of the 5th week, and cardiac activity in an embryo can be identified at 6 weeks.

The double decidual sac sign (DDSS) is a useful feature on early pregnancy ultrasound to confirm an early intrauterine pregnancy when the yolk sac or embryo is still not visualised. It consists of the decidua parietalis (lining the uterine cavity) and decidua capsularis (lining the gestational sac) and is seen as two concentric rings surrounding an anechoic gestational sac.

The double decidual sac sign differentiates normal pregnancy from the pseudo-gestational sac of an ectopic pregnancy. A pseudosac typically appears as an uneven fluid collection situated near the centre of the uterine cavity, lacks the characteristic double decidual reaction, and does not contain embryonic structures. question: What is the diagnosis based on the given image?

explanationHtml:
The given Doppler image indicates normal diastolic flow in the umbilical arteries.

Umbilical artery vessels are characterized by forward, low-resistance flow. As gestation increases, there is a gradual fall in all the resistance indices, so the amount of forward diastolic flow increases. S/D ratio decreases as the period of gestation increases (S represents the peak systolic flow or velocity, and D indicates the end-diastolic flow or velocity).

Abnormal flow patterns in the umbilical artery:

  • Reduced end-diastolic flow: Uteroplacental insufficiency.
  • Absent end-diastolic flow: Fetal compromise (terminate the pregnancy by cesarean section if gestational age is >34 weeks).
  • Reverse end-diastolic flow: Impending doom of death (terminate pregnancy irrespective of gestational age).

Middle cerebral artery: This will show increased diastolic velocity in fetus with hypoxemia.
question: A 26-year-old pregnant woman has the following flow pattern of umbilical arteries on a Doppler study. What does this pattern indicate?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows the lemon sign, which is seen in spina bifida.

The lemon sign is related to changes in the configuration of the fetal frontal bone, which loses convexity and appears concave or linear on ultrasonography. This sign can be detected during the first six months of gestation.

Spina bifida is a common open neural tube defect associated with hydrocephalus and Arnold-Chiari II malformation. It is the most common open neural tube disorder. Spina bifida results from a defect in the vertebral column along with a corresponding defect in the skin, which causes the meninges and spinal nerve roots to be exposed.

The 3 main types of spina bifida:

  • Spina bifida occulta - This is the mildest form of spina bifida. The defect in the vertebral arches is covered by the skin. The splits in the vertebrae are so small that the spinal cord does not protrude. The skin at the site of the lesion may be normal, or it may have some hair growing from it.
  • Meningocele - The defect in the vertebra allows the meninges to protrude through the defect.
  • Myelomeningocele (meningomyelocele) - A defect in the vertebral column allows the spinal cord with the meningeal coverings to protrude.

The image below shows the various types of spina bifida.

The banana sign is another sign that is seen in spina bifida associated with Arnold-Chiari II malformation. Herniation of the brainstem and cerebellar tonsils occurs through the foramen magnum, with the cerebellum surrounding the brainstem, thus giving rise to the appearance of the curved shape of a banana.

Anencephaly is characterised by an open calvarial defect with exposed cranial neural tissue. On ultrasound, the “frog-eye” sign is seen with prominent orbits and absent cranial cerebral tissue.

Omphalocele is a midline anterior abdominal wall defect with herniation of abdominal contents into a membrane-covered sac. Given below is a fetal ultrasound image suggestive of an omphalocele (asterisk).

Holoprosencephaly results from failure of forebrain division, leading to a single ventricular cavity (horseshoe or boomerang-shaped), fused frontal lobes, and corpus callosum abnormalities.
question: A 24-year-old primigravida has come for an antenatal ultrasound examination. The sonographic image obtained is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical picture is suggestive of a breast abscess, and the most appropriate initial imaging modality is ultrasonography (USG).

USG is the investigation of choice for evaluating inflammatory and suppurative breast conditions, as it reliably distinguishes cystic (fluid-filled) lesions from solid masses and can also detect associated features such as axillary lymphadenopathy. It is especially useful in pregnant and lactating women and in patients under 40 years, where dense breast tissue reduces the sensitivity of mammography.

A key clinical feature is localized probe tenderness on USG, which supports an inflammatory or infective process, such as an abscess, and helps distinguish it from a painless solid tumour.

The ultrasound image shown below shows a breast abscess.

Mammography is preferred in women over 40 years, mainly for evaluation of breast lumps or persistent symptoms, including non-resolving puerperal abscesses, to exclude underlying malignancy.

Breast MRI is the most sensitive modality for detecting breast malignancy and is primarily reserved for high-risk patients (genetic predisposition), typically used for screening from around 25–30 years of age.
question: A 29 year old lactating female presents with painful breast lump on the right side since 5 days but denies any history of fever or previous episodes of breast issues. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the investigation of choice?

explanationHtml:
For high-risk screening of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), breast MRI is the investigation of choice, as it is the most sensitive imaging modality.

On MRI, DCIS typically presents as ductal or non-mass-like enhancement, reflecting abnormal proliferation within the ductal system. Screening breast MRI is recommended for women at high risk of breast cancer (known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, strong family history of breast cancer, hereditary cancer syndromes), and is typically initiated between 25 and 30 years of age.

Breast MRI is ideally performed during the second week (follicular phase) of the menstrual cycle. This timing minimizes hormonal influences, as elevated estrogen and progesterone levels during the luteal phase can cause stromal edema and lobular development, leading to physiological enhancement that may obscure or mimic pathology.

Mammography may miss such lesions in younger women due to dense glandular breast tissue, which reduces its sensitivity.

explanationHtml:
Under the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, Form F is for the maintenance of scan records for each pregnant woman undergoing the ultrasound scan.

Form F is the record of the Genetic Clinic / Ultrasound Clinic. This form is maintained for each pregnant woman undergoing an ultrasound or any prenatal diagnostic procedure. It includes patient details, medical indications for the procedure, and declarations signed by both the patient and the doctor. The record must be preserved for a minimum of 2 years, or until the completion of any legal proceedings, whichever is later.

Registration and records under the PCPNDT Act require all centres to be registered, display a no sex determination notice, and maintain records in the prescribed forms, such as:

  • Form D – Maintenance of counselling records for each woman at genetic counselling centres
  • Form E – Maintenance of records by genetic laboratories (Option D)
  • Form F – Maintenance of scan records for each pregnant woman undergoing the ultrasound scan
  • Form G – Written consent of a pregnant woman before undergoing invasive prenatal diagnostic procedures (Option C)

Whereas, Form A is the application for the registration of a clinic/lab/ultrasound centre with the authority under the Act (Option A).

The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 (PCPNDT Act), amended in 2003, is a law that prohibits sex selection, sex determination, disclosure of fetal sex, related advertising, and use of unregistered clinics/machines.

It applies to genetic counselling centres, genetic laboratories, genetic clinics, ultrasound clinics, and imaging centres that use techniques such as ultrasound, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling (CVS), and fetoscopy.

The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 (PCPNDT Act), amended in 2003, is a law that prohibits sex selection, sex determination, disclosure of fetal sex, related advertising, and use of unregistered clinics/machines.

An initial offence is punishable with a prison term of up to three years, along with a monetary penalty of up to ₹ 10,000. In the case of a repeat offence, the penalty increases to a prison term of up to five years, along with a monetary penalty that may reach ₹ 50,000.

explanationHtml:
Hysterosalpingography in a patient with bilateral hydrosalpinx would reveal bilateral dilated fallopian tubes with no free spill.

A hydrosalpinx is a chronic cystic swelling of the fallopian tube that forms after a distal tubal obstruction. The tubes are enormously distended due to filling with clear serous fluid and become retort-shaped. On histology, the tubal plicae appear flattened.

The interstitial end of the tube is open, whereas the fimbrial end is indrawn and closed. This permits the dye to enter but not exit the tube during HSG.

The hysterosalpingogram shown below demonstrates bilateral dilated fallopian tubes with no free spill.

In a normal hysterosalpingography (HSG), free spillage of contrast into the peritoneal cavity indicates normal tubal patency. In contrast, tuberculous salpingitis may show a characteristic “tobacco pouch” appearance, due to rigid, beaded, and irregularly dilated fallopian tubes with distal block and peritubal adhesions.

The hysterosalpingogram shown below demonstrates intrauterine filling defects, which are typically seen in conditions such as endometrial polyps and submucosal fibroids.

explanationHtml:
The X-ray shows a champagne glass pelvis and is suggestive of achondroplasia.

Achondroplasia is a genetic disorder resulting in proximal limb shortening (rhizomelic dwarfism). It is the most common cause of disproportionate dwarfism. The iliac blades are flattened, giving rise to a pelvic inlet that resembles a champagne glass. The acetabular roofs appear relatively flat with a more horizontal orientation, and the sacrosciatic notches are reduced in size.

The image below shows a patient with achondroplasia -

Hip dysplasia usually presents with hip dislocation.

explanationHtml:
In achondroplasia, the tombstone appearance of the pelvis is produced by squaring of the iliac blades rather than by the acetabula.

Other radiological findings seen in achondroplasia include:

  • Large skull with -
    • Prominent forehead
    • Depressed nasal bridge
    • Small, funnel-shaped foramen magnum
  • Epiphyses with V-shaped distal ends and deep intercondylar notches, known as the “chevron sign.
  • Spinal features:
    • Bullet-shaped vertebrae

question: Radiograph of a child with history of delayed walking showed the following findings. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Dense metaphyseal bands are not seen in primary hyperparathyroidism. It is seen in hypoparathyroidism.

Dense metaphyseal bands occur when there is increased bone deposition and/or decreased osteoclastic remodeling at the metaphysis, leading to the appearance of sclerotic lines on radiographs.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by increased osteoclastic bone resorption, which results in bone loss rather than sclerosis. Therefore, dense metaphyseal bands are not a feature of this condition. In contrast, Hypoparathyroidism is associated with dense metaphyseal bands.

The image below shows dense metaphyseal bands (red arrow):

Dense metaphyseal bands are also seen in conditions like lead poisoning, beta thalassaemia, vitamin D intoxication, scurvy, and osteogenesis imperfecta type 5.
question: Which of the following conditions do not cause dense metaphyseal bands?

explanationHtml:
The radiological finding in the image is a dense provisional zone of calcification at the growing metaphysis, known as Frankel’s line, which is characteristic of scurvy.

Radiographic features of scurvy include:

  • Wimberger's ring sign - sharp margination of the epiphysis by a sclerotic rim
  • White line of Frankel - calcified cartilage at metaphyses
  • Trummerfeld zone - radiolucent area located just below Frankel’s line, resulting from inadequate mineral deposition within osteoid tissue
  • Pelkan spurs - due to fractures at the cortical margin
  • Periosteal elevation - due to subperiosteal haemorrhages

Scurvy results from the deficiency of vitamin C, which is required for the hydroxylation of lysine and proline. Hence, a deficiency of vitamin C leads to defective collagen formation, resulting in generalized bleeding tendencies. Early manifestations include irritability, loss of appetite, musculoskeletal pain, and tenderness in the legs.

Later on, the child can have swelling of the knees, ankles, and pseudo paralysis. Additional features may include delayed healing of wounds and fractures, excessive keratin buildup around hair follicles, joint discomfort, and reduced muscle strength. It also results in defective osteoid formation.
question: The knee joint X-ray of a patient with scurvy is given below. What is the radiological finding seen?

correctAnswer: A. Type 1 of the disease is most lethal
explanationHtml:
The clinical features are suggestive of osteogenesis imperfecta. Osteogenesis imperfecta type 2 is the most lethal.

Osteogenesis imperfecta, also known as brittle bone disease, is an inherited connective tissue condition transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern and caused by defects in type I collagen synthesis. It most frequently arises from mutations affecting the COL1A1 and COL1A2 genes.

These mutations lead to the replacement of glycine with another amino acid, resulting in an abnormal triple helix of collagen. This results in the abnormal formation of type 1 collagen.

The main features are joints that are vulnerable to fracture (joint laxity), scleral alterations (blue sclera), dentinogenesis imperfecta, and deafness. Multiple bone fractures are a consequence of bone fragility. Bowing of the long bones, wormian bone (intrasutural bone), and multiple fractures of long bones are common radiological findings that are observed.

A Wormian bone (intrasutural bone) in the skull is shown below:

Management comprises the use of bisphosphonates, along with physiotherapy and walking aids.

As battered baby syndrome can present with multiple fractures secondary to abuse, it is a common differential diagnosis for osteogenesis imperfecta. However, features such as blue sclera, wormian bones, dentinogenesis imperfecta, ligamentous laxity, and a positive family history are seen in osteogenesis imperfecta and are typically absent in battered baby syndrome.

Battered baby syndrome (non-accidental injury) has several radiologic findings that are highly suggestive of physical abuse. These include metaphyseal lesions such as metaphyseal chip fractures, rib fractures in infants younger than one year, and fractures typically associated with high-impact trauma, including those involving the scapula, spinous processes, and sternum.

The presence of multiple fractures at different stages of healing is also a key diagnostic clue indicating repeated injury.

Can be associated with autosomal dominant inheritance
Battered baby syndrome is a differential diagnosis

question: A 7-year-old child presents with recurrent fractures following minimal trauma since early childhood, along with progressive bone deformities and short stature. Radiotracer uptake reflects osteoblastic (bone-forming) activity. Causes include:

Multiple myeloma typically does not show a rim-uptake pattern with a central photopenic area on bone scintigraphy because its lesions are purely osteolytic.
question: Which of the following is not associated with an increased radiotracer uptake at the periphery of the lesion on a bone scan?

explanationHtml:
The given radiograph shows a "bone within-a-bone" appearance. This finding is least likely to be seen in hyperparathyroidism.

Bone-in-bone appearance is when an X-ray shows a dense line of bone inside another bone. It happens due to abnormal bone remodeling. New bone forms on the inner surface of the cortex (endosteal apposition), and this inward thickening, with a thin, translucent zone in between, produces this characteristic appearance in long bones.

The image below shows the bone-in-bone appearance.

Causes of bone-within-bone appearance on a radiograph include:

  • Osteopetrosis
  • Osteoid Osteoma
  • Gaucher disease
  • Sickle cell anemia

Hyperparathyroidism leads to bone resorption rather than bone formation, and therefore does not produce a bone-in-bone appearance.

In greenstick fractures, the inner cortex (concave) bends, and the outer (convex) cortex breaks.

A greenstick fracture is an incomplete break in which one side of the bone’s cortex and periosteum is disrupted, while the opposite side remains continuous and undergoes bending rather than complete separation. This pattern is characteristic of pediatric bones due to their increased elasticity and thicker periosteum.

These fractures are most commonly seen in the shaft of long bones, especially the forearm (radius and ulna), in children.

The given X-ray is consistent with a greenstick fracture, showing breakage on one side with bending on the other.

Note: Torus fracture results from compressive forces, leading to a bulging or buckling of the cortex rather than a clear break. Importantly, both cortices remain intact, which differentiates it from greenstick fractures, where one cortex is disrupted.

There is internal rotation of the humeral head, which causes changes to the normal radiographic contour of the head of the humerus.

Radiological signs described in posterior dislocation of the shoulder in the AP view are as follows:

  • Vacant glenoid sign - Glenoid fossa looks empty as the humeral head has moved away from it

question: A young soccer player presents with complaints of pain in his right shoulder. He fell while alternating from jumping jacks to push-ups during a warm-up drill. His shoulder's radiograph is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario and X-ray findings are suggestive of an inferior shoulder dislocation (luxatio erecta).

The given scenario describes a patient with shoulder pain following forced abduction after a fall. The X-ray demonstrates the humeral head positioned inferior to the glenoid with the shaft of the humerus in an abducted orientation, consistent with an inferior shoulder dislocation.

This injury is rare and typically results from a hyper-abduction force, where the arm is forcefully pulled upward during high-energy trauma. Patients usually present with the affected arm locked in near-complete abduction.

A common complication is cubitus varus deformity (gunstock deformity) due to the malunion of fractured ends. Myositis ossificans is a delayed complication of the fracture.

question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the casualty after a fall on an outstretched hand. An X-ray of the patient is given below. Identify the true statement regarding the condition.

explanationHtml:
The given features and radiograph are suggestive of volar or reverse Barton’s fracture.

A volar (reverse) Barton's fracture is a fracture-dislocation of the volar rim of the distal radius. Dislocation of the radiocarpal joint is the hallmark feature.

The radiographic findings are the following:

  • Comminuted intra-articular fracture of the distal radius
  • Volar rim maintains a relationship with the carpus, and both are displaced proximally
  • Fracture of the radial styloid process with loss of radial inclination

The X-ray below shows Volar (reverse) Barton's fracture.

Barton's fracture is an intra-articular rim fracture of the distal radius. It is of two types.

  • Volar (reverse) Barton's fracture
  • Dorsal Barton's fracture

Volar (reverse) Barton's fracture is the most common type of Barton's fracture. This fracture involves the volar rim of the distal radius. Reverse-type Barton's fracture is similar to Smith’s fracture, but the difference is that the fracture line runs obliquely and extends into the joint surface.

A dorsal Barton's fracture involves fracture-dislocation of the dorsal rim of the radius, representing the less common variant.

The image below shows the lateral and anterior-posterior view of the dorsal-type of Barton's fracture with dorsal displacement.
question: A 40-year-old man presented with severe pain in the wrist after suffering a fall on an outstretched hand during his morning jog. His X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?

The clinical features and radiograph showing a large gap between the scaphoid and lunate are suggestive of scapholunate dissociation.

It is also known as tooth gap sign or Terry Thomas sign, after the English comedian.
question: A 52-year-old woman presented with pain in the right wrist following a fall on the outstretched hand. On examination, tenderness was noted in the anatomical snuff box. Radiograph of her wrist is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Medullary expansion of the distal femoral ends results in loss of the normal concavity, which produces the characteristic Erlenmeyer flask deformity.

Causes of Erlenmeyer flask deformity include:

  • Thalassemia
  • Leukemia
  • Fibrous dysplasia
  • Osteopetrosis
  • Pyle’s (metaphyseal) dysplasia
  • Heavy metal poisoning
  • Niemann Pick disease
question: Which of the following conditions is least likely to cause the following appearance on a radiograph?

explanationHtml:
Ewing's sarcoma is the most likely diagnosis.

Ewing's sarcoma is the 2nd most common bone sarcoma in children. The majority of the patients affected are usually <20 years of age. It has a slight male predominance. The majority of Ewing sarcomas have a balanced translocation between the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 and the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11.

It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones, like the femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and flat bones of the pelvis. Patients present with a painful progressive swelling, fever, and anemia.

Radiographic Features of Ewing's Sarcoma:

  • The lesion could be lytic, sclerotic, or mixed
  • A diaphyseal lesion with irregular destruction (moth-eaten appearance or cracked ice appearance)
  • Periosteal reaction is deposited in layers, giving an onion peel appearance.

The onion-skin (onion-peel) periosteal reaction is classically seen in Ewing sarcoma. It can also be seen in osteosarcoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and other aggressive bone lesions.

Osteosarcoma shows periosteal reaction in the form of a Codman triangle. It corresponds to the longitudinal limit of subperiosteal tumor extension. The Codman triangle can also be seen in Ewing sarcoma.

Giant cell tumor has a characteristic soap bubble appearance.

Unicameral bone cyst has a pathognomonic fallen fragment sign.
question: A 12-year-old boy presents with fever, pain, and swelling over the shaft of the femur. X-ray shows a diaphyseal lesion with an “onion-skin” periosteal reaction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The presence of a double posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) sign on MRI is highly suggestive of a bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus.

In this condition, the displaced fragment of the torn meniscus flips into the intercondylar notch and lies anteroinferior to the PCL, creating the appearance of a second PCL on sagittal MRI images.
