question: A 20-year-old footballer sustained a sliding tackle during a match and fell on the ground in pain. An MRI was done and the double posterior cruciate ligament sign was noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario of hip pain in a patient on long-term steroid therapy with normal examination and radiographs is highly suggestive of Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (AVN). MRI is the most sensitive investigation for detecting early AVN, even before radiographic changes become apparent.

Long-term steroid usage is a risk factor for the development of AVN.

The X-rays are usually normal in the early stages, and the radiograph of the femoral head may show the following changes:

  • Sclerosis of the femoral head
  • Flattening or loss of sphericity of the femoral head
  • Crescent sign – subchondral fracture overlying the necrotic segment of the femoral head
  • In severe stages, it may show femoral head collapse and arthritic changes in the joint

The X-ray below shows flattening of the femoral head and degenerative changes associated with osteonecrosis or AVN.

MRI allows the identification of avascular necrosis of the femoral head in earlier stages and also helps determine the exact stage and extent of the pathologic process. Ficat and Arlet staging is used to stage the disease.

In osteoporosis due to long-term steroid therapy, a normal radiograph is less likely. It typically shows diffusely reduced bone density on X-ray.
question: A 40-year-old man complains of right hip pain while walking up the stairs. He has been on long-term steroid therapy for rheumatoid arthritis for 6 months. Physical examination and radiograph of the hip are unremarkable. What is the best imaging modality for his condition?

explanationHtml:
The procedure depicted in the image represents myelography, an imaging technique used to evaluate spinal canal pathology.

Myelography involves the intrathecal injection of contrast material, followed by imaging under fluoroscopy or CT to visualize the spinal cord, nerve roots, and subarachnoid space. X-ray (fluoroscopic) myelography is particularly useful in assessing conditions such as spondylolisthesis, allowing dynamic evaluation of spinal canal changes during movement.

In current practice, MRI has largely replaced CT myelography due to its non-invasive nature and absence of ionizing radiation, as it does not require intrathecal contrast administration. However, CT myelography remains useful when MRI is contraindicated, such as in patients with non-MRI-compatible implants or severe claustrophobia.

Adhesive arachnoiditis can be diagnosed when the thecal sac is empty. This occurs due to inflammation, which leads to clumping of nerve roots. This leads to an empty sac appearance. It is best observed on T2-weighted MRI scans of the lumbar spine when the thecal sac appears empty.

A cervical rib is a supernumerary or accessory rib arising from the seventh cervical vertebra.

It is more common in females than in males. Usually, it is an incidental finding and doesn't produce any symptoms.

In some individuals, it can cause thoracic outlet syndrome by compressing the brachial plexus or subclavian vessels. Neurological features include pain in the hand when the arm is elevated. Vascular manifestations include differences in pulse intensity between the two arms when the affected extremity is in a certain position and Raynaud's phenomenon.

Methyl diphosphonate (MDP) adsorbs into the hydroxyapatite crystals and gets accumulated in the areas of active bone formation, which can be detected by nuclear imaging.

Scanning with technetium-99m methylene diphosphonate (99mTc-MDP) can demonstrate non-specific reactive changes in bone, which can aid in localizing small lesions, such as an osteoid osteoma.

In hyperparathyroidism, there is resorption of the trabecular bone of the skull (which causes the radiolucent areas) in combination with cystic areas of osteopenia. There is also a loss of definition between the inner and outer tables of the skull.

In multiple myeloma, multiple well-defined "punched out" lytic lesions exist.

The image below shows the multiple punched-out lesions seen in multiple myeloma.

In Paget's disease, the pelvis, spine, skull, and proximal long bones are most frequently affected. Radiological skull changes include:

Radiological features during the early phase of this disease include osteolytic (lucent) regions which is later followed by coarse trabeculae and bony enlargement. Sclerotic changes occur much later in the disease process. The lesions seen are:

  • Osteoporosis circumscripta: large, well-defined lytic lesion
  • Cotton wool appearance: mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions of the skull
  • Diploic widening: both inner and outer calvarial tables are involved, with the former usually more extensively affected

explanationHtml:
This patient now has a fever and swelling on the anterior aspect of his right leg after an injury. This is suggestive of acute osteomyelitis, for which MRI is the investigation of choice.

The characteristic earliest signs of acute osteomyelitis include bone marrow edema, which is seen as a low T1 signal in the bone marrow, along with a high signal on T2 MRI. MRI is also the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of subacute and chronic osteomyelitis.

Investigations of choice for bone diseases:

  • Cortical pathology, like bone tumours, - CT is used
  • Marrow pathology, like avascular bone necrosis, MRI is used.

question: A 3-year-old boy was brought to the casualty with fever and pain in the right leg. There was a history of minor trauma 5 days ago. On examination, a warm, tender swelling was noted on the anterior aspect of the right leg, and the pain worsened on movement.  What is the radiological investigation of choice for this suspected condition?

explanationHtml:
For a calcaneal fracture, a CT is the investigation of choice.

The CT scan is especially valuable for delineating fracture patterns, assessing joint surface involvement, and identifying associated injuries such as medial malleolus fractures. Calcaneal fractures can be difficult to detect on plain radiographs.

A CT scan is also the investigation of choice for suspected tarsal fractures. While CT excels in evaluating cortical bone detail, MRI is superior for detecting stress and occult fractures.

correctAnswer: D. It can be used for hybrid imaging
explanationHtml:
The PET (Positron Emission Tomography) is a nuclear medicine imaging technique that can be used for hybrid imaging.

The PET scan is most commonly combined with CT. This allows correlation of metabolic information from PET with anatomical detail from CT.

PET scanning works by detecting the uptake of positron-emitting radioisotopes in the body, which enables visualization of functional and metabolic processes. Advanced computer algorithms then reconstruct 3D images of tracer distribution, offering insights into tissue function that conventional CT or MRI cannot provide.

This technique is particularly valuable in oncology because tumor cells usually demonstrate increased metabolic activity compared with normal tissues. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a glucose analogue, is the most commonly used PET tracer. After uptake by metabolically active cells, FDG is phosphorylated to FDG-6-phosphate, which cannot undergo further metabolism and therefore becomes trapped intracellularly.

This accumulation enables Positron emission tomography to identify areas of increased metabolic activity. Unlike conventional gamma cameras, PET does not require physical collimators for image reconstruction, resulting in higher sensitivity.

Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is another similar imaging technique, which also provides functional information but utilizes gamma-emitting isotopes rather than positron emitters.

PET

SPECT

Very expensive

Lower cost

Uses positron-emitting radioisotope (tracer) like 18F-FDG

Uses gamma-emitting radioisotopes (tracer) such as Tc-99m, I-123, I-131
Better contrast and spatial resolution Less contrast and spatial resolution

question: Which of the following is true regarding PET (Positron Emission Tomography) scans?

correctAnswer: B. Dual photon peak at 511 keV
explanationHtml:
PET (Positron Emission Tomography) scans are based on the principle of detecting a dual-photon peak at 511 keV.

During a PET scan, a radionuclide tracer (commonly FDG) is administered. The tracer undergoes positron emission, releasing a positron that travels a short distance before annihilating with an electron.

This annihilation produces two high-energy photons moving in opposite directions, each with an energy of 511 keV, which is detected by the PET scanner to generate images of metabolic activity.
question: Which of the following is the principle of PET (Positron Emission Tomography) scan?

explanationHtml:
2-fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose is used in PET scans.

After injection, FDG is taken up by cells and undergoes initial metabolism. The technique is based on the principle that tumor cells exhibit higher metabolic activity than normal tissues.

FDG is phosphorylated to FDG-6-phosphate, which cannot be further metabolized, leading to its accumulation within tumor cells. This accumulation can be detected, measured, and quantified using PET imaging.

The applications of PET include:

  • Oncologic:
    • Detection, staging, drug response
    • Differentiation between radiation necrosis and recurrence
  • Neurologic:
    • Early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease
    • Localisation of seizure focus in the interictal phase
    • Localising eloquent areas (speech, motor function)
  • Cardiac: Identification of hibernating myocardium
question: Which of the following compounds are used in PET scan?

explanationHtml:
On an 18F-FDG PET-CT scan, the urinary bladder demonstrates normal physiological uptake (false positive) due to FDG excretion via the renal system, which can sometimes mimic pathological activity on oncologic imaging.

Areas of normal physiological FDG uptake on PET-CT include:

  • Brain tissue
  • Skeletal muscle, especially after strenuous activity, and laryngeal muscles following speech
  • Myocardium
  • Gastrointestinal tract - intestinal wall
  • Genitourinary tract - as FDG is excreted via the renal system and passes into the collecting systems, urinary bladder
  • Brown fat - FDG accumulates here as glucose and ATP are required for heat production
  • Thymus

explanationHtml:
A photon camera is not used to image gamma radiation in scintigraphy.

The device used for this purpose is the gamma camera, also called a scintillation or Anger camera, which detects gamma rays emitted by radioactive tracers. This technique is known as scintigraphy.

The applications of scintigraphy include:

  • Early drug development
  • Nuclear medical imaging involves viewing and analyzing images of the human body
  • Assess the distribution of medically injected, inhaled, or ingested radionuclides emitting gamma rays
question: Which of the following is not used to detect gamma radiation in scintigraphic imaging?

explanationHtml:
Technetium agents based on technetium-99m (Tc-99m) radioisotopes are the most frequently used agents in nuclear imaging.

Tc-99m is a radioactive isotope that works by emitting gamma rays in the targeted tissue or organ. These gamma rays are then detected and recorded by a specialized gamma camera for medical imaging purposes. The radioactive technetium can be chelated to several different compounds to create specific radiopharmaceuticals and optimize imaging of various structures.

The half-life of Tc-99m is 6 hours. It produces gamma rays of 140 keV. It is a pure gamma emitter as it is in a metastable state. It decays to the stable isotope of ruthenium-99.

Iodine-125, caesium-137, and iridium-192 are used in radiotherapy.
question: Among the following, which isotope is used in nuclear scanning?

explanationHtml:
Tc-HMPAO (technetium-99m hexamethyl propylenamine oxime) SPECT is used for the assessment of cerebral perfusion.

In Alzheimer's disease, the Tc-HMPAO SPECT shows reduced perfusion of the temporoparietal region.

Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) with a gamma camera employs radiotracers that penetrate the blood–brain barrier, such as technetium-99m–labelled HMPAO and 99mTc-ethyl cysteinate dimer.

These agents enable assessment of regional cerebral perfusion and are useful in the evaluation of dementia, cerebrovascular disorders, and in identifying the origin of the epileptic seizures.

In-111 (Indium) DTPA is injected intrathecally to assess CSF flow.

Tc-99m (Technetium) MIBI is used for parathyroid scintigraphy.

Tl-201 (Thallium) is used in myocardial perfusion scanning.
question: An 84-year-old man has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Which of the following can be used to assess his cerebral perfusion?

explanationHtml:
Radioactive isotopes of technetium, labeled to specific compounds, are widely used for bone scintigraphy.

For a bone scan, the patient is injected with a small dose of a radiopharmaceutical, typically 600 MBq of technetium-99m–methylene diphosphonate (Tc-99m MDP). Imaging is performed with a gamma camera, which detects the gamma radiation emitted by the tracer.

MDP shows affinity for hydroxyapatite within bone tissue, preferentially accumulating in areas of active bone formation. This allows identification of regions with increased osteoblastic activity, such as metastatic lesions, fractures, or infection.

The image below is a bone scan demonstrating bony metastases.

Phosphorus (P-32) and Iridium (Ir-192) are used in radiotherapy.
question: An oncologist orders a bone scan to assess for bony metastases in a 49-year-old woman with breast cancer.  The radioactive isotope of which of the following is used?

explanationHtml:
Technetium-99m MAG3 (mercaptoacetyltriglycine) renal scan is useful for evaluating renal transplant function and for detecting post-transplant urinary tract obstruction.

Technetium-99m MAG3 (mercaptoacetyltriglycine) is the most commonly used radiopharmaceutical for dynamic renal scintigraphy (renography). It is cleared predominantly by tubular secretion because of its high protein binding. Therefore, it is not suitable for measuring GFR.

Compared with Technetium-99m DTPA, Tc-99m MAG3 has nearly twice the extraction efficiency, producing superior image quality and a better renal target-to-background ratio, especially in patients with impaired renal function. It is therefore the preferred agent for evaluating renal perfusion, drainage, and transplant function.

In cases of acute rejection, imaging typically demonstrates diminished renal perfusion. Mild hepatobiliary excretion may also result in visualization of the liver and biliary tract.

Technetium-99m DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) is used to evaluate renal structure and morphology, particularly in pediatric imaging for detecting scarring and pyelonephritis. It is an ideal agent for the assessment of the renal cortex.

Technetium-99m DTPA is a glomerular filtration agent used in dynamic renal scintigraphy. It is freely filtered at the glomerulus with negligible tubular secretion or reabsorption, making it suitable for estimating GFR. However, its relatively low extraction efficiency results in lower image quality compared with tubular agents and may slightly underestimate GFR.

Captopril DTPA is used for screening in patients with renovascular hypertension.
question: A 48-year-old woman who underwent a renal transplant 4 months ago comes for follow-up. Which of the following would you perform to assess her renal function?

explanationHtml:
Tc-99m-labelled RBC scan would be useful in patients 1, 3, and 4. The uses of the Tc-99m-labelled RBC scan include assessment of the following:

  • Occult gastrointestinal bleed
  • Vascular lesions like hepatic haemangioma
  • Ectopic splenic tissue - splenosis

Tc-99m labelled leucocytes are used in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

An 18-fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan is used to evaluate tumors, including solitary pulmonary nodules.
question:
Technetium 99m labeled RBC scan is useful in which of the following patients?

  1. A 56-year-old man with hepatic haemangioma
  2. An 18-year-old boy with inflammatory bowel disease
  3. A 60-year-old woman with a positive fecal occult blood test
  4. A 20-year-old man who developed splenosis following trauma
  5. A 66-year-old woman with a solitary pulmonary nodule

correctAnswer: C. To screen patients with renovascular hypertension
explanationHtml:
Tc-99m DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan is not used to screen patients with renovascular hypertension, as this requires dynamic imaging. DMSA is utilized in static imaging studies rather than dynamic scans.

Tc-99m DMSA is specifically used for assessing the renal cortex. It binds to sulfhydryl groups in the proximal tubular cells and demonstrates prolonged cortical retention compared to other radiotracers. This property allows for accurate evaluation of differential renal function.

Unlike dynamic agents such as DTPA or MAG3, DMSA is a static imaging agent. The primary clinical applications of DMSA include:

  • Evaluation of renal structure and cortical morphology
  • Detection of renal scarring
  • Diagnosis of pyelonephritis
  • Assessment of renal anatomical abnormalities

Note: Captopril-enhanced DTPA scans are used for screening patients with suspected renovascular hypertension.

To evaluate a patient with a duplex renal collecting system

question: A DMSA scan can be performed in all of the following cases except:

Tc 99m pertechnetate scan, a radionuclide imaging more accurate in the pediatric age group than in adults for Meckel's diverticulum. It has a very high sensitivity and specificity for bleeding meckel diverticula, but is of little value in children with no history of rectal bleeding.

Other uses of Tc-99m pertechnetate include:

  • Thyroid imaging
  • Parathyroid imaging for distinguishing from the thyroid gland
  • Testicular imaging
  • Gastric emptying studies, intestinal and rectal functional studies.
question: A 2-year-old child is brought with recurrent episodes of blood in his stool. Meckel’s diverticulum is suspected. Which of the following can be used to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
PACS in medical imaging stands for Picture Archiving and Communication System.

PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System) is a digital system used to store, retrieve, transmit, and view medical images. It is integrated with RIS for a smooth radiology workflow.

It includes DICOM viewing software, storage/archival systems, network connectivity, and radiologist workstations, along with post-processing tools like zoom, measurement, and windowing. Images are stored in DICOM format, archived on servers or cloud with redundancy for data safety, and accessed through fast hospital networks.

Advanced PACS also supports protocols, AI integration, and post-processing tools, improving reporting efficiency and workflow. Overall, PACS replaces film-based imaging, reduces cost and space, improves accessibility, and enhances radiology productivity.

Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) is an international standard for storing, transmitting, and viewing medical images along with patient and imaging data. It is used across radiology and other specialties.

A DICOM file (.dcm) has two parts:

  • Header (patient and study information) and
  • Image data (pixel information).

DICOM requires special software to view and allows image processing like windowing and measurements. Limitations include large file size and the need for conversion for use in teaching or publication.

Radiology Information System (RIS) is the central radiology workflow system that links HIS and PACS for seamless data exchange. It manages patient registration, scheduling, worklists, study tracking, and reporting. Each patient has a UHID, and each imaging study has a separate accession number for accurate tracking.

RIS generates a modality worklist for imaging systems, reducing manual errors, while images are stored in PACS using DICOM format and linked back to RIS for reporting. Overall, RIS acts as the backbone of radiology workflow, integrating all systems for efficient and error-free imaging management.

Modern PACS systems include built-in or server-based postprocessing, eliminating the need for separate workstations. These tools enable reconstruction of images in different planes and 3D formats to improve diagnostic accuracy.

Many of these tools are now standard in modern scanners. AI applications are also increasingly integrated into PACS, assisting in image analysis and generating additional processed series for radiologist review.

The Bragg peak effect is pronounced in protons.

Protons are relatively heavy, positively charged particles that gradually lose energy as they travel through human tissue. Their motion can be precisely controlled, allowing them to deliver a maximum radiation dose at a specific depth up to about 32 cm within the body.

As a proton penetrates tissue, the absorbed dose increases slowly while its speed decreases, followed by a sharp rise in energy deposition just before the proton comes to rest. This sharp maximum is known as the Bragg peak.

Because the behavior of protons is highly predictable, the beam can be accurately directed so that the Bragg peak occurs exactly at the tumor site. After this point, the proton has no remaining range, so there is essentially no exit dose.

This unique property makes proton therapy highly effective for targeting tumors, as it concentrates radiation within the tumor while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue, making it a less invasive option for cancer treatment.

Systemic radiotherapy involves administering a radioactive substance orally or parenterally, allowing it to accumulate in a specific organ or a tumour site. This approach is commonly used in radioactive iodine (I-131) therapy for hyperthyroidism and differentiated thyroid cancers.

In contrast, brachytherapy is a type of radiotherapy where radioactive sources are placed inside or close to the target area. It delivers radiation over short distances using interstitial, intracavitary, or surface placement techniques. The following isotopes are used in brachytherapy:

It may be administered as either a low-dose-rate (LDR) or high-dose-rate (HDR) treatment. The major advantage of brachytherapy is the delivery of a high radiation dose to the tumor while minimizing radiation exposure to the surrounding normal tissues because the source is located within or adjacent to the lesion.

Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is a reasonable alternative for people who refuse or cannot tolerate surgery. Here, beams are modified and focused only to concentrate on the tumor and have little effect on the surrounding tissue. It can be done by using:

  • X-knife using a linear accelerator
  • Gamma-knife using Cobalt-60
  • CyberKnife - image-guided linear accelerator using real-time image guidance to deliver radiation from multiple angles.

The patient wears a specialized helmet that is surgically fixed to the skull. The Gamma knife aims gamma radiation through a target point in the patient’s brain. An ablative dose of radiation is thereby sent through the tumour in one treatment session, while surrounding brain tissues are relatively spared.

SRS has been used in the treatment of almost every intracranial lesion, but is commonly used in the treatment of acoustic schwannoma, pituitary adenoma, meningioma, and trigeminal neuralgia.

Therefore, the standard treatment involves maximal safe surgical resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with temozolomide and concurrent fractionated radiotherapy. SRS may, however, be beneficial in cases of focal recurrence, particularly in patients who have already undergone high-dose radiation therapy.

Option C: Tuberculomas are localised granulomatous masses in the CNS resulting from Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. They develop when tuberculous foci, formed during initial bacteremia, coalesce into caseous lesions without causing meningitis.

The primary treatment involves anti-tubercular therapy (ATT), often supplemented with corticosteroids to mitigate inflammation and manage paradoxical reactions (situations where lesions enlarge after initiating ATT). The primary objective of compression ultrasonography (CUS) is to assess venous patency by applying intermittent direct pressure on the veins using the ultrasound probe and observing the vein’s compressibility. In a patient with suspected PE, CUS is used to detect thrombus in the leg veins.

Under normal physiological conditions, peripheral veins are readily compressible upon application of gentle pressure. In the presence of a thrombus, normal venous compressibility is impaired, and the affected vein may demonstrate partial or complete non-compressibility.

Additionally, the echogenic characteristics of the vein vary according to the stage of thrombus development. An acute thrombus, as in a case of acute DVT, is typically anechoic or hypoechoic and may resemble a normal vein; however, the vessel is usually distended and noncompressible. In subacute and chronic stages, the thrombus becomes progressively hyperechoic.

    • A longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant is used to assess splenic injury and left kidney injury.
    • Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region are used to assess Douglas's pouch and bladder.

An "extended FAST or eFAST" scan: Assess left and right thoracic views, in addition to the FAST assessed regions, to look for pneumothorax and hemothorax.
